SECRET
PAGE 01 BEIRUT 05776 181500Z

FM AMEMBASSY BEIRUT
TO SECSTATE WASHDC IMMEDIATE

EXDIS

S E C R E T BEIRUT 05776

SUBJECT: GOL-FEDAYEEN ARRANGEMENT
REF: STATE 94202

SUMMARY: FEDAYEEN REPS IN MIXED COMMISSION CAME UP WITH LIST OF SPECIFIC PROMISES
EVENING MAY 17 ON ACTIONS THEY WOULD TAKE IN ACCORDANCE WITH PRESIDENT FRANGIE'S
DEMAND THAT GOL SOVEREIGNTY HENCEFORTH BE FULLY RESPECTED. LIST COVERS COMMITMENT
NOT TO UNDERTAKE CROSS-BORDER RAIDS, TO STAY WELL BACK FROM SENSITIVE BORDER
AREAS, TO CEASE USING BEIRUT AS INFORMATION/PROPAGANDA HEADQUARTERS, TO REMOVE
HEAVY WEAPONS FROM CAMPS, TO ACKNOWLEDGE SUPREMACY LEBANESE LAW OVER PALESTINIANS,
TO REMOVE ALL "FOREIGN ELEMENTS" (I.E., NON-ARABS) AND TO ALLOW LEBANESE SECURITY
FORCES ACCESS TO CAMPS. GOL FULLY AWARE THAT FEDAYEEN PROMISES MUST BE IMPLEMENTED
AND THEN BE RESPECTED OVER TIME TO BE WORTHWHILE, AND THAT FEDAYEEN GOOD FAITH IN
THIS REGARD IS SUSPECT. ARMY PRESENTLY WORKING OUT DETAILED AGREEMENT WHEREBY
FEDAYEEN WILL BE SUPPOSED TO IMPLEMENT THEIR PROMISES. THESE COMMITMENTS BY
FEDAYEEN APPLY TO ALL 15 REFUGEE CAMPS NOT ONLY THOSE IN BEIRUT AREA. END SUMMARY.

1. IN CONVERSATION WITH FONMIN REPORTED SEPTEL, DIRECTOR GENERAL OF PRESIDENCY
(DIB) BRIEFED CHARGE AND EMBOFF MORNING MAY 18 ON STATUS OF GOL-FEDAYEEN TALKS
WHICH CONCLUDED EVENING MAY 17. DIB AND FONMIN BOTH STRESSED ON SEVERAL OCCASIONS
THAT THERE WAS NO RPT NO AGREEMENT OR EVEN UNDERSTANDING BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN.
RATHER, LATTER HAD MADE SERIES OF COMMITMENTS OR PROMISES TO ARMY NEGOTIATORS
WHICH GOL HAS ACCEPTED AS BASIS FOR NEW RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ITSELF AND ALL
FEDAYEEN IN LEBANON. COMMITMENTS MADE EVENING OF MAY 17 WILL BE DRAWN UP ON PIECE
OF PAPER BY ARMY AND WE CERTAIN OTHER GOVTS WILL RECEIVE COPIES. ARMY TALKING
RIGHT NOW TO FEDAYEEN REPS ABOUT MODALITIES OF IMPLEMENTATION, INCLUDING TIMETABLE.
DIB THEN SUMMED UP (FROM MEMORY) ESSENTIAL POINTS OF FEDAYEEN COMMITMENTS. (THESE
ARE REPORTED AS FOLLOWS BUT MAY NOT BE COMPLETE NOR COMPLETELY ACCURATE. WE SHALL
OBTAIN FURTHER INFO AND PRECISION WHEN AVAILABLE.)

2. ACTIVITY IN CAMPS: FEDAYEEN HAVE AGREED TO CEASE ALL TRAINING IN CAMPS, TO
REMOVE "HEAVY WEAPONS" FROM CAMPS, AND TO CLEANSE CAMPS OF ALL "FOREIGN ELEMENTS"
(I.E., NON-ARABS). ARMY AND FEDAYEEN WORKING OUT DETAILED AGREEMENT ON MEANING OF
HEAVY WEAPONS WHICH WILL BE BASED ON CALIBER, RANGE AND WHETHER OR NOT WEAPON IS
CREW-SERVED OR HANDLED BY SINGLE MAN. TIME-TABLE FOR REMOVAL ALSO BEING ESTABLISHED
SINCE FEDAYEEN ARGUE THAT FOR LOGISTIC REASONS AND TO ALLOW FEAR AND SUSPICION OF
LEBANESE ARMY TO DIE DOWN, REMOVAL OF HEAVY WEAPONS CANNOT TAKE PLACE ALL AT ONCE
AND RIGHT AWAY. IN REMOVAL OF FOREIGNERS, FEDAYEEN MADE ONE EXCEPTION AND THAT IS
THOSE WHO ENGAGED IN MEDICAL WORK. ALL "COMBATTANTS" WILL GO AND THIS EXPLICITLY
INCLUDES TURKS AND IRANIANS AS WELL AS VARIETY OF OTHERS (SOME OF WHOM HAVE BEEN
ROUNDED UP BY LEBANESE ARMY AT CHECKPOINTS OUTSIDE OF CAMPS IN PAST TWO WEEKS).
DIB AND FONMIN AGREED THAT SO-CALLED MEDICAL PERSONNEL WOULD HAVE TO BE WATCHED
CAREFULLY AND SAID THAT FEDAYEEN WOULD HAVE TO BE WATCHED CAREFULLY ON EVERY POINT,
EVERY STEP OF THE WAY.

3. CONTROL OF CAMPS: LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES (ARMY AND CIVILIAN) WILL HAVE
CHECKPOINTS JUST OUTSIDE CAMPS IN STRATEGIC LOCATIONS FROM WHICH THEY CAN OBSERVE
INTERIOR OF CAMPS ON COMINGS AND GOINGS. THERE IS TO BE NO MORE MILITARY TRAINING
IN CAMPS AND CAMPS ARE NO LONGER TO SERVE AS SHELTERS FOR FUGITIVES FROM LEBANESE
JUSTICE. (WE UNDERSTAND FROM SEPARATE RELIABLE SOURCE THAT PALESTINIAN ARMED
STRUGGLE COMMAND WILL STILL HAVE AUTHORITY WITHIN CAMPS BUT WILL COOPERATE CLOSELY
WITH LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES WITH RESPECT TO FUGITIVES FROM JUSTICE.) FONMIN AND
DIB SAID THAT LEBANESE SECURITY FORCES WILL HAVE RIGHT TO ENTER CAMPS BUT WITH
PERMISSION OF FEDAYEEN. FEDAYEEN HAVE NO RIGHT TO CIRCULATE WITH ARMS OUTSIDE OF
CAMPS AND MUST USE ONLY VEHICLES WITH SPECIAL PLATES.

4. INFORMATION/PROPAGANDA: ALL INFO MEDIA SUPPOSED TO BE CONSOLIDATED UNDER PLO
AND THERE IS TO BE NO MORE ATTACKS ON GOL BY FEDAYEEN MEDIA, EVEN VIA VOICE OF
PALESTINE IN BAGHDAD AND DAMASCUS. BEIRUT NO LONGER TO BE USED AS BASE FOR
RELEASING FEDAYEEN COMMUNIQUES AND ANNOUNCEMENTS ALTHOUGH WAFA (PALESTINE NEWS
AGENCY) WILL BE ALLOWED TO CONTINUE TO OPERATE IN LEBANON. WHERE TRACTS AND OTHER
"WILDCAT" FEDAYEEN PUBLICATIONS CONCERNED, GOL FREE TO ACT UNDER LEBANESE LAW AS
IT WOULD AGAINST ANY OTHER SUCH PUBLICATION.

5. BORDER AREAS: FEDAYEEN HAVE AGAIN AGREED TO RESPECT LIMITS DRAWN UP BY ARMY
FOLLOWING SEPT 16-17, 1972 ISRAELI ACTION. THERE ARE TO BE NO RPT NO CROSS-BORDER
ACTIONS OF ANY KIND, FEDAYEEN TO BE ABSENT COMPLETELY FROM WESTERN AREA (VICINITY
RAS NAQURAH) AND AT LEAST 8-10 KMS BACK FROM BORDER IN CENTRAL AREA (VICINITY
BINT JBEIL). IN ARKUB, FEDAYEEN TO BE NORTH OF ROAD FROM HASBAYAH TO CHEBAA
EXCEPT FOR TWO OR THREE SPECIFIED AND CAREFULLY CONTROLLED SPOTS.

6. COMMENT: OBVIOUSLY THERE ARE MANY DETAILS STILL TO BE WORKED OUT IN ARRANGEMENTS
BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN. ARMY IS BEING VERY WARY AND VIGILANT. PUBLIC PRESENTATION
OF ARRANGEMENTS BY GOL AS UNILATERAL CONCESSIONS IS LIKELY BE COUNTERED ON FEDAYEEN
SIDE BY CLAIM THAT IT IS ALL WITHIN CONTEXT CAIRO ACCORDS WHICH STILL IN FORCE.
THIS IS NOT CASE BUT ON OTHER HAND THERE IS A MUTUAL -- ALBEIT ONE-SIDED --
AGREEMENT BETWEEN GOL AND FEDAYEEN. GOL APPEARS TO HAVE COME OUT VERY WELL IN
TERMS OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID. BIG TEST WILL BE IN IMPLEMENTATION, AS GOL AND ARMY
SEEM UNDERSTAND.

HOUGHTON
footnotes: SEPTEL (Separate Telegram): Standard State Department cable shorthand directing the reader to a companion cable filed under a different subject heading and cable number. The two cables in this merged entry are explicitly cross-referenced as SEPTELs: 1973BEIRUT05755 mentions "DIB'S REPORT BEING SENT SEPTEL," referring to 05776; while 05776 opens with "IN CONVERSATION WITH FONMIN REPORTED SEPTEL," referring back to 05755. Filed 90 minutes apart on May 18, 1973, neither is fully intelligible without the other — which is why they are archived here as a merged entry.

Démarche (French: “step” or “move”): A formal diplomatic approach in which one government makes a direct, official representation to another. A démarche is more weighty than an informal contact but does not necessarily carry the force of an ultimatum. What the GOL was requesting here was a coordinated diplomatic campaign by the United States to press Arab Gulf governments, Iran, Jordan, and — above all — the Soviet Union to use their financial and political influence to ensure the fedayeen kept the commitments they had just made. The GOL was, in effect, asking Washington to function as a guarantor of an arrangement the Lebanese themselves doubted would hold.

Saʿiqa (الصاعقة, “Thunderbolt”): Palestinian armed faction founded in 1966 under the direct sponsorship of the Syrian Ba’ath Party. Unlike Fatah, the PFLP, or the PDFLP, Saʿiqa was not an independent Palestinian movement: it was effectively an instrument of Syrian state policy. This is why the GOL’s inability to obtain Saʿiqa’s explicit acceptance of the Melkart commitments was so significant: it meant that Syria’s proxy force — and by extension, Syria — was not bound by any of the arrangements being negotiated. The cable makes this explicit: Frangieh’s specific objective was to get Saʿiqa to sign on, and this “would depend upon the attitude of the SARG.” Syria’s non-commitment was not a gap that could be negotiated around.

Chargé d’Affaires (or simply “Chargé”): The acting head of a diplomatic mission when the Ambassador is absent. The use of “Chargé” rather than “Ambassador” here indicates that Dwight Houghton was not present for the May 18 meeting, with his deputy acting in his stead. Houghton’s name still appears on the cable as the responsible officer. This is standard practice: cables are signed by the Ambassador regardless of who conducts the actual meeting.

Foreign Minister Abou Hamad: The cable uses “Abou Hamad” as the standard rendering of the Lebanese Foreign Minister’s name. Some diplomatic records from this period suggest this is a reference to Fouad Butros (Fuad Butros), who served as Foreign Minister in the cabinet of Prime Minister Takieddine Solh from July 1973. If this meeting took place on May 18, 1973, the incumbent Foreign Minister may have been someone else in the transitional period after the May 1973 crisis — or “Abou Hamad” may be a rendering of a different minister. The cable is consistent in using “Abou Hamad” throughout, suggesting this is a kunya (Arabic patronymic form of address) for a specific individual whose given name is not provided. This uncertainty is noted; the archival identification is provisional.

Presidency Director-General Dib: The recurring GOL interlocutor throughout the May 1973 crisis cables. The Presidency Director-General was the senior official of the Lebanese Presidential Palace, functioning as the head of the presidential administration and a key channel between President Frangieh and foreign diplomats. “Dib” appears in several cables as the GOL’s senior briefing officer on the fedayeen negotiations. His role here — summing up from memory the full terms of the fedayeen commitments — indicates he was at the center of the negotiation.

Mixed Commission: The joint body of Lebanese Army officers and fedayeen representatives established to manage the practical implementation of agreements governing Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon. The Mixed Commission operated under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement, which had created a formal structure for GOL-PLO relations. By May 1973, the Mixed Commission had been the venue for ten days of intensive negotiations following the outbreak of fighting on May 7–8. The evening of May 17 — when the fedayeen made their commitments — was the concluding session of this round of talks.

This is the central legal and political framing of the entire Melkart arrangement, and it was chosen deliberately by the Lebanese government. By insisting the fedayeen commitments were “unilateral promises” rather than “a new GOL-fedayeen agreement,” the Lebanese were attempting to sidestep the Cairo Accords framework. Any new “agreement” would implicitly have operated within that framework — which the fedayeen would use to argue their presence and operations were legitimized under the 1969 accords. Unilateral promises, by contrast, were not framed as bilateral contractual obligations with reciprocal GOL concessions; they were simply undertakings the fedayeen made. This distinction mattered enormously on paper. In practice, the fedayeen would interpret the arrangements as a supplement to the Cairo Accords — exactly as the Embassy predicted in paragraph 6 of 05776.

Kamal Jumblatt (1917–1977): Leader of the Progressive Socialist Party and paramount chief of the Lebanese Druze community. In 1973, Jumblatt was the leading figure of the Lebanese left-wing political coalition that aligned itself with the Palestinian fedayeen and maintained close ties to Syria and the Soviet Union. The Foreign Minister’s identification of Jumblatt as a Soviet “left-wing ally” and thus an indirect channel of Soviet influence on Lebanon documents the GOL’s 1973 threat assessment. Jumblatt would go on to lead the Lebanese National Movement (LNM) — the leftist-Palestinian alliance — during the 1975–76 civil war. He was assassinated in March 1977, almost certainly by Syrian agents, after President Assad turned against him.

This sentence is the Foreign Minister’s own prediction, delivered at the moment of apparent diplomatic success, that the agreement would fail and a worse explosion would follow. The phrase “another, more serious explosion” acknowledges that the May 7–8 fighting was the first such explosion. The GOL is predicting the next one while still sitting in the meeting that resolved the current one. The historical record shows the prediction was correct: the fedayeen did not fully implement the Melkart commitments, the Lebanese Army’s capacity to enforce them degraded, and the “more serious explosion” came in April 1975. Abou Hamad’s words were in the diplomatic record in May 1973.

The GOL’s own summary document for the arrangement that would become known as the Melkart Protocol contains an explicit statement of doubt about the other party’s good faith. This is not an external skeptical assessment — it is the Lebanese government’s own framing, transmitted through U.S. Embassy reporting, on the day after the commitments were made. The Melkart Protocol has sometimes been described in secondary literature as a genuine attempt to regulate Palestinian armed presence. The cable record suggests the GOL itself regarded it as an instrument whose value depended entirely on enforcement — and already doubted the good faith of the party making the promises.

“Foreign elements” (non-Arabs) in the camps: This term is used as a euphemism for international volunteers and fighters who had joined the Palestinian armed organizations — individuals from outside the Arab world who had come to Lebanon to participate in the fedayeen cause. The cable makes clear that the category includes “Turks and Iranians as well as a variety of others,” some of whom had already been rounded up by the Lebanese Army at checkpoints in the preceding two weeks. This documents, from a 1973 U.S. Embassy source, that Palestinian camps in Lebanon housed non-Arab combatants including Turks and Iranians. The international composition of the fedayeen forces was therefore documented in the diplomatic record 50 years before it became a matter of historical dispute.

The explicit naming of “Turks and Iranians” as “combatants” in the Palestinian refugee camps is among the most historically specific details in these cables. Pre-revolutionary Iran (1973) under the Shah was not generally associated with Palestinian armed factions. The Iranian government was a U.S. ally and the Shah had diplomatic relations with Israel. Yet the Embassy’s reporting — drawn from Dib’s direct briefing — names Iranians among the non-Arab combatants whom the fedayeen themselves committed to remove from the camps. This detail is in the U.S. diplomatic record as of May 18, 1973. It has not appeared in standard accounts of the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon.

The phrase “with permission of the fedayeen” qualifies the entire clause about Lebanese sovereignty over the camps. Formally, Lebanese security forces were being granted the right of access. Practically, they would need to ask the fedayeen for permission to exercise that right. The GOL and Dib were apparently satisfied with this formulation — or at least accepted it as the best that could be obtained. The Embassy’s Comment paragraph (para. 6) implicitly registers skepticism: “the big test will be in implementation.” A right of entry that requires the consent of the party being entered is, in practice, not a right of entry.

WAFA (وكالة أنباء فلسطين, Wikalat Anbaʼ Falastin — Palestine News Agency): The official PLO news wire service, founded in 1972. The Melkart commitments required the fedayeen to cease using Beirut as a base for propaganda releases. WAFA was explicitly carved out of this prohibition — it was allowed to continue operating in Lebanon. This carve-out for the PLO’s official news agency, while nominally modest, preserved a key institutional presence in Beirut. WAFA still operates today as the official Palestinian news agency.

The geographical specifics here document the military geography of the Melkart Protocol in a level of detail not generally available in secondary sources. Ras Naqura (also known as Rosh HaNikra) is the Mediterranean coastal point on the Lebanese-Israeli border; total fedayeen exclusion there. Bint Jbeil, in the central south, required an 8–10 km pullback. The Arqoub (العرقوب) — the southeastern corner of Lebanon where the Lebanese, Syrian, and Israeli borders converge, historically the most active base for cross-border fedayeen operations — was subject to the most permissive terms: fedayeen to remain north of the Hasbaya-Shebaa road except for “two or three specified and carefully controlled spots.” The Arqoub had been known informally as “Fatahland” since the late 1960s. The gap between the formal commitment (north of Hasbaya-Shebaa road) and the exceptions (“two or three spots” to be specified) left substantial room for contested interpretation.

Cairo Agreement (November 3, 1969): The foundational document governing PLO–GOL relations, signed by PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat and Lebanese Army Commander General Emile Bustani under Egyptian mediation. The Agreement formally legalized the PLO’s armed presence on Lebanese soil and granted Palestinian organizations authority within the refugee camps. The GOL insisted the Melkart commitments were “unilateral promises” rather than a new agreement specifically to avoid the implication that they operated under the Cairo Accords framework. The Embassy predicted in para. 6 that the fedayeen would nonetheless frame the Melkart arrangement as “within the context of the Cairo Accords” — which is exactly what happened.

Dwight J. Houghton: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1970–1974. These two cables, filed on May 18, 1973, represent Houghton’s reporting on the moment of apparent resolution of the May 1973 crisis — the fedayeen commitments that would be formalized as the Melkart Protocol. Read together with the earlier cables in this archive (1973BEIRUT04974 documenting the April 30 bomb plot; 1973BEIRUT05155 and 1973BEIRUT05159 documenting the May 7–8 fighting; and 1973BEIRUT05437 assessing the likely terms), the Melkart cables are the conclusion of a crisis that was, in the Embassy’s own terms at the time, unlikely to resolve the underlying structural problem. Houghton left Beirut in 1974. He did not see the war that his cables had predicted.

readerNarrative.headline: The Promises They Made: The Melkart Arrangement in Real Time
readerNarrative.subheadline: Two SECRET/EXDIS cables filed 90 minutes apart on May 18, 1973 document the Melkart Protocol as it was happening: the specific commitments the fedayeen made, the Lebanese government’s own doubts about whether they would hold, and the critical gap that would doom the arrangement — Saʿiqa, Syria’s proxy force, never signed.
readerNarrative.summary: On May 18, 1973, U.S. Embassy Beirut filed two classified cables 90 minutes apart documenting the conclusion of the negotiations that produced the Melkart Protocol. The first cable (1973BEIRUT05755) records the Lebanese Foreign Minister and Presidency Director-General briefing the U.S. Chargé on what had been achieved and what American diplomatic support was being requested. The second (1973BEIRUT05776) documents the specific commitments: a pullback from border areas, removal of heavy weapons from camps, no cross-border raids, Lebanese security force access to camps, and removal of non-Arab “foreign elements” — explicitly including Turks and Iranians. Both cables are marked SECRET/EXDIS. Together they confirm: the Lebanese government called these “unilateral promises,” not an agreement; Saʿiqa explicitly did not sign; the GOL’s own diplomats described fedayeen good faith as “suspect”; and Lebanese forces could enter camps only with fedayeen permission.
keyRevelations: The Lebanese government’s own framing, on the day after the commitments were made: the fedayeen concessions were unilateral promises, not an agreement — specifically to avoid the Cairo Accords framework. The Embassy predicted the fedayeen would nonetheless claim the arrangement was “within the context” of those same Accords.

Saʿiqa — Syria’s proxy faction — explicitly did not sign the Melkart commitments. Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP representatives claimed they were speaking for all fedayeen. The GOL did not accept this. Syria’s armed proxy was thus entirely outside the arrangement from the moment it was made.

The GOL’s own summary of the arrangement, transmitted through the U.S. Embassy, states that “fedayeen good faith in this regard is suspect.” This is not an outside assessment. It is the Lebanese government’s own language, on record in May 1973.

Lebanese security forces were granted the right to enter the refugee camps “with permission of the fedayeen.” Sovereignty in name, with the party to be regulated retaining veto power over the act of regulation.

Non-Arab combatants in the Palestinian camps — required to leave under the Melkart terms — explicitly included Turks and Iranians, documented by U.S. Embassy reporting based on the Presidency Director-General’s direct briefing. This is in the diplomatic record as of May 18, 1973.

Foreign Minister Abou Hamad told the U.S. Chargé: “the only way to avoid another, more serious explosion in Lebanon” was full implementation. The Lebanese were predicting the next crisis while celebrating the resolution of the current one.

timeline.label: Fighting breaks out in Beirut
timeline.desc: Palestinian factions open fire on Lebanese Army positions. The Army responds with aircraft and tanks. Prime Minister Hafez resigns at 5 AM on May 8. See cable 1973BEIRUT05159.

timeline.desc: The Mixed Commission — Lebanese Army officers and fedayeen representatives — negotiates terms. The May 12 assessment cable (1973BEIRUT05437) predicts the likely outcome and its limits.

timeline.desc: In the Mixed Commission, Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP representatives present a list of specific promises. Saʿiqa and PFLP/GC do not directly participate. The commitments are made verbally and from memory — the Army has not yet written them up.

timeline.label: Cable 05755: GOL requests U.S. démarches
timeline.desc: The Chargé meets with the Foreign Minister and Presidency Director-General. The GOL asks Washington to press Arab Gulf states, Iran, Jordan, and the USSR to back implementation. Saʿiqa’s non-acceptance is flagged as the critical gap.

timeline.desc: First of the two companion cables: the diplomatic conversation, the U.S. role requested, and the Saʿiqa problem. Marked SECRET/EXDIS.

timeline.desc: Second cable, 90 minutes later: the specific terms — border pullback, heavy weapons removal, camp access, foreign elements, propaganda restrictions. The Embassy notes the GOL’s own doubts about implementation.

timeline.desc: The Lebanese Civil War starts. The Melkart commitments were not implemented. Saʿiqa never signed. The “more serious explosion” the Foreign Minister warned of, on May 18, 1973, arrives.

keyFigures.name: Fonmin Abou Hamad
keyFigures.desc: The cable’s consistent designation for the Lebanese Foreign Minister throughout the May 1973 negotiations. He is the GOL’s most senior voice in these cables — the one who tells the U.S. Chargé that “the only way to avoid another, more serious explosion in Lebanon” is full fedayeen implementation. His prediction was accurate. His name as given in the cables (“Abou Hamad”) appears to be a kunya; the archival identification remains provisional.

keyFigures.name: Suleiman Frangieh
keyFigures.desc: Named in both cables as the driving force behind the demand for fedayeen compliance. The Foreign Minister’s objective to obtain Saʿiqa’s explicit commitment is described as “one of Frangie’s specific objectives.” The same Frangieh who said no to BSO blackmail in April 1973 (cable 1973BEIRUT04974) was now trying to hold Syria’s proxy force to an arrangement that Syria had not sanctioned.

keyFigures.name: Saʿiqa leadership
keyFigures.desc: Saʿiqa’s explicit non-acceptance of the Melkart commitments is the most consequential single fact in these two cables. As an arm of Syrian Ba’ath Party policy rather than an independent Palestinian organization, Saʿiqa’s position reflected Damascus’s decision not to be bound. The entire arrangement was therefore built on a foundation where Syria’s proxy force — the one with the most men and the deepest external backing — was formally outside it.

keyFigures.name: Presidency Director-General Dib
keyFigures.role: GOL senior official, key negotiating interlocutor
keyFigures.desc: The official who briefed the U.S. Chargé on the specific terms of the fedayeen commitments — from memory, the morning after they were made, before the Army had written them up. Dib’s briefing is the primary source for the substantive content of cable 1973BEIRUT05776. His hedge — “these are reported as follows but may not be complete nor completely accurate” — documents the fragility of the arrangement even at the moment of its birth.

keyFigures.name: Dwight J. Houghton
keyFigures.desc: Houghton’s name signs both cables, though it was his Chargé who conducted the May 18 meeting. His Beirut reporting across 1973 — from the April airport bomb plot through the May crisis and these Melkart cables — constitutes the most detailed contemporaneous U.S. documentation of the conditions that would produce the 1975 civil war. He left Beirut in 1974 and did not see what his cables had predicted.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Ninety minutes apart

At 1:15 PM Beirut time on May 18, 1973, the U.S. Embassy sent a SECRET/EXDIS cable to Washington. Ninety minutes later, it sent another. Together, the two cables document one of the most consequential diplomatic moments in modern Lebanese history: the day the Lebanese government believed it had secured the fedayeen’s commitment to respect Lebanese sovereignty.

It was the day of the Melkart Protocol.

The two cables are cross-referenced as SEPTELs — Separate Telegrams, the State Department’s standard method of directing a reader to a companion cable. They were filed 90 minutes apart because the meeting they document covered two distinct subjects that the Embassy judged required separate reporting: the diplomatic conversation (what the Lebanese government had achieved, what it was asking the U.S. to do) and the substance (the specific terms of the fedayeen commitments). Neither cable is fully intelligible without the other. They are archived here together.

What the Lebanese government said it had achieved

The morning of May 18, the U.S. Chargé met at the Lebanese Foreign Ministry with Foreign Minister Abou Hamad, Presidency Director-General Dib, and Foreign Office Secretary-General Sadaqa. The meeting had two purposes: to inform the Lebanese of Washington’s response to their earlier requests (including that the U.S. had again approached the Soviets in Moscow and had been in contact with the Israelis), and to hear the GOL’s account of what had been negotiated with the fedayeen the previous evening.

What Dib reported was framed with deliberate legal precision. The fedayeen — Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP — had made a series of specific commitments the evening of May 17 in the Mixed Commission. But these were, in the GOL’s insistent framing, unilateral promises. Not a new agreement. Not a supplement to the Cairo Accords. Not a bilateral undertaking. Unilateral promises, from the fedayeen to the Lebanese Army, which the GOL would codify on paper and distribute to Arab governments and certain other governments so there would be no misunderstanding about the future relationship.

The distinction was not semantic. It was the entire point. Any “agreement” between the GOL and the fedayeen would implicitly operate within the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement, which had legalized Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon and given the fedayeen formal status. Unilateral promises, by contrast, could be presented as the Lebanese state receiving voluntary compliance from a subordinate party — without the reciprocal concessions that a bilateral agreement would imply.

The Embassy knew this framing would not survive contact with the fedayeen’s own public presentation. Paragraph 6 of cable 05776 says so directly: the GOL’s “unilateral promises” framing “is likely to be countered on the fedayeen side by the claim that it is all within the context of the Cairo Accords which are still in force.”

The gap that was already there

Before the Melkart Protocol had been written up, before its terms had been formally transmitted to Arab governments, before the implementation timetable had been agreed, the Lebanese government had already identified its fatal weakness.

Saʿiqa had not signed.

Saʿiqa — the Syrian Ba’ath Party’s Palestinian faction, effectively an instrument of Syrian state policy — was present in Lebanon in significant numbers. The PFLP/GC, also Syrian-aligned, had also not explicitly committed. Fatah, PFLP, and PDFLP representatives in the Mixed Commission claimed they were speaking for all fedayeen organizations. The GOL did not accept this. The cable is explicit: “GOL DOES NOT RPT NOT ACCEPT THIS AS NECESSARILY SO.”

The problem was structural, not diplomatic. Saʿiqa was not an independent Palestinian organization that could be reasoned with or pressured by Arab states. It reflected “the attitude of the Syrian government.” Frangieh’s specific objective — to obtain Saʿiqa’s explicit commitment — would depend on Damascus. And Damascus had given no sign that it intended to restrain its proxy.

This is why the Foreign Minister identified the Soviet Union as the top priority for U.S. démarches: not because Moscow controlled the fedayeen directly, but because Moscow had influence in Damascus, and Damascus controlled Saʿiqa. The chain of necessary diplomatic interventions was long, and each link was uncertain.

The terms themselves

Cable 05776 — the one filed at 1:15 PM, 90 minutes after the first — documents the actual content of what the fedayeen promised. Dib delivered this briefing from memory, the morning after the commitments were made, before the Army had written them up. The Embassy noted the limitations: “these are reported as follows but may not be complete nor completely accurate.”

The terms, as Dib remembered them, covered five areas. In the camps: cease all military training, remove heavy weapons, remove all non-Arab “foreign elements.” On camp control: Lebanese security forces would have checkpoints outside the camps and the right to enter — but only with the permission of the fedayeen. On information: all media to be consolidated under the PLO, no more attacks on the GOL through fedayeen outlets; Beirut no longer to be used as a base for communiqués — though WAFA, the Palestine News Agency, was explicitly carved out and allowed to remain. On the border: full adherence to the limits set after the September 1972 Israeli action, complete exclusion from the western sector near Ras Naqura, 8–10 kilometer pullback in the central sector near Bint Jbeil, and in the Arqoub — the southeastern zone historically used for cross-border operations — fedayeen to stay north of the Hasbaya-Shebaa road except for two or three specified spots.

On paper, this was a significant set of concessions. The Lebanese government had, in the Foreign Minister’s words, “come out very well in terms of what has been said.”

The problem was in what had not been said, and in who had not been in the room.

Sovereignty with permission

One phrase in cable 05776 encapsulates the fundamental problem with the Melkart arrangement: Lebanese security forces would have the right to enter the camps, “but with permission of the fedayeen.”

This is sovereignty in name, with the party to be regulated retaining veto power over the act of regulation. The Lebanese state’s right of access to territory within its own borders was formally contingent on the consent of the armed organizations occupying that territory. The right existed on paper. In practice, it would only be exercised when the fedayeen chose to allow it.

Dib and the Foreign Minister described the fedayeen’s good faith as “suspect.” They said the fedayeen would have to be watched “on every point, every step of the way.” They said the GOL intended to supervise implementation very closely. But the mechanism for that supervision — security force entry to the camps — was itself subject to fedayeen approval. The watchdog required the watched party’s permission to watch.

Foreign fighters in the camps

One of the Melkart commitments was the removal of non-Arab “foreign elements” from the camps. All “combatants” were to leave — with the sole exception of those engaged in medical work. The cable specifies that this “explicitly includes Turks and Iranians as well as a variety of others.”

This is a precise, contemporaneous, U.S.-sourced documentation of international fighters in the Palestinian camps of Lebanon in 1973. Pre-revolutionary Iran was at that time a U.S. ally, diplomatically recognized by Israel, and governed by the Shah. Yet Iranian combatants were present in the fedayeen camps in sufficient numbers that their removal required explicit mention in the commitments. Turkish fighters were similarly named. The Lebanese Army had been rounding up some of these individuals at checkpoints outside the camps in the two weeks preceding the cable.

This detail is in the diplomatic record as of May 18, 1973. It has not appeared in standard accounts of the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon.

Already predicting the next crisis

The meeting closed with the Foreign Minister and Dib thanking the United States for its support and making a prediction. The only way to avoid “another, more serious explosion in Lebanon,” Abou Hamad said, was for the fedayeen to actually honor their promises and not back away from them over time. Support from the governments the U.S. would approach would be vital.

The phrase “another, more serious explosion” is a reference to the May 7–8 fighting that had just been resolved. The Foreign Minister, sitting in the meeting that marked the resolution, was already predicting the next, worse crisis. He was saying, in diplomatic language: we do not think this will hold, and when it fails, the consequences will be worse than what we just survived.

The prediction was documented in U.S. cables on May 18, 1973.

The next explosion came on April 13, 1975.

What the Melkart Protocol was

Historians have sometimes described the Melkart Protocol as a genuine, if ultimately failed, attempt to regulate Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon. The cable record suggests a more precise characterization: it was an arrangement that the Lebanese government concluded was necessary to survive the immediate crisis, whose durability they doubted from the day it was made, and whose critical structural weakness — Saʿiqa’s non-participation, meaning Syria was not bound — was known to them and documented in real time.

The Melkart Protocol did not fail because anyone misunderstood what it was. It failed because everyone, including the Lebanese government, understood exactly what it was: a set of promises from parties whose good faith was suspect, excluding the party whose behavior mattered most, enforced by a mechanism that required the other party’s permission to operate.

The cables filed at 1:15 PM and 3:00 PM on May 18, 1973, document all of this — in real time, on the day it happened, in language the parties involved chose to put on the record.

cables.subject: Lebanese-Syrian Relations
cables.excerpt: Three weeks after the Melkart Protocol, the Lebanese Foreign Office reads the Embassy an intelligence dossier: Iraqi/Soviet arms arriving at Latakia in Arafat's name; half being distributed to Lebanese leftist groups; and direct Fatah treasury payments to the Sunni Grand Mufti, Kamal Jumblatt, Musa Sadr, and Adnan Hakim. Plus a Syrian disinformation campaign designed to justify future action or provoke preemptive fedayeen attack.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL / LIMDIS · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Not passed to Cairo

1.
Secretary General Sadaqa[1] of the Lebanese Foreign Office asked the Chargé d’Affaires to call on him late morning on June 8. He proceeded to inform the Chargé and the Embassy officer of how the GOL sees the current situation as it concerns the Syrians, the Lebanese left, and the fedayeen.[2] Sadaqa read from several intelligence reports received from Lebanese and Jordanian sources in order to document his case.

2.
The first report was from Lebanese Army G-2 and described by the Army as coming from a completely reliable source, who obtained intelligence from fedayeen sources in Beirut. Main points were: (A) Iraq has offered the fedayeen 6,000 individual weapons, and 2,000 Kalashnikov rifles have arrived at Latakia from the USSR in the name of Arafat;[3] (B) On May 21–22 a top-level fedayeen meeting decided to distribute 4,000 of these individual weapons (after delivery in Lebanon) to various fedayeen units, and 4,000 to various leftist groups (“nationalist” or “progressive” forces).[4]

3.
A second report was received from Jordanian intelligence and concerns a fedayeen plan to take Qlaiaat Airport[5] in North Lebanon, using some Lebanese Army officers to develop intelligence on the airfield and its defenses. The Jordanians also reported smuggling of large quantities of light and heavy weapons to several Lebanese cities and into the Shouf area, where they will be distributed to leftist groups, including those of Kamal Jumblatt[6] and Najah Wakin (pro-Syrian Nasserist deputy).

4.
Another Lebanese report indicates large sums of money given by Arafat to certain Muslim and leftist leaders in order to influence them favorably toward the fedayeen and against the GOL (and Frangieh). Amounts cited included LL 250,000 to Grand Mufti Shaykh Hassan Khaled (Sunni); LL 500,000 to leftist former deputy Adnan Hakim (Sunni); LL 100,000 to Shia leader Imam Musa Sadr; and LL 500,000 to leftist Kamal Jumblatt.[7] Money was reported paid out by Abu Jihad[8] from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh. Another Jordanian report says three fedayeen are being sent to Baghdad to arrange for purchase and delivery to Lebanon of some 930 “Cobra” model wire-guided anti-tank rockets[9] which reportedly have a range of 2 kilometers and are 190 centimeters long. A new fedayeen rocket unit is to be organized and emplaced near the Syrian–Lebanese major border crossing area at Masnaa (where the fedayeen tried unsuccessfully to cut the road and had several pitched battles with the Lebanese Army in early May). Also, some 250 of Kamal Jumblatt’s followers are being sent to Syria for training.

5.
Sadaqa said that while some details of these reports might be questionable, the GOL is convinced they are mostly true and that they represent a clear Syrian and Iraqi threat to Lebanon. This is all the clearer when taken together with extraordinary SARG behavior vis-à-vis the GOL and the closure of the border.[10] The Syrian Foreign Minister has been contacted four or five times by the Lebanese Foreign Minister over the past week, yet has consistently avoided answering questions on what are the basic problems between Syria and Lebanon. Instead he limits comments in official channels to complaints about minor, specific cases (e.g., the temporary arrest of three Syrians on June 6).

6.
However, in public comments by Syrian press and radio, and in what top Syrian officials are saying to Lebanese who have recently visited Damascus (including Raymond Eddé,[11] the Abdullah Yafi group, and Arab League Secretary-General Riad), the Syrians make the worst sort of allegations — that the Lebanese government and army have not lived up to arrangements with the fedayeen and that they are in fact preparing another armed attack in an effort to liquidate the fedayeen. The GOL is forced to conclude that the Syrians are not sincerely interested in resolving any outstanding problems, but rather are trying to exert maximum political and psychological pressure on the GOL and President Frangieh. The danger is that this could either be a pretext for a more active and forceful Syrian/fedayeen attack on Lebanon at some future date, or that the campaign could convince the fedayeen they are really in danger, thereby causing them to start something on their own.[12]

7.
In reply to a question, Sadaqa said that it is obvious the Lebanese Army and GOL are not in any way preparing to attack the fedayeen, although the Army is trying to maintain some control over fedayeen movements and arms smuggling. Thus far, the fedayeen have been unwilling to take any action toward implementation of the most important points of their “arrangements” with the GOL, namely: the removal of heavy and medium arms from camps; the removal of fedayeen regulars from camps; the transfer of fedayeen headquarters out of Lebanon; and the transfer of all training operations out of camps to an agreed area near the border with Syria.[13] Yet the Syrians are telling one and all that it is the GOL which is delinquent in not keeping its bargain with the fedayeen.

8.
In summing up, Sadaqa said that the GOL would appreciate it if the Department considered itself in a position to raise the matter of Syrian behavior and fedayeen non-execution of promises with the Soviets.[14] He said that the GOL does not intend to raise the matter with Ambassador Azimov because the Lebanese have learned the hard way that they cannot place any stock in what Azimov says, which often fails to correspond to Soviet deeds.

9.
Sadaqa added that the grim situation as the GOL sees it means that reinforcement of the Lebanese Army becomes all the more important and urgent. He expressed hope that the USG would soon have a positive reply to the Lebanese request for arms.[15]

10. Comment
What Sadaqa had to say about the Syrians, Lebanese left, and fedayeen is just about what we have been reporting for some time. There is no question but that Syrian economic and political pressure and arms supply is causing serious problems for the GOL, both in bringing the fedayeen to implement their promises and in dealing with indigenous leftist opposition. We would hope that Embassy Moscow or the Department could raise the problem of Lebanese–Syrian–fedayeen relations with the Soviets if the opportunity presents itself, even though we realize it is unlikely to have much effect on the Syrians.

HOUGHTON

EO 11652: GDS
TAGS: PFOR, PINS, LE, SY
SUBJECT: LEBANESE-SYRIAN RELATIONS
REF: BEIRUT 6565

1. SECGEN SADAQA OF LEBANESE FONOFFICE ASKED CHARGE CALL ON HIM LATE MORNING
JUNE 8. HE PROCEEDED INFORM CHARGE AND EMB OFF OF HOW GOL SEES CURRENT
SITUATION AS IT CONCERNS SYRIANS, LEBANESE LEFT AND FEDAYEEN. SADAQA READ
FROM SEVERAL INTELLIGENCE REPORTS RECEIVED FROM LEBANESE AND JORDANIAN
SOURCES IN WAY OF DOCUMENTING HIS CASE.

2. FIRST REPORT WAS FROM LEBANESE ARMY G-2 AND DESCRIBED BY ARMY AS COMING
FROM COMPLETELY RELIABLE SOURCE, WHO OBTAINED INTELLIGENCE FROM FEDAYEEN
SOURCES IN BEIRUT. MAIN POINTS WERE: (A) IRAQ HAS OFFERED FEDAYEEN 6,000
INDIVIDUAL WEAPONS AND 2,000 KALASHNIKOV RIFLES HAVE ARRIVED AT LATAKIA FROM
USSR IN NAME OF ARAFAT; (B) ON MAY 21-22 TOP LEVEL FEDAYEEN MEETING DECIDED
DISTRIBUTE 4,000 OF THESE INDIVIDUAL WEAPONS (AFTER DELIVERY IN LEBANON) TO
VARIOUS FEDAYEEN UNITS AND 4,000 TO VARIOUS LEFTIST GROUPS ("NATIONALIST"
OR "PROGRESSIVE" FORCES);

3. SECOND REPORT RECEIVED FROM JORDANIAN INTELLIGENCE AND CONCERNS FEDAYEEN
PLAN TO TAKE QLAIAAT AIRPORT IN NORTH LEBANON USING SOME LEBANESE ARMY
OFFICERS TO DEVELOP INTELLIGENCE ON AIRFIELD AND ITS DEFENSES. JORDANIANS
ALSO REPORTED SMUGGLING OF LARGE QUANTITIES LIGHT AND HEAVY WEAPONS TO
SEVERAL LEBANESE CITIES AND INTO SHOUF AREA WHERE THEY WILL BE DISTRIBUTED
TO LEFTIST GROUPS, INCLUDING THOSE OF KAMAL JUMBLATT AND NAJAH WAKIN (PRO
SYRIAN NASSERIST DEPUTY).

4. ANOTHER LEBANESE REPORT INDICATES LARGE SUMS OF MONEY GIVEN BY ARAFAT TO
CERTAIN MOSLEM AND LEFTIST LEADERS IN ORDER INFLUENCE THEM FAVORABLY TOWARD
FEDAYEEN AND AGAINST GOL (AND FRANGIE). AMOUNTS CITED INCLUDED LL250,000 TO
GRAND MUFTI SHAYKH HASSAN KHALED (SUNNI); LL500,000 TO LEFTIST FORMER DEPUTY
ADNAN HAKIM (SUNNI); LL100,000 TO SHIA LEADER IMAM MUSA SADR; AND LL500,000
TO LEFTIST KAMAL JUMBLATT. MONEY REPORTED PAID OUT BY ABU JIHAD FROM FATAH
TREASURY AT NABATIYEH. ANOTHER JORDANIAN REPORT SAYS THREE FEDAYEEN BEING
SENT TO BAGHDAD TO ARRANGE FOR PURCHASE AND DELIVERY TO LEBANON OF SOME 930
"COBRA" MODEL WIRE GUIDED ANTI TANK ROCKETS WHICH REPORTEDLY HAVE RANGE OF
2 KILOMETERS AND ARE 190 CENTIMETERS LONG. NEW FEDAYEEN ROCKET UNIT TO BE
ORGANIZED AND EMPLACED NEAR SYRIAN LEBANESE MAJOR BORDER CROSSING AREA AT
MASNAA (WHERE FEDAYEEN TRIED UNSUCCESSFULLY CUT ROAD AND HAD SEVERAL PITCHED
BATTLES WITH LEBANESE ARMY IN EARLY MAY). ALSO SOME 250 OF KAMAL JUMBLATTS
FOLLOWERS BEING SENT TO SYRIA FOR TRAINING.

PAGE 03 BEIRUT 06768 081837Z

5. SADAQA SAID THAT WHILE SOME DETAILS OF THESE REPORTS MIGHT BE QUESTIONABLE,
GOL IS CONVINCED THEY ARE MOSTLY TRUE AND THAT THEY REPRESENT A CLEAR SYRIAN
AND IRAQI THREAT TO LEBANON. THIS ALL THE CLEARER WHEN TAKEN TOGETHER WITH
EXTRAORDINARY SARG BEHAVIOR VIS A VIS GOL AND CLOSURE OF BORDER. SYRIAN
FONMIN HAS BEEN CONTACTED FOUR OR FIVE TIMES BY LEBANESE FONMIN OVER PAST
WEEK YET HAS CONSISTENTLY AVOIDED ANSWERING QUESTIONS ON WHAT ARE BASIC
PROBLEMS BETWEEN SYRIA AND LEBANON. INSTEAD HE LIMITS COMMENTS IN OFFICIAL
CHANNELS TO COMPLAINTS ABOUT MINOR, SPECIFIC CASES (EG, TEMP ARREST OF 3
SYRIANS ON JUNE 6).

6. HOWEVER IN PUBLIC COMMENTS BY SYRIAN PRESS AND RADIO AND IN WHAT TOP
SYRIAN OFFICIALS SAYING TO LEBANESE WHO HAVE RECENTLY VISITED DAMASCUS
(INCLUDING RAYMOND EDDE, ABDULLAH YAFI GROUP, AND ARAB LEAGUE SECGEN RIAD)
SYRIANS MAKE WORST SORT OF ALLEGATIONS THAT LEBANESE GOVT AND ARMY HAVE NOT
LIVED UP TO ARRANGEMENTS WITH FEDAYEEN AND THAT THEY ARE IN FACT PREPARING
ANOTHER ARMED ATTACK IN EFFORT LIQUIDATE THE FEDAYEEN (SEE SEPTEL FOR MORE
DETAILS). GOL IS FORCED TO CONCLUDE THAT SYRIANS NOT SINCERELY INTERESTED
IN RESOLVING ANY OUTSTANDING PROBLEMS BUT RATHER TO EXERT MAXIMUM POLITICAL
AND PSYCHOLOGICAL PRESSURE ON GOL AND PRES FRANGIE. DANGER IS THAT THIS
COULD EITHER BE PRETEXT FOR MORE ACTIVE AND FORCEFUL SYRIAN/FEDAYEEN ATTACK
ON LEBANON AT SOME FUT DATE OR THAT CAMPAIGN COULD CONVINCE FEDAYEEN THEY
ARE REALLY IN DANGER, THEREBY CAUSING THEM TO START SOMETHING ON THEIR OWN.

7. IN REPLY TO QUESTION SADAQA SAID THAT IT OBVIOUS LEBANESE ARMY AND GOL
NOT IN ANY WAY PREPARING TO ATTACK FEDAYEEN, ALTHOUGH ARMY TRYING MAINTAIN
SOME CONTROL OVER FEDAYEEN MOVEMENTS AND ARMS SMUGGLING. THUS FAR FEDAYEEN
HAVE BEEN UNWILLING TAKE ANY ACTION TOWARD IMPLEMENTATION OF MOST IMPORTANT
POINTS OF THEIR "ARRANGEMENTS" WITH GOL, NAMELY THE REMOVAL OF HEAVY AND
MEDIUM ARMS FROM CAMPS; THE REMOVAL OF FEDAYEEN REGULARS FROM CAMPS; THE
TRANSFER OF FEDAYEEN HEADQUARTERS OUT OF LEBANON; AND THE TRANSFER OF ALL
TRAINING OPERATIONS OUT OF CAMPS TO AGREED AREA NEAR BORDER WITH SYRIA. YET
SYRIANS ARE TELLING ONE AND ALL THAT IT IS GOL WHICH DELINQUENT IN NOT
KEEPING ITS BARGAIN WITH FEDAYEEN.

PAGE 04 BEIRUT 06768 081837Z

8. IN SUMMING UP, SADAQA SAID THAT GOL WOULD APPRECIATE IT IF DEPT CONSIDERED
ITSELF IN POSITION RAISE MATTER OF SYRIAN BEHAVIOR AND FEDAYEEN NON EXECUTION
OF PROMISED WITH SOVS. HE SAID THAT GOL DOES NOT INTEND RAISE MATTER WITH
AMB AZIMOV BECAUSE LEBANESE HAVE LEARNED HARD WAY THAT THEY CANNOT PLACE
ANY STOCK IN WHAT AZIMOV SAYS, WHICH OFTEN FAILS TO CORRESPOND TO SOV DEEDS.

9. SADAQA ADDED THAT GRIM SITUATION AS GOL SEES IT MEANS THAT REINFORCING
OF LEBANESE ARMY BECOMES ALL MORE IMPORTANT AND URGENT. HE EXPRESSED HOPE
THAT USG WOULD SOON HAVE POSITIVE REPLY TO LEBANESE REQUEST FOR ARMS.

10. COMMENT: WHAT SADAQA HAD TO SAY ABOUT SYRIANS, LEBANESE LEFT AND FEDAYEEN
IS JUST ABOUT WHAT WE HAVE BEEN REPORTING FOR SOMETIME. THERE IS NO QUESTION
BUT THAT SYRIAN ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL PRESSURE AND ARMS SUPPLY IS CAUSING
SERIOUS PROBLEMS FOR GOL BOTH IN BRINGING FEDAYEEN TO IMPLEMENT THEIR
PROMISES AND IN DEALING WITH INDIGENOUS LEFTIST OPPOSITION. WE WOULD HOPE
THAT EMBASSY MOSCOW OR DEPT COULD RAISE PROBLEM OF LEBANESE-SYRIAN-FEDAYEEN
RELATIONS WITH SOVS IF OPPORTUNITY PRESENTS ITSELF, EVEN THOUGH WE REALIZE
IT UNLIKELY HAVE MUCH EFFECT ON SYRIANS.

HOUGHTON

footnotes: Sadaqa: Secretary General of the Lebanese Foreign Office (Fonoffice), one of the Embassy's most frequent Lebanese government contacts in the 1973 cable series. He also appears in cable 1973BEIRUT05437 (May 12, 1973) as a source on Presidency thinking. In this cable, Sadaqa is functioning as the Lebanese government's chosen channel for relaying an intelligence dossier to the United States — a diplomatic request for action, framed as an informational briefing.

The tripartite frame — "Syrians, Lebanese left, and fedayeen" — is itself analytically significant. The Lebanese Foreign Office is presenting these three not as separate problems but as a linked system: Syrian state pressure, indigenous Lebanese leftist mobilization, and armed Palestinian presence operating in concert. The subsequent paragraphs document specific financial and logistical links tying all three together — Syrian arms flowing to both fedayeen and Lebanese leftists, and Arafat personally financing Lebanese Muslim and leftist political figures.

"2,000 Kalashnikov rifles have arrived at Latakia from the USSR in the name of Arafat": this is a specific, dated logistical fact. Latakia is Syria's principal Mediterranean port. The attribution "in the name of Arafat" — rather than to the PLO as an institution — is documented here in Lebanese Army G-2 intelligence reporting passed to U.S. diplomats. Soviet weapons flowing through a Syrian port to Palestinian armed factions in Lebanon is the operational form of the "discreet" Soviet support for the fedayeen that cable 1973BEIRUT05437 identified at the level of political assessment.

The May 21–22 fedayeen meeting's decision to distribute 4,000 of 6,000 weapons to Lebanese leftist groups (described as "nationalist" or "progressive" forces) is one of the most important facts in this cable. It documents a deliberate PLO policy of arming Lebanese domestic factions — not only Palestinian fighters. The word "nationalist" in quotation marks is the Embassy marking the ideological label used by those factions themselves. This arms transfer — from Iraqi/Soviet-supplied fedayeen stockpiles to Lebanese leftists — is the physical mechanism behind the alliance that would become the Lebanese National Movement (LNM) in 1975.

Qlaiaat Airport: the military airport in the Akkar plain of northern Lebanon, near the Syrian border. Fedayeen plans to seize it — using Lebanese Army officers to develop intelligence on its defenses — would constitute a direct armed assault on Lebanese sovereign territory. The infiltration of Lebanese Army officers as intelligence sources for foreign armed factions is the operational form of the "state within a state" problem that successive cables in this archive document.

Kamal Jumblatt (1917–1977): leader of the Lebanese Progressive Socialist Party (PSP), hereditary leader of the Druze community in the Shouf region, and — by 1975 — leader of the Lebanese National Movement. This cable documents two distinct relationships between Jumblatt and the Syrian/Palestinian alignment: (1) weapons smuggling to his followers in the Shouf; (2) 250 of his followers being sent to Syria for military training. And in paragraph 4, it also documents LL 500,000 in direct financial payments from Arafat's Fatah treasury to Jumblatt personally. Jumblatt would be assassinated in the Shouf on March 16, 1977 — an act widely attributed to Syrian agents after his opposition to Syrian intervention in Lebanon.

This paragraph contains one of the most consequential intelligence reports in this archive: a detailed itemization of direct financial payments from Arafat's Fatah treasury to specific named Lebanese political and religious leaders. The recipients crossed confessional lines — a Sunni Grand Mufti, a leftist Sunni former deputy, a Shia religious leader (Imam Musa Sadr), and a Druze-descended leftist political leader (Kamal Jumblatt). The amounts in Lebanese pounds (LL), adjusted for 1973 values, range from approximately USD 30,000 (Musa Sadr) to approximately USD 150,000 each (Hakim and Jumblatt). The inclusion of Musa Sadr in this list is particularly significant: the charismatic Shia cleric who founded the Movement of the Deprived (precursor to Amal) was politically independent, but the Embassy's reporting documents him as a recipient of PLO funding in June 1973, 15 months before his Movement launched and five years before his 1978 disappearance in Libya. The presence of these payments on the factual record — through Lebanese Army G-2 intelligence, captured in U.S. diplomatic reporting — is a documentary fact about the pre-war political economy of Lebanon that does not appear in standard accounts.

Abu Jihad (Khalil al-Wazir, 1935–1988): Fatah co-founder and the PLO's principal operational commander for military affairs. Here he is identified as the paymaster of Fatah's Lebanese political influence operations, operating from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh. His role as both military operations chief and disbursing officer for political payments illustrates the integration of military and political functions within Fatah. Abu Jihad was assassinated by Israeli commandos at his home in Tunis on April 16, 1988.

"Cobra" wire-guided anti-tank rockets: the reference is to the Bölkow/MBB "Cobra" anti-tank guided missile, a West German design widely exported in the 1960s and 1970s. A fedayeen request to purchase 930 units through Baghdad for deployment near the Syrian-Lebanese border at Masnaa — the principal highway crossing between the two countries — would represent a dramatic upgrade in fedayeen anti-armor capability, specifically sited to contest Lebanese Army mechanized forces along the critical east-west road corridor.

Syrian closure of the border: Syria had closed the Lebanese-Syrian border following the May 1973 fighting, imposing significant economic pressure on Lebanon. Lebanese transit trade — the economic backbone of the Lebanese financial sector — depended heavily on Syrian overland routes to the Gulf. The border closure, combined with the political pressure campaign documented in this cable, constituted a coordinated strategy of economic coercion.

Raymond Eddé (1913–2000): leader of the Lebanese National Bloc, prominent Maronite political figure and former presidential candidate. Syrian overtures to Eddé in Damascus illustrate the breadth of Syrian political contact with Lebanese figures — reaching even across the sectarian lines that Syrian policy would otherwise exploit. Eddé would later oppose Syrian intervention in the Lebanese civil war and spent his final decades in self-imposed exile in Paris.

The cable's assessment — that the Syrian campaign "could convince the fedayeen they are really in danger, thereby causing them to start something on their own" — identifies a specific mechanism of deliberate destabilization: persuading the fedayeen that a threat exists in order to induce them to take military action. This is the pattern of manufactured crisis that successive cables in this archive document. The Embassy is naming it here in June 1973, 22 months before the civil war began.

This list of unimplemented fedayeen commitments is the substantive content of the Melkart Protocol and related May 1973 agreements, which cable 1973BEIRUT05776 documented in real time. The fedayeen had made written promises regarding (1) removal of heavy and medium arms from camps; (2) removal of regulars from camps; (3) transfer of headquarters out of Lebanon; and (4) relocation of training to designated border areas. Three weeks after these commitments were made, Sadaqa documents to U.S. diplomats that none had been honored. The "state within a state" was consolidating its position through selective non-compliance.

The Lebanese Foreign Office's request that the United States raise the Lebanese-Syrian-fedayeen issue with the Soviet Union — and explicit refusal to raise it with the Soviet Ambassador in Beirut — documents Lebanese diplomatic assessment that Soviet Ambassador Azimov was not a reliable channel for substantive communication with Moscow. The Lebanese government is asking the United States to undertake the diplomatic representation it feels it cannot undertake directly. This request places the U.S. Embassy in a specific position within the regional diplomatic architecture of the period.

The "Lebanese request for arms": Lebanon had submitted a formal request to the United States for enhanced military assistance in the aftermath of the May 1973 crisis. Sadaqa's pairing of the intelligence dossier with the arms request — in the same meeting, as the final substantive point — is a clear diplomatic tactic: establish the severity of the threat, then anchor the case for U.S. weapons to match. The cable is, among other things, a document in the Lebanese state's attempt to obtain American military backing for an army the Embassy had assessed in cable 1973BEIRUT05437 as limited to 6,000 combat troops against 15,000 fedayeen fighters.

readerNarrative.headline: The Paymaster's Ledger: Arafat's Payments to Lebanese Leaders, Documented
readerNarrative.subheadline: A Lebanese Foreign Office briefing, filed June 8, 1973, passed to the U.S. Embassy a detailed intelligence dossier: Soviet and Iraqi arms flowing through Latakia to Arafat; Lebanese leftist factions receiving half those weapons; and direct cash payments from the Fatah treasury to Lebanon's Grand Mufti, to Kamal Jumblatt, to Imam Musa Sadr, and to a former Sunni deputy. Also: Syria's parallel campaign to convince the fedayeen Lebanon was preparing to liquidate them.
readerNarrative.summary: Three weeks after the Melkart Protocol was supposed to regularize the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon, the Lebanese Foreign Office summoned the U.S. Chargé to hand over an intelligence dossier. Secretary General Sadaqa read from Lebanese Army G-2 and Jordanian reports documenting three simultaneous developments: Iraq had offered 6,000 weapons and the USSR had delivered 2,000 Kalashnikovs at Latakia in Arafat's name; a May 21–22 fedayeen meeting decided to distribute half those weapons to Lebanese leftist groups; and Arafat had personally paid LL 250,000 to the Sunni Grand Mufti, LL 500,000 to leftist deputy Adnan Hakim, LL 100,000 to Shia leader Musa Sadr, and LL 500,000 to Kamal Jumblatt, from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh. Meanwhile Syria was telling visiting Lebanese that the Lebanese government was preparing to liquidate the fedayeen — a claim the Embassy assessed as designed either to justify future Syrian action or to drive the fedayeen into preemptive attack. Sadaqa asked the U.S. to raise the matter with Moscow because the Lebanese had learned the hard way they could not trust Soviet Ambassador Azimov. The cable closes with a concrete Lebanese ask: urgent U.S. weapons for the Lebanese Army.
keyRevelations: Arafat personally funded a cross-confessional roster of Lebanese political figures from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh: LL 250,000 to Sunni Grand Mufti Hassan Khaled, LL 500,000 to Adnan Hakim, LL 100,000 to Imam Musa Sadr, LL 500,000 to Kamal Jumblatt. The paymaster was Abu Jihad (Khalil al-Wazir).

A May 21–22 fedayeen meeting decided to distribute half of a 6,000-weapon Iraqi/Soviet shipment to Lebanese leftist groups — the physical basis for the armed alliance that became the Lebanese National Movement in 1975.

2,000 Kalashnikov rifles arrived at Latakia from the USSR “in the name of Arafat.” Latakia is Syria's principal port; the shipment crossed Syrian territory en route to Lebanon. This is the operational form of the “discreet” Soviet support assessed in 1973BEIRUT05437.

Syria was running a parallel disinformation campaign telling visiting Lebanese politicians that Beirut was preparing another armed attack to liquidate the fedayeen — an assessment the Embassy flagged as either a pretext for Syrian action or designed to push the fedayeen into a preemptive strike.

The Lebanese Foreign Office asked the U.S. to raise the matter with Moscow because the Lebanese had learned they could not trust Soviet Ambassador Azimov. Sadaqa also coupled the dossier with an explicit request: urgent U.S. arms for the Lebanese Army.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Three weeks after the agreement

The Melkart Protocol had been reached on May 17, 1973. The Lebanese Army and Palestinian factions had exchanged written commitments on heavy weapons, camp security, training locations, and the operational posture of the fedayeen inside Lebanon. It was supposed to be the end of the May crisis.

On June 8, 1973 — three weeks later — the Secretary General of the Lebanese Foreign Office summoned the U.S. Chargé and read him an intelligence dossier. None of the Melkart commitments had been implemented. Instead, the situation had gotten worse.

The arms supply

Iraq had offered the fedayeen 6,000 individual weapons. Two thousand Kalashnikov rifles had arrived at the Syrian port of Latakia, from the USSR, addressed in Arafat's name. A top-level fedayeen meeting on May 21–22 had decided how to distribute the weapons when they reached Lebanon: 4,000 to fedayeen units, and 4,000 to Lebanese leftist groups described as "nationalist" or "progressive" forces. Jordanian intelligence added that three fedayeen were being sent to Baghdad to arrange the purchase and delivery of 930 wire-guided anti-tank rockets for a new rocket unit to be emplaced near the Syrian-Lebanese border crossing at Masnaa.

The arithmetic was not subtle. Half of the incoming fedayeen arms inventory was going to Lebanese militia formations, not to Palestinian fighters. This was the material base of an armed alliance between the PLO and indigenous Lebanese leftist factions — the physical assembly of what would, two years later, become the Lebanese National Movement.

The payments

Paragraph 4 of the cable contains the most detailed information in the pre-war archive about direct financial relations between Arafat's Fatah and Lebanese political figures. The list is specific: LL 250,000 to Grand Mufti Shaykh Hassan Khaled; LL 500,000 to leftist former deputy Adnan Hakim; LL 100,000 to Shia leader Imam Musa Sadr; LL 500,000 to Druze leftist Kamal Jumblatt. The payments crossed confessional lines. The paymaster, the cable reports, was Abu Jihad — Khalil al-Wazir — operating from the Fatah treasury at Nabatiyeh.

These were substantial sums. In 1973 Lebanese pounds, they translate to roughly USD 30,000 to USD 150,000 per recipient at contemporary exchange rates — meaningful political financing by any measure, and especially so for a religious scholar (the Grand Mufti) or for a political figure whose public identity rested on principled independence (Musa Sadr).

The Syrian campaign

In parallel, Sadaqa documented a Syrian information operation. The Syrian Foreign Minister had refused to answer substantive questions from his Lebanese counterpart over four or five contacts in a week, limiting himself to minor specific grievances like the temporary arrest of three Syrians on June 6. But in Damascus, visiting Lebanese politicians — including the Maronite Raymond Eddé, the Abdullah Yafi group, and Arab League Secretary-General Mahmoud Riad — were being told by top Syrian officials that the Lebanese government was preparing another armed attack to liquidate the fedayeen.

The Embassy's assessment was that this was a pretext-manufacturing operation. The Syrian allegation — that Lebanon was planning to liquidate the fedayeen — could serve either as justification for subsequent Syrian military action, or as a means to convince the fedayeen they were genuinely threatened and drive them into preemptive action of their own. The cable names this mechanism. It does not wait for scholarly retrospective to identify the pattern.

The diplomatic ask

Sadaqa asked the United States to raise the Lebanese-Syrian-fedayeen question with the Soviet Union. The Lebanese government explicitly did not intend to raise it with the Soviet Ambassador in Beirut — because, Sadaqa said, the Lebanese had learned the hard way that they could not place any stock in what Ambassador Azimov said. Soviet words and Soviet deeds, in the Lebanese assessment, did not correspond.

He coupled this with a direct request: urgent U.S. weapons for the Lebanese Army. The intelligence dossier and the arms request were delivered in the same meeting. The cable captures them in the same text. The connection between them was not rhetorical but operational: the Lebanese state, facing the arms flow and political payments documented in the preceding paragraphs, was asking the United States for matching military assistance.

What the record shows

This cable is the pre-war Lebanese financial and logistical record. It documents, on the factual level, what the political-assessment cables (1973BEIRUT05437, 1973STATE086221) described at the level of judgment: a coordinated Syrian-Palestinian-Soviet-Iraqi system of arms and money flowing through Lebanon to destabilize Lebanese state sovereignty. The recipients were named. The amounts were specified. The paymaster — Abu Jihad — was identified. The ports and border crossings were located.

None of this appears in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon. It is in the documentary record because a Lebanese Secretary General read it aloud to a U.S. Chargé on the morning of June 8, 1973, and the Chargé's cable preserved it.

cables.subject: Trouble Ahead for Lebanon
cables.excerpt: Nine days before Israeli-Syrian disengagement, addressed to Kissinger's travel party: Israeli retaliation policy is counterproductive. It killed three Lebanese children on May 21, radicalized Fatah moderates, pushed Maronite deputies to call for Soviet SAMs, and was closing the one mechanism (1973-style GOL-fedayeen confrontation) by which the Lebanese state might have constrained the armed Palestinian presence. Iraq and Libya would try to derail disengagement through Lebanon.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified SECRET / LIMDIS · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Jerusalem copy for Secretary Kissinger's travel party

Summary
Repeated Israeli attacks on targets in Lebanon, in the context of an announced Israeli hard line toward Palestinians, have caused significant casualties among non-combatant Palestinians and Lebanese civilians, as well as some losses among fedayeen.[1] The result to date has been to increase Palestinian anger toward Israel, increase Lebanese popular resentment against Israel and the GOL, and increase the problems for the GOL — but not to bring any visible movement by the GOL toward the possibility of armed confrontation with the fedayeen. The GOL anticipates further increase in its problems with Palestinians and Israel after the Israeli–Syrian disengagement agreement,[2] and is consulting with other Arab governments in search of support.

Although we can understand the reasons for present Israeli policy regarding the fedayeen, Palestinians and Lebanon, we do not believe it will prove any more effective than it has in the past, and its counter-productivity will increase. We therefore suggest that at an appropriate time the USG might wish to discuss the entire question with the GOI.

1. The Israeli signal
The Israeli naval attack on the Palestinian refugee camp near Tyre on May 19, the speeches of May 20 by Mrs. Meir, Dayan and Begin,[3] and the Israeli air attacks of May 21 appear to the Lebanese as a clear signal that the GOI, in the aftermath of Ma’alot,[4] has taken a firm decision to return to the policy adopted after Munich but abandoned by mid-1973 of striking “terrorists” wherever they are found — using a variety of methods including strikes on refugee camps which, as in 1972–73, almost always produce no military results but a large number of innocent victims among Palestinians and often among Lebanese. As a result, the strong impression left with Palestinians is that “the only good Palestinian is a dead one.”[5] The Lebanese population is angry at both Israel and the GOL. While basic antipathy toward the fedayeen remains, many Lebanese now feel sorry for them.

2. Doubts as to efficacy
Although we can understand why GOI leaders may believe they have no choice but to make statements such as those of May 20, and to follow an aggressive policy of taking the attack to the fedayeen, our doubts as to the efficacy of this sort of action vis-à-vis the fedayeen in Lebanon and the GOL and Army remain as stated in Beirut 5573. This applies particularly to rather indiscriminate attacks on refugee camps, Lebanese border villages, and sometimes fedayeen encampments near villages.

3. Militancy up, moderation down
The net short-term effect of recent Israeli attacks on refugee camps and other targets, and of official GOI statements regarding terrorists, appears to have been: increased militancy on the part of fedayeen leaders, including those from the more moderate Fatah organization;[6] decline of moderate influence; and somewhat more aggressive reaction of the Lebanese Army in replying to IDF attacks and/or border incursions. This reflects the present mood of political leaders, since even Maronite deputies are calling for acquisition of the Soviet SAM air defense system.[7] Recent Israeli overflights of Beirut have been regularly greeted by anti-aircraft fire where before there was usually none.

The sea attack on Rachidiyeh camp[8] was met by return fire from all available Lebanese artillery, apparently with intent to hit the attacking vessels if at all possible. IDF patrols moving in Lebanese territory in the Arkub area also seem to be receiving more and closer fire from the Lebanese Army, whose units now appear to be nearer to the border and in greater strength than in the recent past. The IDF, as is its custom when fired upon from whatever source, is responding in kind and taking closer aim; and in the most recent incident on May 20 near Chebaa in Arkub, they lightly wounded five Lebanese soldiers.

4. Civilian casualties and the absence of “May 1973” dynamic
IAF attacks on May 21, on targets apparently believed to be fedayeen camps in Arkub and near Tyre in southwest Lebanon, caused few casualties among fedayeen and Palestinians (most of whom have moved from their old haunts since the IAF began wide-ranging strikes after Kiryat Shmona) but did result in the death of three Lebanese children, with three children and two elderly persons seriously wounded and fifteen other Lebanese civilians less seriously wounded.[9] The hostility of the local populace — many of whom have also left their homes as a result of constant Israeli shelling and air attacks — has not to date produced any sign that the GOL might be forced into armed confrontation with the fedayeen such as occurred in May 1973.[10] Quite to the contrary, we see signs of momentary improved fedayeen–Lebanese Army relations.

5. What comes next
The GOL is aware of the likelihood Lebanon will face still greater problems from Israel, the fedayeen, and radical Arab states (i.e., Iraq and Libya) following the Israeli–Syrian disengagement agreement. The government fears that under present circumstances the fedayeen will feel they have no choice but to step up actions against Israel, concentrating where possible on inside operations.[11] Israeli policy of retaliation is already tougher than it has been since right after the Munich (and Lod) tragedies. And Iraq and Libya will in all probability be using their political, human, and financial resources to encourage the fedayeen to attack Israel and take an intransigent attitude regarding political settlement. Their objective would be to create enough trouble between Israel, Palestinians and Lebanon to threaten the disengagement agreement and the Geneva Conference.[12]

6. Arab consultations
In anticipation of this onslaught, the GOL is beginning to consult closely with other Arab governments to see what support it can find — beginning with the meeting of Arab League Defense and Foreign Ministers which just ended in Cairo.[13] We shall try to keep abreast of the progress of GOL consultations, and of problems which develop inside Lebanon. We would appreciate information which other addressees might be able to develop on this, particularly Cairo, Damascus, and Jidda.

7. Recommendation
In view of the foregoing, we recommend discussion at an appropriate time and level with the GOI of its intentions regarding the fedayeen, Palestinians, and Lebanon. As noted above, and borne out in the past, the apparent Israeli policy of repeated attacks on targets in Lebanon is unlikely to have any positive effect on what Arab terrorists do inside Israel, but is likely to have a negative effect on Palestinians, Lebanese, and perhaps other Arab states — resulting in increased terrorism in Israel.[14]

GODLEY[15]

SUBJECT: TROUBLE AHEAD FOR LEBANON

SUMMARY: REPEATED ISRAELI ATTACKS ON TARGETS IN LEBANON IN CONTEXT
ANNOUNCED ISRAELI HARD LINE TOWARD PALESTINIANS HAVE CAUSED SIGNIFICANT
CASUALTIES AMONG NON-COMBATTANT PALESTINIANS AND LEBANESE CIVILIANS AS
WELL AS SOME LOSSES AMONG FEDAYEEN. RESULT TO DATE HAS BEEN TO INCREASE
PALESTINIAN ANGER TOWARD ISRAEL, AND INCREASE LEBANESE POPULAR RESENTMENT
VS. ISRAEL, AND GOL, AND INCREASE IN PROBLEMS FOR GOL BUT NOT RPT NOT TO
BRING ANY VISIBLE MOVEMENT BY GOL TOWARD POSSIBILITY OF ARMED
CONFRONTATION WITH FEDAYEEN. GOL ANTICIPATES FURTHER INCREASE IN ITS
PROBLEMS WITH PALESTINIANS AND ISRAEL AFTER ISRAELI-SYRIAN DISENGAGEMENT
AGREEMENT AND IS CONSULTING WITH OTHER ARAB GOVTS. IN SEARCH OF SUPPORT.
ALTHOUGH WE CAN UNDERSTAND REASONS FOR PRESENT ISRAELI POLICY RE
FEDAYEEN, PALESTINIANS AND LEBANON, WE DO NOT BELIEVE IT WILL PROVE ANY
MORE EFFECTIVE THAN IT HAS IN PAST AND ITS COUNTER-PRODUCTIVITY WILL
INCREASE. THEREFORE WE SUGGEST THAT AT APPROPRIATE TIME USG MIGHT WISH
DISCUSS ENTIRE QUESTION WITH GOI. END SUMMARY.

1. ISRAELI NAVAL ATTACK ON PALESTINIAN REFUGEE CAMP NEAR TYR ON MAY 19,
SPEECHES MAY 20 BY MRS. MEIR, DAYAN AND BEGIN AND ISRAELI AIR ATTACKS OF
MAY 21 APPEAR TO LEBANESE AS CLEAR SIGNAL THAT GOI, IN AFTERMATH OF
MA'ALOT, HAS TAKEN FIRM DECISION TO POLICY ADOPTED AFTER MUNICH BUT
ABANDONED BY MID-1973 OF STRIKING "TERRORISTS" WHEREVER THEY ARE FOUND,
USING VARIETY METHODS INCLUDING STRIKES ON REFUGEE CAMPS WHICH, AS IN
1972-73, ALMOST ALWAYS PRODUCE NO MILITARY RESULTS BUT LARGE NUMBER
INNOCENT VICTIMS AMONG PALESTINIANS AND OFTEN AMONG LEBANESE. AS RESULT
STRONG IMPRESSION LEFT WITH PALESTINIANS IS THAT ONLY GOOD PALESTINIAN
IS DEAD ONE. LEBANESE POPULATION ANGRY AT ISRAEL, AND GOL. WHILE BASIC
ANTIPATHY TOWARD FEDAYEEN REMAINS MANY LEBANESE NOW FEEL SORRY FOR THEM.

2. ALTHOUGH WE CAN UNDERSTAND WHY GOI LEADERS MAY BELIEVE THEY HAVE NO
CHOICE BUT TO MAKE STATEMENTS SUCH AS THOSE OF MAY 20, AND TO FOLLOW
AGGRESSIVE POLICY OF TAKING ATTACK TO FEDAYEEN, OUR DOUBTS AS TO EFFICACY
OF THIS SORT OF ACTION VIS-A-VIS FEDAYEEN IN LEBANON AND GOL AND ARMY
REMAIN AS STATED BEIRUT 5573. THIS APPLIES PARTICULARLY TO RATHER
INDISCRIMINATE ATTACKS ON REFUGEE CAMPS, LEBANESE BORDER VILLAGES AND
SOMETIMES FEDAYEEN ENCAMPMENTS NEAR VILLAGES.

3. NET SHORT-TERM EFFECT OF RECENT ISRAELI ATTACKS ON REFUGEE CAMPS AND
OTHER TARGETS AND OFFICIAL GOI STATEMENTS RE TERRORISTS APPEARS TO HAVE
BEEN INCREASED MILITANCY ON PART FEDAYEEN LEADERS, INCLUDING THOSE FROM
MORE MODERATE FATAH ORGANIZATION, DECLINE OF MODERATE INFLUENCE, AND
SOMEWHAT MORE AGGRESSIVE REACTION OF LEBANESE ARMY IN REPLYING TO IDF
ATTACKS AND/OR BORDER INCURSIONS. THIS REFLECTS PRESENT MOOD OF POLITICAL
LEADERS, SINCE EVEN MARONITE DEPUTIES ARE CALLING FOR ACQUISITION SOV SAM
AIR DEFENSE SYSTEM. RECENT ISRAELI OVERFLIGHTS OF BEIRUT HAVE BEEN
REGULARLY GREETED BY ANTI-AIRCRAFT FIRE WHEN BEFORE THERE WAS USUALLY
NONE. SEA ATTACK ON RACHIDIYEH CAMP WAS MET BY RETURN FIRE FROM ALL
AVAILABLE LEBANESE ARTILLERY, APPARENTLY WITH INTENT HIT ATTACKING
VESSELS IF AT ALL POSSIBLE. IDF PATROLS MOVING IN LEBANESE TERRITORY IN
ARKUB AREA ALSO SEEM BE RECEIVING MORE AND CLOSER FIRE FROM LEBANESE
ARMY WHOSE UNITS NOW APPEAR TO BE NEARER TO BORDER AND IN GREATER
STRENGTH THAN RECENT PAST. IDF, AS IS ITS CUSTOM WHEN FIRED UPON FROM
WHATEVER SOURCE, IS RESPONDING IN KIND AND TAKING CLOSER AIM, AND IN
MOST RECENT INCIDENT ON MAY 20 NEAR CHEBAA IN ARKUB, LIGHTLY WOUNDED
FIVE LEBANESE SOLDIERS.

4. IAF MAY 21 ATTACKS ON TARGETS WHICH APPARENTLY BELIEVED TO BE FEDAYEEN
CAMPS IN ARKUB AND NEAR TYR IN SOUTHWEST LEBANON CAUSED FEW CASUALTIES
AMONG FEDAYEEN AND PALESTINIANS (MOST OF WHOM HAVE MOVED FROM OLD HAUNTS
SINCE IAF BEGAN WIDE-RANGING STRIKES AFTER KIRYAT SHIMONA) BUT DID
RESULT IN DEATH OF THREE LEBANESE CHILDREN, WITH THREE CHILDREN AND TWO
OLD PERSONS SERIOUSLY WOUNDED AND FIFTEEN OTHER LEBANESE CIVILIANS LESS
SERIOUSLY WOUNDED. HOSTILITY OF LOCAL POPULACE, MANY OF WHOM HAVE ALSO
LEFT THEIR HOMES AS RESULT CONSTANT ISRAELI SHELLING AND AIR ATTACKS,
HAS NOT TO DATE PRODUCED ANY SIGN THAT GOL MIGHT BE FORCED INTO ARMED
CONFRONTATION WITH FEDAYEEN SUCH AS OCCURRED IN MAY 1973. QUITE TO THE
CONTRARY WE SEE SIGNS OF MOMENTARY IMPROVED FEDAYEEN LEBANESE ARMY
RELATIONS.

5. GOL IS AWARE OF LIKELIHOOD LEBANON WILL FACE STILL GREATER PROBLEMS
FROM ISRAEL, FEDAYEEN AND RADICAL ARAB STATES (I.E., IRAQ AND LIBYA)
FOLLOWING ISRAELI-SYRIAN DISENGAGEMENT AGREEMENT. GOVT. FEARS THAT UNDER
PRESENT CIRCUMSTANCES FEDAYEEN WILL FEEL THEY HAVE NO CHOICE BUT TO
STEP-UP ACTIONS VS. ISRAEL, CONCENTRATING WHERE POSSIBLE ON INSIDE
OPERATIONS. ISRAELI POLICY OF RETALIATION ALREADY TOUGHER THAN IT HAS
BEEN SINCE RIGHT AFTER MUNICH (AND LOD) TRAGEDIES. AND IRAQ AND LIBYA
WILL IN ALL PROBABILITY BE USING THEIR POLITICAL, HUMAN AND FINANCIAL
RESOURCES ENCOURAGE FEDAYEEN TO ATTACK ISRAEL AND TAKE INTRANSIGENT
ATTITUDE RE POLITICAL SETTLEMENT. THEIR OBJECTIVE WOULD BE TO CREATE
ENOUGH TROUBLE BETWEEN ISRAEL, PALESTINIANS AND LEBANON TO THREATEN
DISENGAGEMENT AGREEMENT AND GENEVA CONFERENCE.

6. IN ANTICIPATION OF THIS ONSLAUGHT, GOL IS BEGINNING CONSULT CLOSELY
WITH OTHER ARAB GOVTS. TO SEE WHAT SUPPORT IT CAN FIND, BEGINNING WITH
MEETING OF ARAB LEAGUE DEFENSE AND FOREIGN MINISTERS WHICH JUST ENDED
IN CAIRO. WE SHALL TRY KEEP ABREAST OF PROGRESS GOL CONSULTATIONS, AND
OF PROBLEMS WHICH DEVELOP INSIDE LEBANON. WE WOULD APPRECIATE INFO WHICH
OTHER ADDRESSEES MIGHT BE ABLE DEVELOP ON THIS, PARTICULARLY CAIRO,
DAMASCUS AND JIDDA.

7. VIEW FOREGOING RECOMMEND DISCUSSION AT APPROPRIATE TIME AND LEVEL
WITH GOI OF ITS INTENTIONS RE FEDAYEEN, PALESTINIANS AND LEBANON. AS
NOTED ABOVE, AND BORNE OUT IN PAST, APPARENT ISRAELI POLICY OF REPEATED
ATTACKS ON TARGETS IN LEBANON UNLIKELY HAVE ANY POSITIVE EFFECT ON WHAT
ARAB TERRORISTS DO INSIDE ISRAEL BUT IS LIKELY HAVE NEGATIVE EFFECT ON
PALESTINIANS, LEBANESE AND PERHAPS OTHER ARAB STATES RESULTING IN
INCREASED TERRORISM IN ISRAEL.

GODLEY
