footnotes: This cable marks a shift in the Embassy's reporting frame. The 1973 cables were preoccupied with fedayeen/Syrian pressure on the Lebanese state. This May 1974 cable inverts the lens: the primary pressure on the Lebanese state is now coming from Israeli retaliation. The civilian casualty pattern — documented here with specific numbers — had altered Lebanese public sentiment toward the Palestinians from antipathy to sympathy, and toward Israel from baseline hostility to active anger. The cable's title, "Trouble Ahead for Lebanon," marks this shift.

Israeli-Syrian Disengagement Agreement: signed May 31, 1974, nine days after this cable was filed, on the Golan Heights front. Brokered by Secretary Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy following the October 1973 Yom Kippur War. The agreement separated Israeli and Syrian forces, established a UN buffer zone (UNDOF), and reduced the risk of conventional war on the Syrian front. The cable anticipates — correctly — that Israeli military resources freed from the Syrian border would enable a more aggressive policy toward Palestinian armed activity based in Lebanon, and that radical Arab states (Iraq, Libya) would work to derail the agreement by provoking Israeli-Palestinian-Lebanese instability.

The May 20 speeches by Golda Meir (Prime Minister), Moshe Dayan (Defense Minister), and Menachem Begin (Opposition Leader): coming two days after the May 18 IDF attack on Palestinian positions near Tyre and two days before the Ma'alot attack response. These speeches publicly articulated what the Embassy frames as a return to the post-Munich policy of striking Palestinian armed targets "wherever they are found." The cable's characterization — that this policy had been "abandoned by mid-1973" — is significant: it implies an Israeli strategic recalibration in mid-1973 that lasted approximately ten months before being reversed after Ma'alot.

Ma'alot: the Ma'alot massacre of May 15, 1974. Three members of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) crossed from Lebanon into northern Israel, entered a school in the town of Ma'alot where students were on an overnight field trip, and took 105 hostages. In the Israeli rescue operation, 22 students and four others were killed. The attack prompted an immediate Israeli military response against Palestinian targets in southern Lebanon, including the May 19 naval attack referenced here. Ma'alot is the direct proximate cause of the Israeli policy recalibration documented in this cable.

"The only good Palestinian is a dead one" — the Embassy's stark characterization of the message that Palestinians (and, the cable implies, Lebanese observers) drew from the May 1974 Israeli posture. This is a quotation-marked phrase not attributed to a specific Israeli official; the cable is reporting the interpretive impression created by Israeli actions and statements. The quotation marks are doing the work of distancing the U.S. Embassy from endorsing the characterization while recording that this is how the actions were being received by their immediate audience.

"Including those from the more moderate Fatah organization": this is a notable assessment from the U.S. Embassy in 1974, characterizing Fatah as "more moderate" relative to other PLO factions (DFLP, PFLP, PFLP-GC, Sa'iqa). The specific attribution of rising militancy even within Fatah — attributed to Israeli attacks rather than to internal radicalization — complicates the reading that Fatah was uniformly disposed to negotiation. It documents the mechanism by which Israeli retaliation strengthened PLO hardliners against moderates.

"Even Maronite deputies are calling for acquisition of the Soviet SAM air defense system": this sentence captures a significant political shift. Maronite Christian deputies — typically the political bloc most aligned with Western powers and most hostile to the fedayeen — were, by May 1974, publicly calling for Soviet air defense missile systems as a response to Israeli overflights of Beirut. The request is doubly revealing: it documents the depth of Lebanese national feeling against Israeli airspace violations, and it documents how that feeling was transcending the normal sectarian political alignments. The Maronites were not abandoning their pro-Western posture in general, but the direct experience of Israeli overflights was producing policy preferences that would have been unthinkable a year earlier.

Rachidiyeh camp: Palestinian refugee camp in southern Lebanon, south of Tyre. The May 19, 1974 Israeli naval attack on Rachidiyeh is one of the Israeli actions this cable identifies as triggering the Lebanese Army's shift toward more aggressive return fire against IDF operations.

The casualty figures — three Lebanese children killed, three children and two elderly persons seriously wounded, fifteen other Lebanese civilians less seriously wounded — are specific. The cable notes that fedayeen had "moved from their old haunts" after the IAF began wide-ranging strikes post-Kiryat Shmona (April 1974), meaning the May 21 strikes hit targets the fedayeen had already evacuated. The military effect was negligible; the civilian effect was substantial. This pattern — Israeli strikes on evacuated targets producing primarily civilian casualties — is the factual basis for the cable's judgment that the policy is "counter-productive."

"Has not to date produced any sign that the GOL might be forced into armed confrontation with the fedayeen such as occurred in May 1973" — the cable explicitly contrasts May 1974 with May 1973. The key distinction: in 1973, fedayeen provocations led the Lebanese Army to confront them; in 1974, Israeli attacks on Palestinian camps and Lebanese villages were producing solidarity between Lebanese civilians and fedayeen, closing rather than opening the path to Lebanese state action against the armed Palestinian presence. This is a structurally important shift in the pre-war dynamic.

"Inside operations": attacks on targets inside Israel itself, as distinct from cross-border raids or attacks on Israeli targets outside Israel. The cable anticipates — correctly — that the fedayeen would respond to intensified Israeli pressure by shifting toward more inside-Israel operations. The Kiryat Shmona attack (April 11, 1974) and Ma'alot attack (May 15, 1974) were both inside-Israel operations; more would follow. The pattern the cable identifies — Israeli pressure → increased inside-operations → more Israeli pressure → further destabilization of Lebanon — is a feedback loop the Embassy names in May 1974.

The assessment that Iraq and Libya would try to derail the disengagement agreement and Geneva Conference by creating trouble between Israel, the Palestinians, and Lebanon is stated here as prospective. The Geneva Conference (held December 1973, suspended thereafter) was the framework through which Kissinger hoped to consolidate post-war Arab-Israeli diplomacy; Iraq and Libya opposed it as Arab "rejectionist" states. The cable documents the Embassy's understanding that Lebanon's internal stability was an instrument for radical Arab opposition to regional peace efforts — not an incidental casualty of Palestinian armed activity.

The Arab League Defense and Foreign Ministers meeting in Cairo that "just ended" at the time of this cable was the precursor to the Arab Defense Council meeting documented in cable 1974BEIRUT07889 (July 9, 1974). The Lebanese diplomatic sequence — consult with Arab states in May, attend formal ADC meeting in July, manage the outcome — is the Lebanese state's attempt to construct Arab cover for its refusal to confront the fedayeen militarily, paired with its refusal to accept the terms under which other Arab states (particularly Kuwait) were prepared to provide support.

The cable's recommendation that the U.S. raise the entire question with the Government of Israel is notable for what it does not say. It does not condemn Israeli policy. It explicitly concedes that Israeli leaders "may believe they have no choice." What it does is pose the efficacy question: does the policy actually reduce terrorism? The Embassy's answer is that it does not, and that its negative externalities — Palestinian radicalization, Lebanese state destabilization, threat to disengagement and Geneva — outweigh its deterrent value. The recommendation is measured: raise the question "at an appropriate time and level." This is a diplomatic hedge; the substantive judgment is that the policy is harmful.

G. McMurtrie Godley: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon from June 1974 to July 1976, succeeding Ambassador William Buffum (who had served briefly after Houghton's 1974 departure). Godley's signature on this May 22 cable — before his formal arrival in June 1974 — likely reflects his imminent posting. Godley had previously served as Ambassador to Laos during the peak of U.S. covert operations in Southeast Asia. His tenure in Beirut would span the full period of the outbreak and first-year escalation of the Lebanese Civil War, beginning April 13, 1975.

readerNarrative.headline: Trouble Ahead for Lebanon: The Embassy Warns Kissinger
readerNarrative.subheadline: Filed May 22, 1974 — nine days before the Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement and addressed to Secretary Kissinger's traveling party in Jerusalem — this SECRET cable tells the U.S. government that Israeli retaliation against Palestinian targets in Lebanon is counterproductive: producing dead Lebanese children, radicalizing Fatah moderates, pushing even Maronite deputies to demand Soviet SAMs, and threatening the disengagement agreement itself. And warns what comes after disengagement: Iraq and Libya will work to derail it through Lebanon.
readerNarrative.summary: On May 22, 1974 — one week after the Ma'alot attack, three days after the Israeli naval strike on Rachidiyeh camp, one day after Israeli air strikes killed three Lebanese children, and nine days before the Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement was signed — the U.S. Embassy in Beirut filed a SECRET/LIMDIS cable addressed partly to Secretary Kissinger's travel party in Jerusalem. The message: Israeli retaliation policy is not working. It is producing civilian casualties, radicalizing Fatah moderates, strengthening Iraqi and Libyan hands, and creating a feedback loop in which every Israeli strike pushes the fedayeen toward inside-Israel operations that provoke the next Israeli strike. The cable warns that after disengagement, Iraq and Libya will work to derail it by creating Israeli-Palestinian-Lebanese trouble. It recommends a U.S. conversation with the Government of Israel about its entire policy toward Lebanon. The cable is signed GODLEY — the ambassador who would be in post when the civil war began 11 months later.
keyRevelations: Israeli air strikes on May 21, 1974 killed three Lebanese children and wounded seventeen more Lebanese civilians, while producing few fedayeen casualties because the targets had been evacuated after Kiryat Shmona. The Embassy assessed the pattern as “counter-productive.”
Even Maronite deputies — Lebanon's most pro-Western political bloc — were publicly calling for acquisition of Soviet SAM air defense systems in response to Israeli overflights of Beirut.

The Embassy identified a feedback loop: Israeli retaliation → Palestinian radicalization (even within Fatah's moderate wing) → more inside-Israel operations → more Israeli retaliation → destabilization of Lebanon.
The cable explicitly warned that Iraq and Libya would try to derail the Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement and Geneva Conference by fomenting Israeli-Palestinian-Lebanese conflict.

The title — “Trouble Ahead for Lebanon” — is the cable's own word. And the recommendation, addressed implicitly to Secretary Kissinger, was: raise the entire question with the Government of Israel at an appropriate level.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The week Lebanon changed

In the seven days before this cable was filed, the Lebanese situation was transformed. On May 15, Palestinian militants crossed from southern Lebanon into northern Israel and took over 100 hostages at a school in Ma'alot; 22 students died in the rescue. On May 19, Israeli naval forces attacked a Palestinian refugee camp near Tyre. On May 20, Golda Meir, Moshe Dayan, and Menachem Begin publicly announced a return to the post-Munich policy of striking "terrorists" wherever they were found. On May 21, Israeli air strikes hit Arkub and targets near Tyre — killing three Lebanese children and wounding seventeen other Lebanese civilians. The fedayeen camps had been largely evacuated after the April 11 Kiryat Shmona attack.

On May 22, the U.S. Embassy in Beirut filed this cable. It was SECRET, LIMDIS, addressed to the Secretary of State, to the Defense Intelligence Agency, and — unusually — to the American Consul in Jerusalem "for Secretary's party." Secretary Kissinger was in the region conducting shuttle diplomacy; the Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement was nine days away. The Embassy wanted Lebanon on the agenda.

What had shifted

The cable's structural insight is that the Israeli policy of retaliation against Palestinian targets in Lebanon was not producing its intended deterrent effect — and was producing unintended strategic consequences that would make the broader regional situation worse.

Specifically: Israeli strikes were producing few fedayeen casualties, because the fedayeen had evacuated after the April Kiryat Shmona attacks. They were producing substantial civilian casualties, including dead Lebanese children. They were producing Lebanese solidarity with the Palestinians — such that "many Lebanese now feel sorry for them," even among populations that retained basic antipathy toward the fedayeen. And they were producing a specific political signal: Maronite deputies, the most pro-Western bloc in Lebanese politics, were openly calling for acquisition of Soviet SAM air defense systems. A year earlier this would have been unthinkable.

The Fatah moderation problem

A crucial passage: the Embassy documented increased militancy on the part of fedayeen leaders "including those from the more moderate Fatah organization." The frame — Fatah as the moderate PLO faction, relative to DFLP, PFLP, PFLP-GC, and Sa'iqa — was the U.S. Embassy's operating assessment in 1974. The observation that Israeli attacks were pushing Fatah moderates toward militancy, not just the already-radical factions, identified a mechanism by which Israeli policy was actively strengthening PLO hardliners against the figures within Fatah most potentially amenable to negotiation.

The May 1973 contrast

The most important single sentence in the cable, analytically, is the one explicitly contrasting May 1974 with May 1973:

"The hostility of the local populace has not to date produced any sign that the GOL might be forced into armed confrontation with the fedayeen such as occurred in May 1973. Quite to the contrary we see signs of momentary improved fedayeen-Lebanese Army relations."

In May 1973, Palestinian provocations had driven the Lebanese Army into confrontation with the fedayeen. In May 1974, Israeli attacks on Palestinian camps and Lebanese villages were producing the opposite pattern: Lebanese-Palestinian solidarity and improved fedayeen-Army relations. The path to Lebanese state action against the armed Palestinian presence — fragile in 1973 — was closing in 1974. Israeli retaliation policy was, inadvertently, shutting off the one mechanism by which the Lebanese state might have been able to constrain the fedayeen.

After disengagement

The cable's second analytical insight is prospective. The Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement, to be signed May 31, would reduce the strategic demands on Israeli forces on the Golan front. More Israeli military attention and resources would become available for the Lebanese frontier. At the same time, radical Arab states — Iraq and Libya — would have motive and means to derail the agreement by fomenting Israeli-Palestinian-Lebanese conflict. Their objective, the Embassy assessed, would be to threaten not just disengagement but the Geneva Conference framework.

The fedayeen, under pressure, would turn increasingly to inside-Israel operations — the cable uses exactly this phrase. And inside-Israel operations would produce further Israeli retaliation. The feedback loop was, by May 1974, self-reinforcing.

The recommendation

The Embassy's recommendation was measured. Not condemnation. Not a demand. A suggestion: that the United States Government, at an appropriate time and level, raise the entire question with the Government of Israel. Did the policy actually reduce terrorism inside Israel? The Embassy's judgment was that it did not — that it was likely to increase terrorism inside Israel — and that its harmful effects on Palestinians, Lebanese, and the broader Arab world outweighed the deterrent case for it.

The cable was addressed, in part, to Kissinger's party in Jerusalem because the Secretary was at that moment negotiating the regional peace architecture that the dynamics documented here would undermine. The Embassy's question, in diplomatic form, was whether the United States would use its leverage with Israel on Lebanon while it still had that leverage. The record of the subsequent 11 months — through April 13, 1975 — does not suggest that the question was pressed.

cables.subject: Arab Defense Council Meeting
cables.excerpt: SECRET/EXDIS/NOFORN readout of the July 3-4, 1974 Arab Defense Council meeting in Cairo, given by Presidential Adviser Dib. Kuwait's FM circulated a draft treating the PLO and Lebanon as equal claimants on LL 50 million defense funding each. The Kuwaiti questioned Lebanon's 'Arab' status; PM Solh threatened to walk. Privately the Kuwaiti FM admitted the PLO had threatened his life. Sa'iqa leader Mohsen, believed personally profiting from Kuwaiti money, led the attacks. Syria's Khaddam — provocateur in 1973 — moderated.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified SECRET / EXDIS / NOFORN · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Two sections transmitted as separate cables (BEIRUT 7889 01-02 of 02)

Summary
A high-ranking GOL source who was present at the Arab Defense Council (ADC) meeting in Cairo has confirmed our impression that the GOL successfully managed to deflect offers of Arab military assistance.[1] He also provided some interesting insights into the positions adopted by the various Arab delegations.

1. The readout meeting
We called yesterday afternoon, July 8, on Presidential Adviser Boutros Dib,[2] who accompanied Prime Minister Takieddine Solh,[3] Foreign Minister Naffah, and Minister of Defense Maalouf to Cairo for the Arab Defense Council meeting July 3–4. We complimented Dib on the meeting’s outcome, since from press accounts it appeared that the Lebanese objective of not accepting all-out Arab military assistance had been achieved while at the same time maintaining Lebanon’s position in the Arab world. Dib said that the Lebanese had succeeded, but that it had involved acrimonious and often extremely tough exchanges with Arab colleagues.

2. The Kuwaiti draft
The principal problem, and a rather unexpected one, was the position of Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sabah,[4] who, prior to the plenary session July 3, had circulated a draft resolution which treated the PLO and GOL on an equal footing and which provided for 50 million Lebanese pounds to be accorded each to the GOL and the PLO on an equal basis for defense.[5] The Kuwaiti representative appeared to the GOL delegation to be “more PLO than the PLO,” and he led the hard-line Arabs in subsequent discussions. The Kuwaiti position was particularly resented by the Lebanese — for, according to the latter, the Kuwaitis showed total disregard for Lebanese sovereignty and all that the GOL had done for the PLO, as well as the sufferings borne by the Lebanese due to this “hospitality.”

In pre-plenary discussions the Lebanese rejected Kuwait’s position, arguing not only Lebanese sovereignty but also the fact that Kuwaiti generosity to the PLO would jeopardize the current fragile peace along the border and result in Israeli reprisals.[6] The Kuwaiti representative at one point questioned Lebanese “Arab” status, to which Prime Minister Takieddine Solh replied that if this assertion were not withdrawn immediately, the Lebanese would not attend the ADC meeting. As a result, the Kuwaiti representative withdrew his paper.

3. Plenary and closed sessions
The plenary session on the afternoon of July 3 was, according to Dib, relatively anodyne, with each delegation making anticipated public statements. The ensuing closed sessions, at which only delegation chiefs (Foreign Ministers and/or Ministers of Defense) were present, were, however, acrimonious. They coincided with working meetings, either with all delegations represented or in smaller groups.

4. Delegation-by-delegation behavior
Dib described the behavior of the various delegations along the following lines:

Egyptians were gracious hosts, saying relatively little but showing understanding of the Lebanese position.

Syrians were most helpful in supporting the GOL position. Foreign Minister Khaddam[7] acted wisely and, on several occasions, as moderator between the GOL and the Sa’iqa representative Mohsen.[8]

Sa’iqa delegation, led by Muhsen, was particularly violent, supporting the Kuwaitis and frequently attacking the Lebanese. (As noted REFTEL, Muhsen has continued to criticize the GOL since returning from Cairo.) Dib said the GOL delegation was convinced that Muhsen personally profited immensely from “Kuwaiti generosity”.[9]

Kuwaiti delegation, in addition to what is indicated above, appeared, according to Dib, terrified of the PLO. At an initial private discussion, the Kuwaiti representative, when challenged by the Lebanese regarding the relative status of Palestinians in Lebanon versus Kuwait, stated that his life had been threatened by the PLO and gave every appearance of permitting this threat to govern his actions.[10]

Algerian delegation under Bouteflika’s leadership[11] showed great statesmanship as a moderating element. On one occasion, however, Bouteflika advanced a lengthy legal argument regarding PLO rights having been accepted at the UN, but he formally withdrew his comments when attacked by Naffah, the GOL Foreign Minister.

Iraqi and Libyan delegations caused no great problems for the GOL in that most of their venom appeared directed against the Syrians and Egyptians for having agreed to disengagement.[12] Dib said the GOL delegation was surprised by the degree of their vehemence, which the Syrians and Egyptians handled in the most dignified manner.

5. The Saudi delegation
The Saudi Arabian delegation was headed by the Saudi Chief of Staff and Representative to the Arab League. The absence of Saudi Minister of Defense Sultan at the outset caused the GOL delegation some concern, but their concern was somewhat mollified when informed that Sultan was probably absent to save his punch for some later occasion, should the meeting turn out badly.[13]

6. GOL delegation internals
Dib said that the GOL delegation was in total harmony, and that the non-Muslims — e.g., Foreign Minister Naffah and Minister of Defense Maalouf — took pains to protect Muslim Prime Minister Solh from attacks by other Arabs.[14] Solh behaved most effectively, particularly as he was smarting from early Kuwaiti attacks that the GOL was not behaving as an Arab state.

7. The “Secret Resolutions”
The final “Secret Resolutions,” according to Dib, contained three clauses which were totally acceptable to the GOL:

(A) Diplomatic pressure would be brought on the “Great Powers” — i.e., the U.S. — to persuade Israel not to continue action against Lebanon. (In this connection Dib pointed out that fedayeen activity from Lebanon should cease.)

(B) Unspecified aid would be accorded the GOL in its efforts to improve its defensive position. (Dib commented that Minister of Defense Maalouf pointed out that Lebanon’s LL 2.2 billion defense program over the next five years was a big burden on the GOL but it would be met. If other states desired to contribute to this program, assistance would of course be most welcome provided no strings attached.)[15]

(C) The Council agreed that the PLO represented the Palestinian people and that it would be supported in its struggle to regain its homeland. Dib emphasized that this had already been agreed to at Algiers[16] and that there was no specific reference to material or financial assistance to the PLO in Lebanon.

8. Caveat
We recognize the foregoing is obviously one-sided. We believe, however, that the atmospherics set forth above might be in interest, and it is a relatively accurate description of the Lebanese delegation’s views and impressions of the meeting. Repeatedly Dib emphasized the sensitivity of the foregoing and requested that it not only be strictly NOFORN but used only on a need-to-know basis.[17]

GODLEY

1. SUMMARY: HIGH-RANKING GOL SOURCE WHO PRESENT AT ARAB DEFENSE COUNCIL
(ADC) MEETING IN CAIRO HAS CONFIRMED OUR IMPRESSION (REFTEL) THAT GOL
SUCCESSFULLY MANAGED DEFLECT OFFERS OF ARAB MILITARY ASSISTANCE. HE ALSO
PROVIDED SOME INTERESTING INSIGHTS INTO POSITIONS ADOPTED BY VARIOUS
ARAB DELS. END SUMMARY.

2. CALLED YESTERDAY AFTERNOON, JULY 8, ON PRESIDENTIAL ADVISER BOUTROS
DIB, WHO ACCOMPANIED PRIMIN TAKIEDDINE SOLH, FONMIN NAFFAH AND MINDEF
MAALOUF TO CAIRO FOR ARAB DEFENSE COUNCIL MEETING JULY 3-4. COMPLIMENTED
DIB ON MEETING'S OUTCOME, FOR FROM PRESS ACCOUNTS IT APPEARED THAT
LEBANESE OBJECTIVE OF NOT REPEAT NOT ACCEPTING ALL-OUT ARAB MILITARY
ASSISTANCE HAD BEEN ACHIEVED WHILE AT SAME TIME MAINTAINING LEBANESE
POSITION IN THE ARAB WORLD. DIB SAID THAT LEBANESE HAD SUCCEEDED BUT
THAT IT HAD INVOLVED ACRIMONIOUS AND OFTEN EXTREMELY TOUGH EXCHANGES
WITH ARAB COLLEAGUES. PRINCIPAL PROBLEM, AND RATHER UNEXPECTED ONE, WAS
POSITION OF KUWAITI FONMIN SABAH WHO, PRIOR TO PLENARY SESSION JULY 3,
HAD CIRCULATED DRAFT RESOLUTION WHICH TREATED PLO AND GOL ON AN EQUAL
FOOTING AND WHICH PROVIDED FOR 50 MILLION REPEAT 50 MILLION LEBANESE
POUNDS TO BE ACCORDED EACH TO GOL AND PLO ON AN EQUAL BASIS FOR DEFENSE.
KUWAITI REP APPEARED TO GOL DEL TO BE MORE PLO THAN THE PLO, AND HE LED
THE HARD-LINE ARABS IN SUBSEQUENT DISCUSSIONS. KUWAITI POSITION WAS
PARTICULARLY RESENTED BY THE LEBANESE, FOR ACCORDING TO THE LATTER,
KUWAITIS SHOWED TOTAL DISREGARD FOR LEBANESE SOVEREIGNTY AND ALL THAT
GOL HAD DONE FOR PLO, AS WELL AS SUFFERINGS BORNE BY LEBANESE DUE TO
THIS HOSPITALITY (SIC). IN PRE-PLENARY DISCUSSIONS LEBANESE REJECTED
KUWAIT'S POSITION, ARGUING NOT ONLY LEBANESE SOVEREIGNTY BUT ALSO FACT
THAT KUWAITI GENEROSITY TO PLO WOULD JEOPARDIZE CURRENT FRAGILE PEACE
ALONG BORDER AND RESULT IN ISRAELI REPRISALS. KUWAITI REP AT ONE POINT
QUESTIONED LEBANESE "ARAB" STATUS, TO WHICH PRIME MINISTER TAKIEDDINE
SOLH REPLIED THAT IF THIS ASSERTION WERE NOT WITHDRAWN IMMEDIATELY,
LEBANESE WOULD NOT REPEAT NOT ATTEND ADC MEETING. AS RESULT, KUWAITI
REP WITHDREW HIS PAPER.

3. PLENARY SESSION AFTERNOON JULY 3 WAS, ACCORDING TO DIB, RELATIVELY
ANODYNE WITH EACH DELEGATION MAKING ANTICIPATED PUBLIC STATEMENTS.
ENSUING CLOSED SESSIONS AT WHICH ONLY DELEGATION CHIEFS (FORNMIN AND/OR
MINS DEF) WERE PRESENT, WERE, HOWEVER, ACRIMONIOUS. THEY COINCIDED
WITH WORKING MEETINGS, EITHER WITH ALL DELEGATIONS REPRESENTED OR IN
SMALLER GROUPS.

4. DIB DESCRIBED BEHAVIOR OF VARIOUS DELEGATIONS ALONG FOLLOWING LINES:
EGYPTIANS WERE GRACIOUS HOSTS, SAYING RELATIVELY LITTLE BUT SHOWING
UNDERSTANDING OF LEBANESE POSITION. SYRIANS WERE MOST HELPFUL IN
SUPPORTING GOL POSITION. FORMIN KHADDAM ACTED WISELY AND ON SEVERAL
OCCASIONS AS MODERATOR BETWEEN GOL AND SA'IQA REP MOHSEN. SA'IQA DEL,
LED BY MUHSEN, WAS PARTICULARLY VIOLENT, SUPPORTING KUWAITIS AND
FREQUENTLY ATTACKING LEBANESE. (AS NOTED REFTEL, MUHSEN HAS CONTINUED
TO CRITICIZE GOL SINCE RETURNING FROM CAIRO.) DIB SAID GOL DEL WAS
CONVINCED THAT MUHSEN PERSONALLY PROFITED IMMENSELY FROM "KUWAITI
GENEROSITY". KUWAITI DEL, IN ADDITION TO WHAT IS INDICATED ABOVE,
ACCORDING TO DIB, APPEARED TERRIFIED OF PLO. AT INITIAL PRIVATE
DISCUSSION, KUWAITI REP, WHEN CHALLENGED BY LEBANESE RE RELATIVE STATUS
OF PALESTINIANS IN LEBANON AND KUWAIT, STATED THAT HIS LIFE HAD BEEN
THREATENED BY PLO AND GAVE EVERY APPEARANCE OF PERMITTING THIS THREAT
TO GOVERN HIS ACTIONS. ALGERIAN DEL UNDER BOUTEFLIKA'S LEADERSHIP
SHOWED GREAT STATESMANSHIP AS A MODERATING ELEMENT. ON ONE OCCASION,
HOWEVER, BOUTEFLIKA ADVANCED LENGTHY LEGAL ARGUMENT RE PLO RIGHTS
HAVING BEEN ACCEPTED AT UN BUT HE FORMALLY WITHDREW HIS COMMENTS WHEN
ATTACKED BY NAFFAH, GOL FORNMIN. IRAQ AND LIBYAN DELS CAUSED NO REPEAT
NO GREAT PROBLEMS FOR GOL IN THAT MOST OF THEIR VENOM APPEARED DIRECTED
AGAINST SYRIANS AND EGYPTIANS FOR HAVING AGREED TO DISENGAGEMENT. DIB
SAID GOL DEL SURPRISED BY DEGREE OF THEIR VEHEMENCE, WHICH SYRIANS AND
EGYPTIANS HANDLED IN MOST DIGNIFIED MANNER.

ISRAEL NOT REPEAT NOT TO CONTINUE ACTION AGAINST LEBANON (IN THIS
CONNECTION DIB POINTED OUT THAT FEDAYEEN ACTIVITY FROM LEBANON SHOULD
CEASE); B) UNSPECIFIED AID WOULD BE ACCORDED GOL IN ITS EFFORTS TO
IMPROVE ITS DEFENSIVE POSITION (DIB COMMENTED THAT MINDEF MAALOUF

WOULD BE SUPPORTED IN ITS STRUGGLE TO REGAIN HOMELAND. DIB EMPHASIZED
THAT THIS HAD ALREADY BEEN AGREED TO AT ALGIERS AND THAT THERE WAS NO
REPEAT NO SPECIFIC REFERENCE TO MATERIAL OR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PLO
IN LEBANON.

8. WE RECOGNIZE FOREGOING IS OBVIOUSLY ONE-SIDED. BELIEVE, HOWEVER,
ATMOSPHERICS SET FORTH ABOVE MIGHT BE IN INTEREST, AND IT IS A
RELATIVELY ACCURATE DESCRIPTION OF LEBANESE DEL'S VIEWS AND IMPRESSIONS
OF THE MEETING. REPEATEDLY DIB EMPHASIZED THE SENSITIVITY OF FOREGOING
AND REQUESTED THAT IT NOT ONLY BE STRICTLY NOFORN BUT USED ONLY ON A
NEED-TO-KNOW BASIS.

footnotes: The Arab Defense Council (ADC) meeting of July 3-4, 1974 in Cairo was convened in the aftermath of the May 31 Israeli-Syrian disengagement agreement and the intensified Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon documented in cable 1974BEIRUT05740. The Arab League framework provided for collective defense arrangements; Lebanon's strategic objective at the meeting was to obtain diplomatic support against Israeli retaliation without accepting Arab military assistance that would have further compromised its sovereignty and triggered more Israeli action. The phrase "deflect offers of Arab military assistance" captures the Lebanese state's core dilemma in this period: accepting Arab military aid would have required hosting additional foreign armed elements on Lebanese soil and would have provoked Israeli escalation; refusing it required walking a diplomatic tightrope of appearing loyal to Arab solidarity while protecting Lebanese sovereignty.

Boutros Dib: Presidential Adviser to President Suleiman Frangieh, one of the Embassy's most senior Lebanese sources. Dib appears in the 1973 cable series (1973BEIRUT05437) as a Presidency source and here in 1974 as a member of the GOL delegation to the ADC. His role as the Embassy's channel for confidential readouts of sensitive Lebanese diplomatic engagements is a structural feature of U.S.-Lebanese communication in the pre-war period.

Takieddine Solh (1908–1988): Sunni Muslim Prime Minister of Lebanon, June 1973 – October 1974. His government — assessed in cable 1974BEIRUT11970 as characterized by "do-nothingness" — would collapse in the fall of 1974. Solh's presence at the ADC meeting, and his direct confrontation with the Kuwaiti representative who questioned Lebanese "Arab" status, documents a rare moment of Lebanese firmness from a government whose general characteristic was passivity. A Sunni PM defending Lebanese sovereignty against a hostile Kuwaiti (Sunni) delegation illustrates the complexity of intra-Sunni Arab politics that the sectarian frame obscures.

Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah: Kuwaiti Foreign Minister (1963–2003), later Emir of Kuwait (2006–2020). His role at the July 1974 ADC meeting — circulating a draft resolution treating Lebanon and the PLO as equal claimants on Arab defense funding, and openly questioning Lebanon's Arab status — is documented here. The Kuwaiti position is analytically significant: Kuwait was not a radical Arab state but rather a pro-Western Gulf monarchy whose Palestinian population was large and politically influential. The cable's suggestion that Sabah's actions were partly driven by personal threats from the PLO — "his life had been threatened by the PLO" — is a striking allegation preserved in the diplomatic record.

LL 50 million for each of the GOL and PLO, on equal footing, for defense: this is the specific proposal the Lebanese delegation rejected. Equating a sovereign state with an armed non-state actor — and funding them equally for defense activities on Lebanese territory — would have formally elevated the PLO to parity with the Lebanese state in the Arab League framework, with structural implications for Lebanese sovereignty far beyond the monetary value of the proposal. This is the concrete diplomatic form of the "state within a state" dynamic that successive cables in this archive document. LL 50 million in 1974 was approximately USD 15-20 million at contemporary exchange rates.

The Lebanese argument — that Arab military aid to the PLO in Lebanon would jeopardize the "fragile peace along the border and result in Israeli reprisals" — accepted the implicit logic of the feedback loop documented in cable 1974BEIRUT05740: arming the fedayeen would produce Israeli retaliation would produce Lebanese instability. The GOL's diplomatic strategy was to prevent the first link in this chain by rejecting Arab support that would arm the fedayeen further. This was the policy choice for which Solh's government was simultaneously most successful diplomatically and most criticized politically.

Abdul Halim Khaddam (1932–2020): Syrian Foreign Minister (1970–1984), later Vice President. Khaddam's appearance in this cable as a "wise moderator" stands in sharp contrast to his role in the 1973 cable series, where cable 1973BEIRUT05159 (May 8, 1973) reported Khaddam deliberately misrepresenting negotiating terms during the May 1973 crisis. The inversion is notable: in 1973, Khaddam was the Syrian provocateur; in 1974, following Syrian-Israeli disengagement, Khaddam played moderator. Syrian policy toward Lebanon was shifting. The cable's observation that Khaddam "moderated between the GOL and Sa'iqa" is particularly revealing, because Sa'iqa was a Syrian-controlled Palestinian faction — meaning Khaddam was moderating between Lebanon and a PLO faction Syria itself directed. Syria was using its control of Sa'iqa as leverage in Arab diplomacy.

Zuhair Mohsen (also spelled Muhsen; 1936–1979): leader of Sa'iqa, the Syrian-backed Palestinian faction within the PLO. Mohsen was one of the most militant and outspoken Palestinian leaders, famous for his 1977 statement that "there is no difference between Jordanians, Palestinians, Syrians, and Lebanese... Only for political reasons do we carefully underline our Palestinian identity." His position at the ADC supporting the Kuwaiti draft resolution — attacking the Lebanese delegation from within the Arab framework — and his continued criticism of the GOL after returning to Beirut (noted as having been documented in REFTEL) illustrate the tactical alignment of Syrian-backed Palestinian factions with Kuwaiti policy despite the two being from very different points on the Arab political spectrum. Mohsen was assassinated in Cannes in 1979.

"Muhsen personally profited immensely from Kuwaiti generosity": this is a specific allegation — that the Sa'iqa leader was receiving direct Kuwaiti payments — preserved in the U.S. diplomatic record on the basis of a statement by the Lebanese presidential adviser. The allegation is consistent with the broader pattern documented in cable 1973BEIRUT06768 (June 8, 1973), which recorded Arafat's direct payments to Lebanese political figures from the Fatah treasury. The emerging picture, across these cables, is of a political economy in which Palestinian faction leaders were intermediaries for Gulf Arab state funding to be directed into Lebanese political operations — with personal enrichment for the intermediaries as a structural feature of the system.

"His life had been threatened by the PLO": this is the most striking single sentence in the cable. A Kuwaiti Foreign Minister — sovereign of a major Arab state — admitting in private diplomatic discussion that his public policy positions were being driven by PLO death threats against him personally. The Lebanese delegation's reading — that this fear "governed his actions" — is recorded as the GOL assessment of the Kuwaiti position. This observation, preserved in the U.S. diplomatic record, is a factual datum about the operational pressure under which Gulf Arab states were making Palestinian-related policy in 1974.

Abdelaziz Bouteflika (1937–2021): Algerian Foreign Minister (1963–1979), later President of Algeria (1999–2019). Bouteflika was the "moderating element" at the ADC meeting — consistent with Algeria's position as a radical-but-responsible Arab actor in this period. His formal withdrawal of a legal argument on PLO UN rights after being attacked by Lebanese Foreign Minister Naffah illustrates the specific diplomatic deference Bouteflika was willing to extend to Lebanese sensitivities, even at the cost of PLO positional advocacy.

Iraq and Libya directed their criticism at Syria and Egypt (for accepting disengagement) rather than at Lebanon — exactly the pattern cable 1974BEIRUT05740 predicted: radical Arab states working to derail the post-war diplomatic architecture. The Embassy had forecast this dynamic on May 22; the ADC meeting of July 3-4 confirmed it. The Lebanese delegation's "surprise at the degree of their vehemence" documents that even experienced Lebanese diplomats underestimated the intensity of intra-Arab disagreement about post-October 1973 Middle East diplomacy.

"To save his punch for some later occasion, should the meeting turn out badly": Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz al-Saud, Saudi Defense Minister (1963–2011), was absent from the outset of the ADC meeting. The Saudi delegation explanation — that Sultan was being held in reserve for a later contingency — suggests the Saudi assessment that the ADC meeting might "turn out badly" (from a Saudi perspective), requiring higher-level Saudi intervention if outcomes proved adverse. Saudi Arabia's approach to Arab collective defense diplomacy, as reflected here, was characterized by graduated escalation reserved for contingencies — a pattern consistent with Saudi diplomatic style across the period.

"Non-Muslims took pains to protect Muslim Prime Minister Solh from attacks by other Arabs": the inversion captured here is diplomatically striking. In the Lebanese confessional system, the Prime Minister is constitutionally Sunni Muslim. At this meeting, the Christian Foreign Minister (Naffah) and Christian Defense Minister (Maalouf) were publicly defending their Sunni Prime Minister against attacks from Sunni Arab states (Kuwait in particular). The internal Lebanese delegation dynamic — Christians defending Muslim leadership against Muslim external attacks — illustrates that Lebanese sovereignty concerns, at least at the governmental level, had transcended confessional alignment in ways that Lebanon's critics in the Arab world did not expect.

LL 2.2 billion (approximately USD 800 million to USD 1 billion at 1974 exchange rates) five-year defense program: this is a specific commitment by the Lebanese Ministry of Defense documented here. The caveat — "no strings attached" — signals the Lebanese insistence that any Arab financial assistance not carry political conditions that would compromise Lebanese sovereignty or force Lebanese state engagement against the fedayeen, or for them. Cable 1974BEIRUT11970 (October 2, 1974) notes that parliamentary inertia had prevented significant progress in strengthening the Lebanese Army over the next three months, despite the announced defense program — documenting the gap between GOL declared commitments and GOL legislative capacity.

The Algiers Arab League Summit of November 1973 — the first Arab League summit after the October Yom Kippur War — formally recognized the PLO as "the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people," a formulation that would be enshrined in subsequent Arab collective positions and ultimately endorsed by the UN General Assembly in Resolution 3236 of November 1974. Dib's emphasis that the ADC meeting merely reiterated what had been agreed at Algiers — without specific reference to PLO operations in Lebanon — documents the GOL's careful calibration: supporting the PLO's political role in principle while resisting its operational role on Lebanese territory.

NOFORN and "need-to-know basis": the tightest handling restriction combination. NOFORN prohibits sharing with foreign governments, which given the cable's contents (detailed readouts of other Arab delegations' private positions, including specific allegations about individual foreign leaders' corruption, personal fears, and motivations) was essential. The classification — SECRET/EXDIS/NOFORN — is among the most restrictive in the State Department system. The cable was written on the understanding that it would not circulate beyond a small U.S. readership. That it now appears in the public record is a function of Freedom of Information Act declassification processes half a century after the events.

readerNarrative.headline: More PLO Than the PLO: Kuwait's Draft at the Arab Defense Council
readerNarrative.subheadline: Filed July 9, 1974, SECRET/EXDIS/NOFORN. The Lebanese presidential adviser's readout of the Arab Defense Council meeting in Cairo: Kuwait tried to equate the PLO with the Lebanese state, proposing LL 50 million each in defense funding. The Kuwaiti FM questioned Lebanon's Arab status — and privately admitted his life had been threatened by the PLO. Saudi Arabia kept its defense minister in reserve 'for when things turned bad.' Syria, surprisingly, moderated.
readerNarrative.summary: On July 8, 1974, U.S. Ambassador Godley's deputy called on Presidential Adviser Boutros Dib for a readout of the July 3-4 Arab Defense Council meeting in Cairo. Dib gave him one on condition of strictest handling: SECRET/EXDIS/NOFORN, need-to-know basis only. The cable reports what Dib said: Kuwait's Foreign Minister Sabah circulated a draft resolution treating the PLO and Lebanon as equals, with LL 50 million each for defense. The Kuwaiti representative questioned Lebanese 'Arab' status — prompting PM Solh to threaten walking out. In private, the Kuwaiti FM admitted the PLO had threatened his life. The Sa'iqa representative Zuhair Mohsen was 'particularly violent,' and the Lebanese delegation believed he was personally profiting from Kuwaiti money. Syrian FM Khaddam, who had been a provocateur in 1973, played moderator in 1974. Iraq and Libya attacked Syria and Egypt for having accepted disengagement. Saudi Arabia kept its Defense Minister absent from the outset 'to save his punch for later' if the meeting went badly. The Lebanese non-Muslim ministers took pains to defend the Muslim PM from attacks by other Arabs. The final resolutions — the 'Secret Resolutions' — papered over everything.
keyRevelations: Kuwait's Foreign Minister circulated a draft resolution at the Arab Defense Council proposing LL 50 million each for the PLO and the Lebanese government, treating an armed non-state actor as diplomatically equal to a sovereign state within Arab League defense architecture.
The Kuwaiti FM questioned Lebanon's 'Arab' status in open ADC discussion. Prime Minister Solh threatened to walk out; the Kuwaiti withdrew the paper.
In private diplomatic conversation, the Kuwaiti FM admitted his life had been threatened by the PLO — and, the Lebanese assessed, this fear was governing his positions.

The Lebanese delegation was convinced that Sa'iqa leader Zuhair Mohsen personally profited immensely from “Kuwaiti generosity” — consistent with the pattern of faction leaders as intermediaries for Gulf money into Lebanese political operations.
Syria had reversed its 1973 role: FM Khaddam, who had been a provocateur in 1973, played moderator in 1974 — moderating even between Lebanon and Sa'iqa, a Syrian-controlled Palestinian faction.

Iraq and Libya directed their venom not at Lebanon but at Syria and Egypt for having agreed to disengagement — confirming cable 1974BEIRUT05740's May forecast that radical Arab states would work to derail the post-war diplomatic architecture.

keyFigures.name: Boutros Dib
keyFigures.role: Presidential Adviser to President Frangieh; GOL delegate at ADC
keyFigures.desc: Dib's function across the 1973–1974 cable series is as the Embassy's most senior Lebanese source on Presidency thinking. He accompanied Prime Minister Solh to the Cairo ADC meeting and provided this detailed readout to the Embassy on condition of the tightest possible handling. The texture of his readout — candid, unflattering to several Arab states, protective of his own delegation's members — reflects the confidence established between the Frangieh Presidency and the U.S. Embassy by 1974.

keyFigures.name: Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah
keyFigures.role: Kuwaiti Foreign Minister, 1963–2003; Emir of Kuwait, 2006–2020
keyFigures.desc: The Kuwaiti delegation chief at the July 1974 ADC meeting. His draft resolution treating the PLO and Lebanon as equal claimants on Arab defense funding, his questioning of Lebanese 'Arab' status, and his private admission that the PLO had threatened his life, are documented in this cable. He would later become Emir of Kuwait and was widely respected as a diplomat; the 1974 moment captured here represents an unusual alignment between Kuwaiti Gulf pragmatism and PLO radicalism, attributable in part, per the cable, to personal fear.

keyFigures.name: Zuhair Mohsen
keyFigures.desc: Mohsen led the most militant anti-GOL attacks at the ADC meeting, supporting the Kuwaiti draft. The Lebanese delegation believed he was personally profiting from Kuwaiti payments. He is famous for his 1977 statement that there was 'no difference between Jordanians, Palestinians, Syrians, and Lebanese... Only for political reasons do we carefully underline our Palestinian identity.' Assassinated in Cannes, 1979.

keyFigures.name: Abdul Halim Khaddam
keyFigures.desc: Khaddam had been the Syrian provocateur in the 1973 crisis, deliberately misrepresenting Lebanese positions (see cable 1973BEIRUT05159). By July 1974, with Israeli-Syrian disengagement in place, he was playing moderator at the ADC meeting — even moderating between Lebanon and Sa'iqa, a Palestinian faction Syria itself controlled. The inversion documents a shift in Syrian policy toward Lebanon in 1974.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The call on Dib

On the afternoon of July 8, 1974, four days after the Arab Defense Council meeting in Cairo ended, a U.S. Embassy officer called on Presidential Adviser Boutros Dib in Beirut. Dib had accompanied Prime Minister Solh, Foreign Minister Naffah, and Defense Minister Maalouf to the meeting. The Embassy officer complimented Dib on the outcome — press accounts suggested Lebanon had successfully avoided committing to Arab military assistance while maintaining its Arab-world position. Dib confirmed the success and then gave a detailed readout of how it had been achieved.

Ambassador Godley filed the cable the next day under the tightest handling restrictions available: SECRET, EXDIS (Exclusive Distribution), NOFORN (No Foreign nationals), and transmitted in two sections. Dib had requested that the material be used "only on a need-to-know basis." He was being candid about Arab delegations in a way he could only be candid if he was confident the readout would not surface in Arab diplomatic channels.

The Kuwaiti draft

The central incident of the ADC meeting was the Kuwaiti initiative. Before the plenary session on July 3, Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah circulated a draft resolution that proposed LL 50 million each for the Government of Lebanon and the PLO, to be distributed on equal terms for defense purposes. To the Lebanese delegation, this was unacceptable in principle: it treated a sovereign state and an armed non-state actor as diplomatically equivalent within an Arab League collective defense framework. The Lebanese rejection argued both Lebanese sovereignty and practical consequences — arming the PLO further would "jeopardize the current fragile peace along the border and result in Israeli reprisals."

The exchange escalated. The Kuwaiti representative questioned Lebanese "Arab" status. Prime Minister Solh — a Sunni Muslim politician from one of Lebanon's most prominent political families — replied that if the assertion were not withdrawn immediately, the Lebanese delegation would not attend the ADC meeting. The Kuwaiti withdrew the paper.

Fear as foreign policy

But the more striking piece of Dib's readout was what he said the Kuwaiti delegation had admitted in private discussion. When Lebanese representatives pressed the Kuwaitis on the discrepancy between Kuwait's maximalist PLO advocacy at the ADC and Kuwait's own domestic handling of its large Palestinian population, the Kuwaiti Foreign Minister stated that his life had been threatened by the PLO — and, in Dib's characterization, "gave every appearance of permitting this threat to govern his actions."

A sovereign Gulf foreign minister, acknowledging in private diplomatic conversation that his public policy was being driven by assassination threats from an armed non-state actor. Preserved in the U.S. diplomatic record. The cable does not embellish or moralize; it records the observation as Dib made it.

The Sa'iqa paymaster picture

The Sa'iqa representative Zuhair Mohsen — the same figure who would become famous three years later for declaring that Palestinian identity was a political construction — led the most aggressive attacks on the Lebanese delegation at the ADC, supporting the Kuwaiti draft. The Lebanese delegation's assessment, transmitted through Dib: Mohsen was personally profiting immensely from "Kuwaiti generosity." The allegation is consistent with cable 1973BEIRUT06768, which had documented Arafat's direct payments from the Fatah treasury to Lebanese religious and political leaders. Across the 1973–1974 cable record, the picture that emerges is of a political economy in which Palestinian faction leaders function as intermediaries for state funding flows — with personal enrichment as a structural feature, not an aberration.

Khaddam, moderator

The 1974 Syrian posture at the ADC was strikingly different from 1973. Foreign Minister Khaddam — who in cable 1973BEIRUT05159 was documented deliberately misrepresenting Lebanese negotiating positions during the May 1973 crisis — here acts as "wise moderator," repeatedly mediating between the Lebanese delegation and the Sa'iqa representative. The irony is specific: Sa'iqa was a Syrian-controlled Palestinian faction. Khaddam was mediating between Lebanon and a group his own government directed. Syrian control of Sa'iqa was functioning as diplomatic leverage — Syria could produce moderation by constraining Sa'iqa, and could produce confrontation by unleashing it. In July 1974, with Israeli-Syrian disengagement fresh, Syria was choosing moderation.

The rejectionists' target

Iraq and Libya, as cable 1974BEIRUT05740 had forecast in May, were working against the post-October 1973 diplomatic architecture. But their venom at the ADC was directed not at Lebanon — which had taken a pro-PLO political position rhetorically while rejecting it materially — but at Syria and Egypt for having accepted disengagement. The Lebanese delegation was "surprised by the degree of their vehemence." The rejectionist Arab states were attacking the moderate Arab states. The diplomatic coalition that had unified during the October war was fracturing along the lines the May cable had predicted.

Sultan in reserve

One detail captures Saudi Arabia's characteristic posture. The Saudi delegation at the outset was headed by the Saudi Chief of Staff and the Saudi Arab League representative — not by Defense Minister Prince Sultan, whose attendance would have been the normal Saudi level. The Lebanese were told that Sultan was probably being held back "to save his punch for some later occasion, should the meeting turn out badly." The Saudi calculation was that the ADC meeting might go wrong from a Saudi perspective, and that intervening at the highest level was an option to be preserved for a later contingency. The graduated, conservative Saudi approach to Arab diplomacy was structural.

Lebanese internal dynamics

The cable's sixth paragraph contains an observation that would be easy to overlook but captures something important about pre-war Lebanese politics. Within the GOL delegation, Christian Foreign Minister Naffah and Christian Defense Minister Maalouf "took pains to protect Muslim Prime Minister Solh from attacks by other Arabs." Sunni Arab attacks on a Sunni Lebanese Prime Minister, deflected by his Christian cabinet colleagues. The confessional system's external stress points ran at right angles to its internal stress points — Lebanese Christians and Muslims, in government service, defended each other against external attacks that used confessional frames against them.

That solidarity would not hold indefinitely. Nine months after this cable was filed, the Lebanese civil war began. But in July 1974, in Cairo, a Lebanese delegation internally unified across confessional lines defeated a Kuwaiti proposal that would have equated the Lebanese state with an armed non-state actor operating on Lebanese territory.

The resolutions that papered over everything

The final "Secret Resolutions" contained three clauses, all acceptable to the GOL: diplomatic pressure would be applied to the "Great Powers" (i.e., the United States) to restrain Israeli action against Lebanon; unspecified aid would be provided to the GOL for its defensive position; and the PLO was re-recognized as the representative of the Palestinian people consistent with the Algiers summit language. There was no specific reference to material or financial assistance to the PLO in Lebanon. The Lebanese had succeeded in obtaining the rhetorical Arab solidarity they needed while avoiding the substantive commitments that would have further eroded their sovereignty.

The success was temporary. Cable 1974BEIRUT11970, filed three months later, would document the Solh government's collapse. The Arab resolutions of July 1974 went into the record. The Lebanese internal disintegration continued.

cables.subject: Situation in Lebanon
cables.excerpt: SECRET Embassy post-mortem of the 15-month Solh government, filed the morning after it collapsed. Ambassador Godley's verdict: Solh's major accomplishment was to survive by avoiding every difficult decision. What that passivity enabled: Syrian SA-7 missiles to the fedayeen, Christian militia arming after the Cyprus partition, Iraqi-Libyan hired assassins in Beirut, Musa as-Sadr's rising Shia political movement, and a fiscal state where only 11.8% of revenue came from income tax because no one dared enforce tax laws on the well-to-do. The Embassy's prediction: Lebanon would "muddle through until 1976." Civil war broke out six months later.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified SECRET · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review (May 28, 2004) · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Transmitted in three sections (BEIRUT 11970 01-03 of 03)

Summary
Although Lebanon is in a sorry state by American standards, a new government will change little, and the country will probably muddle through at least until 1976.[1]

1. Purpose of this cable
The demise of the Takieddine Solh government prompts us to submit the following evaluation of its achievements over the past 15 months,[2] along with an assessment of the current situation in Lebanon and the problems it can be expected to pose for any successor government. A fuller analysis will follow by airgram.

2. The record of the Solh government
In our last detailed report on the situation in Lebanon (A-11 of January 25), we listed the Solh government’s achievements as decidedly meager in most aspects of Lebanon’s domestic and foreign affairs. Its major accomplishment was to survive while avoiding or postponing difficult decisions as long as possible. Over the past eight months of its life, it carried this approach to the point of almost total inaction. This passivity, coupled with a modest amount of good luck, enabled the Solh government to withstand threats of direct/overt Arab assistance to the fedayeen in Lebanon,[3] but it also ruled out any effective progress in bringing fedayeen presence and activities in Lebanon under greater GOL control.

Internally — with the exception of the passage of a bill increasing pensions for ministers and deputies, and a slight but highly controversial lurch in the direction of civil service reform (our A-39 of March 4) — the Solh government can justly claim to have made no positive achievements — whether by legislative action, executive decree, or administrative fiat — since the beginning of 1974. In short, it managed to make its already notorious reputation for “do-nothingness” even more deserved than before.

3. President Frangieh’s decline
President Frangieh’s[4] original reputation as a tough, no-nonsense decision-maker and advocate of law and order suffered badly during the life of the Solh cabinet. His reluctance to use his potential power to overcome parliamentary and cabinet inertia in making controversial decisions became increasingly pronounced, and he showed himself more and more preoccupied with petty family and political developments in his Zghorta hometown than with national affairs.[5]

The result has been a swelling upsurge in public criticism directed at Frangieh’s person and family, which caused him periodically to hit back at his detractors in a variety of ways — including use of the GOL administrative and police apparatus to harass and intimidate his adversaries (and, in so doing, also foreign businessmen).

4. The social and economic malaise
Fifteen months of governmental inertia and continuing parliamentary somnolence have not failed to exacerbate Lebanon’s increasingly acute economic, financial and social problems, thereby contributing greatly to public uncertainty and unrest over the direction in which the country appears to be heading. While Beirut continues to be a boom-town with land values skyrocketing and modern buildings going up like mushrooms, Lebanon’s basic economic problems (e.g., inflation, pollution, increased cost of living, pressing developmental needs in the south and elsewhere) are still not being faced, and its myriad social problems (e.g., lack of adequate social security and public housing) are being ignored almost in toto.[6]

While we hear more and more talk of the rich getting richer and the poor getting no relief, nothing is being done to change this or to combat the ever-increasing venality that prevails (especially at the highest levels in the capital). Reports of major scandals (e.g., in the Tobacco Authority and Beirut Port and Municipality) involving top government officials, although not uncommon in Lebanon, have contributed to erosion of confidence in the country’s hitherto sacrosanct financial-economic “establishment”. In addition, only 11.8 percent of GOL revenue comes from income tax, but no one apparently dares — least of all the GOL — to enforce observance of existing tax laws by the well-to-do and use that revenue to improve economic and social conditions generally.[7]

5. The fedayeen “state within a state”
Another area which has lately pointed up the GOL’s incapacity to govern is the internal security sector. Relations between the GOL and the fedayeen remain much as they were at the beginning of 1974, with both sides remaining wary of each other but with their responsible leaders still anxious to avoid a repetition (or worse) of the confrontation which occurred in May 1973.[8]

At the same time, however, the fedayeen “state within a state” has continuously improved its military capability vis-à-vis the Lebanese Army with constant clandestine importation of arms from Syria (including SA-7 missiles to hamper LAF air attacks), construction of new bunkers and other defensive works within refugee camps.[9] Although efforts have also been made by the GOL to increase the Lebanese Army’s strength over the past 15 months, no significant progress has been realized so far due to parliamentary inertia.[10]

In any event, mindful of its proven inability to confront the fedayeen successfully, GOL leadership remains unwilling to risk incurring heavy human and economic losses and placing severe internal strains on the Lebanese body politic that a renewed confrontation with the fedayeen would almost certainly entail.

(In the meantime, most Lebanese continue to view the Palestinian problem as the major threat to Lebanon’s future security. While some are cautiously optimistic that external forces may produce some kind of solution, most question how this would affect Palestinians residing in Lebanon and how the latter could be induced to return to whatever form of Palestinian “entity” might emerge from the current ME settlement effort. While most concern is centered in Christian quarters, even many Moslems are pessimistic, for they see the continued presence of nearly 350,000 Palestinians in this country as a threat to the multi-confessional balance and the continued existence of Lebanon as they know it.)[11]

6. Lawlessness, militias, and Cyprus
To make matters worse, the GOL’s apathy and/or helplessness — accompanied by the unprecedented socio-economic malaise mentioned above, plus student unrest and labor agitation (see below) — have contributed to a rising tide of outright lawlessness. Public thuggery — including shootings, kidnappings, muggings, roadblocks, and intimidations carried out by a variety of scofflaw “armed elements” (not all of them Palestinians, by any means) — has reached proportions unacceptable even to easy-going Lebanese.

There has also been a marked increase in efforts by various foreign governments (particularly Iraq and Libya) to foment all sorts of domestic turmoil through press incitement, propaganda wars, street agitation, and the use of hired assassins or bullies to combat their real or imagined opponents here.[12]

At the same time, the incidence of lethal feuds and brawls among confessional, family and tribal “militia” groups has risen. (Christian concern, in particular, over a Moslem “threat” in the aftermath of events in Cyprus has lent impetus to enlarging Christian “militia” groups and increases in their armaments, albeit light.)[13] The tendency of many Lebanese to resort to indiscriminate use of firearms to mark public and private celebrations has also increased at a galloping pace, to the point where the Solh government’s pronouncements regarding ensuring civil order were being greeted with open ridicule.

This factor appears to have played a major role in forming the general consensus that the Solh government had outlived any usefulness it might once have enjoyed in binding up inter-confessional and Lebanese-Palestinian wounds inflicted during the traumatic disturbances of May-June 1973.

7. Foreign policy
In international affairs, the Solh government continued the traditional Lebanese policy of doing nothing to jeopardize its image as an Arab state in good standing. Some further improvement was made in relations with Syria over the past eight months, but Foreign Office decision-making has been reduced to the lowest-common denominator in order to ensure that the GOL avoided “trouble” as much as possible. (While the Solh cabinet thus abdicated any more forceful role it might have played in regional affairs, the GOL has in private heartily endorsed Secretary Kissinger’s efforts aimed at a Middle East settlement.)[14]

While Solh and his junketing Foreign Minister continued their peregrinations throughout the Arab world and elsewhere, the Foreign Office handled only the most routine matters and accurately reflected the government’s do-nothing position. It even proved impossible to select a new Foreign Office Secretary General.

8. Labor
On the labor scene, the Confederation of Lebanese Labor (CLL), which had wrung far more material concessions from the Solh government than from any previous government, stood by passively while the Solh cabinet unraveled and finally collapsed. However, there are definite signs that with unfulfilled popular expectations rising and leftist activity flourishing, labor demands will be a factor attracting increased attention in the months to come. Interestingly enough, labor is the one element on the Lebanese scene not based on confessional lines, and it could well become a springboard from which future leaders will emerge to reform (or destroy) Lebanon’s traditional social-political structure.[15]

9. Student unrest
The Solh government was faced last spring with considerable student unrest centered principally at AUB,[16] but with ramifications throughout the entire local university community. Basic causes appear to reflect general student restlessness that we have witnessed world-wide. They are aggravated in Lebanon, however, by student grievances against the do-nothing government, by organized (and frequently subsidized) Palestinian agitation, and by their feeling of being lost in a leaderless society.

The majority of Lebanese youth is antagonistic to the traditional Lebanese socio-confessional structure and is seeking new outlets for their energies. Many reject social restraints deemed essential by older generations. Multi-religious marriages among the elite, anathema to most of their elders, are occurring at an ever-increasing rate, and many parents are incapable of understanding the ideals espoused by their offspring.

10. Imam Musa as-Sadr
One new element that has appeared on the local scene is the charismatic Shiite Imam Musa as-Sadr, who has turned long-ignored Shi’a grievances into a political force to be reckoned with and who is being wooed assiduously by all non-Sunni elements.[17] Backed by Syrian weapons, money and influence, and enjoying a degree of financial support from Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states, the Imam has become not only his people’s most popular leader, but also spokesman on behalf of Lebanon’s underprivileged majority against its affluent minority regardless of religious affiliation.

It is still too early to say precisely in what direction his current protest campaign will take him, but he will certainly make a bid to supplant the existing feudal Shiite political leadership headed by Parliamentary Speaker Kamel al-Assad.[18] The Imam’s social consciousness apparently has not yet led him to espouse far-out leftist causes, but his criticism of GOL inertia has led him to be viewed by many “establishment” elements as a leftist threat to the existing system.

11. Political outlook
At this writing, Lebanon has no government. How long this situation will continue no one really knows, although if the cabinet crisis is not resolved within the next fortnight it will probably become prolonged. In any event, we think that prospects for any future Lebanese government to cope with the problems outlined above, or even to improve appreciably on the abysmal record of the Solh cabinet, are not bright, given:

(A) Absence of leadership or even elementary guidance on the part of Pres. Frangieh;

(B) Ingrained tendency of the country’s “traditional” politicians — both in and out of power — to pursue personal goals at the expense of national objectives;

(C) Total incapacity of Parliament to respond to even the most pressing public demands; and

(D) Demonstrated inability of the Lebanese system to reform itself from within.

Thus no political element really wants a strong, ergo effective government.[19] In addition, as the time draws nearer for parliamentary and presidential elections in 1976, one can expect further erosion of the GOL’s ability to govern as politicians of all stripes jostle and maneuver in anticipation of future presidential/parliamentary possibilities.

12. The “house of cards” argument
In most countries, the foregoing gloomy picture would lead one to anticipate major politico-social upheavals. Although such convulsions could occur in Lebanon at some future date, we believe that the Lebanese system will somehow continue to muddle through for the next few years — at least until the presidential election in 1976. The basic reason for this belief is the lack of alternatives and the country’s delicate balance along confessional and economic lines.[20]

None of the major forces currently competing in Lebanon yet sees any advantage in destroying the existing system without running a serious risk of having its own position suffer as a result. Criticism of the system will undoubtedly increase, but no one is able to offer any workable substitute. (Worth noting that, with the possible exception of “socialist” Kamal Jumblatt, not a single leading political figure or group in Lebanon today has devised any coherent program to alleviate the situation described above, nor does anyone appear to be thinking ahead regarding possible programs for the future.)[21]

Checks and balances which have traditionally characterized Lebanon’s peculiar “house-of-cards” structure are so delicate that most Lebanese realize any attempt to tinker with part of that structure would bring the whole system tumbling down.

13. The prediction
Thus, while recent press reports, such as those written by Jonathan Randall and others,[22] give an essentially accurate description of conditions in Lebanon, it is our opinion that in the absence of some highly extraordinary accident or unforeseen development, we will not soon see a major change in this country. Its structure is fragile, but realization of that fragility by most Lebanese will enable Lebanon to muddle through for some time to come.

GODLEY
