readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The morning of April 13, 1975

Pierre Gemayel — the founder of Lebanon’s largest Christian militia party, the Kataeb — and Camille Chamoun, a former president of Lebanon, attended mass that Sunday morning at a church in Ain el-Rummaneh, a Christian suburb of southeast Beirut. Members of Gemayel’s party militia and Lebanese government police were stationed in the area. It was, in effect, a gathering of the Maronite Christian political establishment.

8:00 AM — First incident

The Embassy’s cable records that a Volkswagen, driven by an individual the cable describes as Palestinian and reportedly affiliated with an armed organization operating in Lebanon, approached the street on which the church stood. A policeman asked the driver not to use that route. An altercation followed; some accounts reported to the Embassy stated the driver threatened the policeman and was disarmed. The vehicle then departed.

This incident — documented in paragraphs 1 of this cable, filed before noon on April 14, 1975 — does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13.

9:30 AM — Second incident

Approximately ninety minutes later, the cable records, a second vehicle arrived at the same location. The Embassy’s account states it carried four armed individuals who opened fire on bystanders, fatally wounding three, before departing. The cable cites no motive; it records what was reported.

This incident — also documented in this cable, which was on file at the State Department before noon on April 14, 1975 — does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13. The subsequent event, at 11:00 AM, does.

11:00 AM — The bus

About ninety minutes after that, a bus carrying Palestinian passengers entered Ain el-Rummaneh. The passengers were traveling from the Shatila refugee camp in southwest Beirut to the Tel Zaartar refugee camp in the northeast — a route that, on this particular Sunday morning, took them through a neighborhood where Palestinian gunmen had just killed three men ninety minutes earlier.

The U.S. Embassy specifically noted in this cable that the bus’s presence “may have been accidental” — that the passengers may not have known they were driving through a violent situation. But the Kataeb opened fire. Twenty-six people aboard were killed.

This is the event that almost every account of April 13, 1975 treats as the sole incident of the day, and as the unprovoked act that started the Lebanese Civil War.

That evening — further incidents documented in this cable

As the day continued, the Embassy recorded additional incidents. Approximately fifteen rockets were fired from the Borj al Barajneh camp toward Haret Hreik, a residential area of Beirut; the cable notes the apparent target was a party office within that neighborhood. A commercial property was destroyed. A factory near the morning’s location was burning.

These events are recorded in this cable, filed before noon on April 14, 1975. They do not appear in the standard accounts of April 13. The bus attack — also documented in this cable — does.

The night of April 13 — a city fractures

By nightfall, gunfire was reported across a dozen neighborhoods. Barricades went up. Two men opened fire on a Kataeb office near Beirut’s commercial center and were killed by guards. Fighting spread to within blocks of the Holiday Inn hotel in downtown Beirut — a building that would itself become a military fortress within months.

The Lebanese Army, the cable notes, appeared to be standing down. An unconfirmed report reaching the Embassy stated that Army units near the fighting had been ordered not to intervene.

The political response

According to this cable, PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat spent the night of April 13 in contact with Arab governments — directly and through their ambassadors in Beirut — requesting diplomatic pressure on the Lebanese government regarding the bus attack. The cable records that these contacts focused on what they described as Kataeb “culprits.”

The cable’s use of quotation marks around that word is standard Embassy practice when attributing claims without endorsing them. The cable’s own paragraphs 1 and 2 contain the Embassy’s documentation of the two incidents that preceded the event these diplomatic contacts were referencing.

Simultaneously, the cable records, Kamal Jumblatt — leader of the coalition of Lebanese leftist parties allied with the PLO — called for the removal of Kataeb ministers from the Lebanese cabinet. The cable notes this without characterizing the motive; the timing is part of the documentary record.

The ambassador’s verdict

Ambassador Godley’s cable, dispatched at the highest urgency level before noon on April 14, closes with a sentence of striking pessimism:

“To this moment, the elements of a ‘Lebanese solution’ to the crisis are not apparent.”

Lebanon had always managed its crises through negotiation among its community leaders — a system of managed compromise that kept the country’s contradictions contained. Godley was signaling, within hours of the first shots, that this system had broken down.

He was right. The war lasted fifteen years.

cables.subject: Beirut Situation Report — 1500Z
cables.excerpt: The afternoon SITREP for April 14 contains three new facts about April 13: two of the four gunmen in the 9:30 AM attack were Libyan nationals; an Iraqi-backed faction claimed 18 of the bus passengers as its members; and the Palestinian funeral was deliberately postponed to organize a larger demonstration.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 05 July 2006 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Although the situation for the time being seems quieter, Beirut continues tense and the situation remains dangerous. Unofficial Lebanese channels of “reconciliation” have swung into action in an effort to resolve the crisis. The expected funeral for Palestinian “martyrs” in the April 13 clashes did not take place at 1000Z according to Lebanese Army G-2,[1] and that hurdle remains to be faced. Emissaries from two Arab capitals are reportedly scheduled to arrive shortly to help calm the situation. On the other hand, in view of a report that Phalangists plan to bring heavy weapons into the capital during the night, tonight and tomorrow morning could bring a dangerous escalation. We continue to have no reports of American citizens injured and incidents thus far have not assumed an explicit anti-American character.

1.
Hard information on developments in Beirut and other parts of the country continues to be elusive. A number of reported clashes, again centering on Phalange installations, have been received during the day. The Phalange headquarters on Charles Helu Street, near Martyrs Square[2] in the heart of the city, came under attack at approximately 1000Z [10:00 AM GMT] and was hit by three RPG anti-tank rockets, with no indication of casualties. In the downtown and Hamra area, banks and other businesses closed early, and eyewitnesses report large crowds at neighborhood food stores as residents stocked up for a possible siege.

2.
The main surprise of the afternoon was the apparent postponement of the Palestinian funeral expected at 1000Z. Lebanese Army G-2 reported the funeral was a non-event, stating that the GOL does not know why it did not take place. Palestinians apparently did pick up the bodies of slain compatriots from Quarantina Hospital (at least one Phalangist reportedly killed in the accompanying confrontation). An American correspondent reported hearing at approximately 1200Z that the funeral might be postponed until April 15 to provide time for Palestinians and leftist forces to “do it up right.”[3] Consequently, the postponement — which bends common Muslim burial practice — might portend even more disruptive proceedings tomorrow. One local newspaper source reports a minimum of seven killed (we suspect more), with four deaths occurring in Ain Ramanneh as a result of anti-tank rockets.

3.
Radio Lebanon at 1000Z reported 14 persons — unidentified but presumably Phalangists — were in GOL custody on charges of provoking the original incidents on Sunday. Prime Minister Solh had reportedly given Phalangist leader Pierre Gemayel until this morning to turn over those guilty. We remain skeptical that either the Phalange surrendered members or the GOL seized them, although it cannot be excluded that some armed men on the periphery of the action have been picked up. Likewise, we discount a report we have received that Palestinians turned over to the GOL seven fedayeen implicated in Sunday’s clashes.[4]

4.
We have heard that the Phalange militia intends to bring machine-guns, rockets, and mortars into Beirut tonight to reinforce their positions. It is also rumored that former President Chamoun’s “Tigers”[5] are presently setting up mortars just below Beit Meri[6] to provide Palestinians in Tel Zaartar camp — who have apparently spent the day bombarding surrounding neighborhoods — with a demonstration of fire power.[7]

5.
The GOL, prominent political figures, and possibly the “moderate” fedayeen leadership have apparently swung into action during the day in an effort to contain the situation. Saeb Salam[8] told the Ambassador this morning that he had been in touch over the last 24 hours with Pierre Gemayel and indicated other similar consultations were taking place. Salam, however, is blaming not only the Phalange for the situation but the entire government for a lack of leadership. Arafat has allegedly returned from Damascus and held discussions with GOL leaders and is scheduled to meet tonight with Arab ambassadors. The Moroccan ambassador told the Ambassador today that President Assad of Syria[9] had dispatched a special emissary to Beirut to tell Syrians — including, presumably, Saiqa[10] — to “cool it.” We have just heard a report that Arab League Secretary-General Mahmud Riad, bearing a message from Sadat,[11] is arriving Beirut this evening to calm the parties to the dispute.

6.
Few additional details regarding the events that sparked the present confrontation are available. We have heard that two of the four persons in the second car — referenced in paragraph 2 of Beirut 4749 — which allegedly fired on Phalangists in Ain Ramanneh were in fact Libyan nationals.[12] In addition, the Iraq-supported Arab Liberation Front (ALF)[13] has now issued a statement asserting that 18 of the Palestinians killed on the bus were its members.[14] The involvement of such elements — if true, and conceivably even if not — might present the GOL and “moderate” PLO leadership with ingredients, if both sides really desire, for a “no win, no loss” solution. This remains, however, to be seen.

7.
All American citizens continue to be safe as far as we are aware. There is little evidence that the ugly mood in town has assumed an anti-American character, although this could happen if the situation deteriorates. As the Department is aware, we are associated with the Phalange in the eyes of some Lebanese.[15] We have been informing Embassy staff — non-essential members of which were dismissed at 1400Z — and inquiring American citizens to stay home.

8 & 9.
Elsewhere in the country the situation remains as reported in the reference cable. All roads into Beirut remain open at this time with the exception of the Sidon road. The Embassy is maintaining a normal duty schedule tonight. This will be our last situation report until tomorrow morning unless significant developments require a report prior to that time.

GODLEY[16]

C O N F I D E N T I A L BEIRUT 4794

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS LE PLO
SUBJECT: BEIRUT SITREP - 1500Z
REF: BEIRUT 4749

SUMMARY: ALTHOUGH SITUATION FOR TIME BEING SEEMS QUIETER, BEIRUT CONTINUES TENSE AND SITUATION REMAINS DANGEROUS. UNOFFICIAL LEBANESE CHANNELS OF "RECONCILIATION" HAVE SWUNG INTO ACTION IN EFFORT TO RESOLVE CRISIS. EXPECTED FUNERAL FOR PALESTINIAN "MARTYRS" IN APRIL 13 CLASHES DID NOT RPT NOT TAKE PLACE AT 1000Z ACCORDING TO LEBANESE ARMY G-2 AND THAT HURDLE REMAINS TO BE FACED. EMISSARIES FROM TWO ARAB CAPITALS REPORTEDLY SCHEDULED TO ARRIVE HERE SHORTLY TO HELP CALM SITUATION. ON OTHER HAND, IN VIEW OF REPORT THAT PHALANGISTS PLAN TO BRING HEAVY WEAPONS INTO CAPITAL DURING NIGHT, TONIGHT AND TOMORROW MORNING COULD BRING DANGEROUS ESCALATION OF SITUATION. WE CONTINUE TO HAVE NO REPORTS OF AMCITS INJURED AND INCIDENTS THUS FAR HAVE NOT ASSUMED EXPLICIT ANTI-AMERICAN CHARACTER. END SUMMARY.

1. HARD INFORMATION ON DEVELOPMENTS IN BEIRUT AND OTHER PARTS OF COUNTRY CONTINUES TO BE ELUSIVE. NUMBER OF REPORTED CLASHES, AGAIN CENTERING ON PHALANGE INSTALLATIONS, HAVE BEEN RECEIVED DURING DAY. PHALANGE HEADQUARTERS IN CHARLES HELU ST., NEAR MARTYRS SQUARE IN HEART OF CITY, CAME UNDER ATTACK ABOUT 1000Z AND WAS HIT BY THREE RPG ANTI-TANK ROCKETS, BUT THERE NO INDICATION OF CASUALTIES. IN DOWNTOWN AND HAMRA AREA, BANKS AND OTHER BUSINESSES CLOSED EARLY AND EYE-WITNESSES REPORT LARGE CROWDS AT NEIGHBORHOOD FOOD STORES AS RESIDENTS STOCKED UP FOR POSSIBLE SIEGE.

2. MAIN SURPRISE OF AFTERNOON WAS APPARENT POSTPONEMENT OF PALESTINIAN FUNERAL EXPECTED AT 1000Z. LEBANESE ARMY G-2, WHO REPORTED FUNERAL WAS NON-EVENT, SAID GOL DOES NOT RPT NOT KNOW WHY IT DID NOT TAKE PLACE. PALESTINIANS APPARENTLY DID PICK UP BODIES OF SLAIN COMPATRIOTS FROM QUARANTINA HOSPITAL (AT LEAST ONE PHALANGIST REPORTED KILLED IN ACCOMPANYING FRAY). AMERICAN CORRESPONDENT, HOWEVER, REPORTED HEARING RUMOR AT ABOUT 1200Z THAT FUNERAL MIGHT BE POSTPONED UNTIL APR 15 TO PROVIDE TIME FOR PALESTINIANS AND LEFTIST FORCES TO DO IT UP RIGHT. CONSEQUENTLY, POSTPONEMENT, WHICH BENDS COMMON MUSLIM BURIAL PRACTICE, MIGHT PORTEND EVEN MORE DISRUPTIVE PROCEEDINGS TOMORROW. PROBABLY NO ONE KNOWS EXTENT OF CASUALTIES FROM TODAY'S ALTERCATIONS BUT ONE LOCAL NEWSPAPER SOURCE REPORTS MINIMUM OF SEVEN (WE SUSPECT MORE) KILLED, WITH FOUR DEATHS OCCURRING IN AIN RAMANNEH AS RESULT OF ANTI-TANK ROCKETS.

3. RADIO LEBANON AT 1000Z REPORTED 14 PERSONS (UNIDENTIFIED BUT PRESUMABLY PHALANGISTS) WERE IN GOL CUSTODY ON CHARGES OF PROVOKING ORIGINAL INCIDENTS ON SUNDAY. PM SOLH HAD REPORTEDLY GIVEN PHALANGIST LEADER, PIERRE GEMAYEL, UNTIL THIS MORNING TO TURN OVER THOSE GUILTY. WE REMAIN SKEPTICAL THAT EITHER PHALANGE SURRENDERED MEMBERS OR GOL SEIZED THEM, ALTHOUGH IT CANNOT BE EXCLUDED THAT SOME ARMED MEN ON PERIPHERY OF ACTION HAVE BEEN PICKED UP. LIKEWISE, WE DISCOUNT REPORT WE HAVE RECEIVED THAT PALESTINIANS HAVE TURNED OVER TO GOL SEVEN FEDAYEEN IMPLICATED IN SUNDAY'S CLASHES.

4. WE HAVE HEARD PHALANGE MILITIA INTENDS TO BRING MACHINE-GUNS, ROCKETS AND MORTARS INTO BEIRUT TONIGHT TO REINFORCE THEIR POSITIONS. IT IS ALSO RUMORED THAT FORMER PRES CHAMOUN'S "TIGERS" PRESENTLY SETTING UP MORTARS JUST BELOW BEIT MERI TO PROVIDE PALESTINIANS IN TEL ZAARTAR CAMP, WHO HAVE APPARENTLY SPENT DAY BOMBARDING SURROUNDING NEIGHBORHOODS, WITH DEMONSTRATION IN FIRE POWER.

5. GOL, PROMINENT POLITICAL FIGURES AND POSSIBLY "MODERATE" FEDAYEEN LEADERSHIP HAVE APPARENTLY SWUNG INTO ACTION DURING DAY IN EFFORT TO CONTAIN SITUATION. SAEB SALAM TOLD AMB MORNING APR 14 THAT HE HAD BEEN IN TOUCH IN LAST 24 HOURS WITH PIERRE GEMAYEL AND INDICATED OTHER SIMILAR CONSULTATIONS WERE TAKING PLACE. SALAM, HOWEVER, BLAMING NOT ONLY PHALANGE FOR SITUATION BUT ENTIRE GOVT FOR LACK OF LEADERSHIP. ARAFAT HAS ALLEGEDLY RETURNED FROM DAMASCUS AND HELD DISCUSSIONS WITH GOL LEADERS AND IS SCHEDULED TO MEET TONIGHT WITH ARAB AMBS HERE. MOROCCAN AMB TOLD AMB TODAY THAT PRES ASSAD OF SYRIA HAD DISPATCHED SPECIAL EMISSARY TO BEIRUT TO TELL SYRIANS, INCLUDING PRESUMABLY SAIQA, TO COOL IT. WE HAVE JUST HEARD REPORT THAT ARAB LEAGUE SYG MAHMUD RIAD BEARING MESSAGE FROM SADAT IS ARRIVING BEIRUT THIS EVENING TO CALM PARTIES TO DISPUTE.

6. FEW ADDITIONAL DETAILS RE EVENTS WHICH SPARKED PRESENT CONFRONTATION ARE AVAILABLE. WE HAVE HEARD TWO OF FOUR PERSONS IN SECOND CAR (REFTEL PARA 2) WHICH ALLEGEDLY FIRED ON PHALANGISTS IN AIN RAMANNEH WERE IN FACT LIBYANS. IN ADDITION, IRAQ-SUPPORTED ARAB LIBERATION FRONT (ALF) HAS NOW ISSUED STATEMENT ASSERTING THAT 18 OF PALESTINIANS KILLED ON BUS WERE ITS MEMBERS. INVOLVEMENT OF SUCH ELEMENTS IF TRUE (AND CONCEIVABLY EVEN IF NOT) MIGHT PRESENT GOL AND "MODERATE" PLO LEADERSHIPS WITH INGREDIENTS, IF BOTH SIDES REALLY DESIRE, FOR "NO WIN, NO LOSS" SOLUTION. THIS REMAINS, HOWEVER, TO BE SEEN.

7. ALL AMCITS CONTINUE TO BE SAFE SO FAR AS WE AWARE. THERE IS LITTLE EVIDENCE THAT UGLY MOOD IN TOWN HAS ASSUMED ANTI-AMERICAN CHARACTER, ALTHOUGH THIS COULD HAPPEN IF SITUATION DETERIORATES. AS DEPT AWARE WE ARE ASSOCIATED WITH THE PHALANGE IN THE EYES OF SOME LEBANESE. WE HAVE BEEN INFORMING EMBASSY STAFF (NON-ESSENTIAL MEMBERS OF WHICH DISMISSED AT 1400Z) AND INQUIRING AMCITS TO STAY HOME.

8. ELSEWHERE IN COUNTRY SITUATION REMAINS AS REPORTED REFTEL. ALL ROADS INTO BEIRUT REMAIN OPEN AT THIS TIME WITH EXCEPTION OF SIDON ROAD WHICH PROBLEMATIC.

9. EMBASSY MAINTAINING NORMAL DUTY SCHEDULE TONIGHT. THIS WILL BE OUR LAST SITREP UNTIL TOMORROW MORNING UNLESS SIGNIFICANT DEVELOPMENTS REQUIRE REPORT PRIOR THAT TIME.

GODLEY

CONFIDENTIAL NNN
footnotes: G-2: military intelligence branch of the Lebanese Army. The Army G-2’s report that the funeral did not occur — and that the GOL did not know why — documents the state’s lack of visibility into Palestinian decision-making in Beirut on April 14, 1975.

Martyrs Square: Beirut’s central public plaza, the symbolic heart of the city. An attack on the Phalange headquarters adjacent to Martyrs Square signals that the violence had reached the city center, not just the suburban neighborhoods of April 13.

The Embassy’s American correspondent source reports that the funeral postponement was deliberate and strategic — designed to allow time to organize a larger, more impactful demonstration. The phrase “do it up right” is the Embassy’s paraphrase of the source’s characterization. The postponement “bends common Muslim burial practice,” which ordinarily requires interment within 24 hours of death. This deliberate breach of religious custom to maximize political impact is documented in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of the April 14 funeral.

The Embassy explicitly discounts two claims: (a) that Phalange surrendered members to the GOL, and (b) that Palestinians turned over seven fedayeen. Both claims had circulated in Lebanese media and diplomatic channels. The Embassy’s skepticism is based on its own sources and judgment. This skepticism about the arrests — which would later prove important in the ceasefire negotiations documented in cable 1975BEIRUT04860 — is on the record in this cable as of April 14.

The Tigers (Numur): the militia of former President Camille Chamoun’s National Liberal Party (NLP). Though distinct from the Kataeb (Phalange), the Tigers were among the principal Maronite militia forces and would operate alongside the Kataeb in the civil war’s early phase.

Beit Meri: a highland village in the Metn district, approximately 15 kilometers east of Beirut, overlooking the capital and the Lebanese coast. The positioning of mortars there would allow fire over a wide area of Beirut.

The cable documents that Tel Zaartar’s Palestinian forces had “apparently spent the day bombarding surrounding neighborhoods” on April 14. This ongoing bombardment of civilian areas is documented here. Read alongside cable 1975BEIRUT04829, which documents the same camp’s situation on April 15, the two cables together establish a pattern of military activity from the camp across these days.

Saeb Salam (1905–2000): prominent Lebanese Sunni political leader who served multiple terms as Prime Minister. He was one of the key cross-communal brokers in Lebanese politics. His meetings with Gemayel on April 13–14, and his attribution of blame to “the entire government for lack of leadership” rather than solely to the Phalange, are documented in this cable on the basis of a direct conversation with the Ambassador.

Hafez al-Assad (1930–2000): President of Syria 1971–2000. His dispatch of a special emissary to tell Syrian-aligned forces in Lebanon to “cool it” within 24 hours of April 13 is documented in this cable on the basis of what the Moroccan ambassador told the U.S. ambassador. This is one of the earliest documented Syrian diplomatic interventions in the April 1975 crisis.

Saiqa (also: Sa’iqa): the Syrian-backed Palestinian armed organization, formally the “Vanguards of the Popular Liberation War.” Saiqa operated in Lebanon under Syrian direction and was among the Palestinian armed groups active in the April 1975 fighting. Assad’s instruction to “cool it” — directed specifically at Saiqa and other Syrian-aligned forces — is documented here.

Anwar Sadat (1918–1981): President of Egypt 1970–1981. His transmission of a calming message through Arab League SYG Riad within 24 hours of April 13 reflects Egypt’s role as a regional stabilizer at this time. Sadat would receive the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978 for the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

This paragraph contains information this cable characterizes as heard rather than confirmed: two of the four individuals in the second car — the vehicle that arrived at approximately 9:30 AM on April 13 and opened fire on bystanders near the church, killing three Kataeb members (documented in cable 1975BEIRUT04749, paragraph 2) — were in fact Libyan nationals, not Palestinian. If accurate as reported, this means the attack that killed three people and directly precipitated the bus massacre was carried out, in part, by citizens of a third country acting within Palestinian armed structures in Lebanon. This specific fact appears in this cable, filed April 14, 1975. It does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13.

Arab Liberation Front (ALF): a Palestinian faction established in 1969 under the sponsorship of the Iraqi Ba’ath Party government. The ALF was a constituent organization of the PLO but operated under Iraqi direction rather than independent Palestinian leadership. Its involvement in the April 13 incidents would implicate Iraqi state sponsorship in the events that initiated the Lebanese Civil War.

The ALF’s claim that 18 of the 26 Palestinians killed on the bus were its members is documented in this cable. If accurate, it means that the majority of the bus passengers were not general Palestinian refugees or civilians in the ordinary sense, but members of a specific Iraqi-backed armed organization. This claim appears in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of April 13, 1975.

The Embassy’s candid statement that “we are associated with the Phalange in the eyes of some Lebanese” is a remarkable self-assessment for a classified diplomatic cable. The U.S. Embassy’s acknowledgment of this perception — and its potential to generate anti-American violence if the situation deteriorated — appears in this cable on record at the State Department as of April 14, 1975.

G. McMurtrie Godley (1917–1999), U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon. This is the fourth cable filed by Godley in the April 13 crisis sequence, following 1975BEIRUT04749 (April 14, AM), 1975BEIRUT04829 (April 15, noon), and 1975BEIRUT04860 (April 16). The four cables together provide continuous situational documentation from the first hours of the civil war through the first ceasefire negotiations.

readerNarrative.headline: The Day After: Three Details the Record Does Not Carry
readerNarrative.subheadline: This cable, filed the afternoon of April 14, 1975, documents three specific facts about April 13 that do not appear in the standard historical account: the national identity of two of the gunmen in the 9:30 AM attack, the stated membership of bus passengers in an Iraqi-backed faction, and the deliberate postponement of the funeral to organize a larger demonstration.
readerNarrative.summary: Filed at 3:00 PM on April 14, 1975, this situation report contains new information about the April 13 incidents that reaches the State Department record the following afternoon. Two of the four gunmen in the 9:30 AM attack that killed three Kataeb members were Libyan nationals, not Palestinians. An Iraqi-backed faction claimed 18 of the 26 people killed on the bus were its members. And the Palestinian funeral, which had been expected that morning, was deliberately postponed — in breach of standard Muslim burial practice — to allow time to organize a larger event. Each of these facts appears in this cable. None appears in the standard account.
keyRevelations: This cable records that two of the four gunmen in the 9:30 AM attack on April 13 — the incident that killed three Kataeb members and directly preceded the bus massacre — were Libyan nationals. This fact appears in paragraph 6 of this cable. It does not appear in the standard historical account of April 13.

The Iraq-supported Arab Liberation Front (ALF) issued a statement claiming that 18 of the 26 people killed on the bus were its members. If accurate, the majority of bus passengers were members of a specific Iraqi-backed armed faction, not general Palestinian civilians. This appears in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account.

The Palestinian funeral, expected at 10:00 AM, was deliberately postponed. An Embassy source characterized the reason as providing time to “do it up right” — organizing a larger event. This postponement “bends common Muslim burial practice.” It is documented in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account.

The Embassy documents that Palestinian forces in Tel Zaartar had spent the day bombarding surrounding neighborhoods on April 14. This ongoing action is recorded in this cable alongside the diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire.

The Embassy candidly notes: “As Dept aware we are associated with the Phalange in the eyes of some Lebanese.” This self-assessment, on record at the State Department on April 14, 1975, documents the U.S. Embassy’s awareness of how its relationships were perceived by Lebanese communities.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The afternoon of April 14

By 3:00 PM on April 14, 1975 — twenty-seven hours after April 13 — the U.S. Embassy filed this situation report. Beirut was quieter than the previous day but deeply tense. The anticipated Palestinian funeral had not occurred. Diplomatic activity had intensified sharply across Arab capitals.

And new information had arrived about April 13 itself.

What this cable documents about April 13 that the standard account does not

Paragraph 6 of this cable contains three specific pieces of information about April 13 that do not appear in the standard historical account of that day.

First: two of the four people in the second car — the vehicle that arrived at approximately 9:30 AM at Ain Ramanneh, opened fire on bystanders, killed three Kataeb members, and drove away — were Libyan nationals, not Palestinians. The Embassy presents this as information it had heard, not as confirmed fact. But it is in the diplomatic record as of April 14, 1975. The standard account does not mention the national identity of the gunmen.

Second: the Iraq-supported Arab Liberation Front issued a statement claiming that 18 of the 26 people killed on the bus were its members. If accurate, the majority of the bus passengers were not ordinary Palestinian civilians or refugees, but members of a specific Iraqi-backed armed faction operating within the Palestinian political structure in Lebanon. The Embassy notes that this information, “even if not” true, might provide both sides with a diplomatic exit. The standard account does not reference the ALF’s claim or the membership of bus passengers in any armed organization.

Third: the Palestinian funeral, ordinarily required within 24 hours under Islamic practice, was deliberately postponed. An American correspondent reported hearing that the postponement was organized to allow time to “do it up right” — to stage a larger, more politically impactful event on April 15. The Embassy characterizes this as portending “even more disruptive proceedings tomorrow.”

The diplomatic response: within 24 hours

The same afternoon, the cable documents a remarkable concentration of Arab diplomatic activity. Former Prime Minister Saeb Salam had met with the U.S. Ambassador in the morning and reported cross-communal consultations. Arafat had returned from Damascus. Syria’s Assad had dispatched a special emissary to tell Syrian-aligned forces in Beirut to stand down. And Arab League Secretary-General Mahmoud Riad was arriving Beirut that evening bearing a message from Egyptian President Sadat.

The speed of the regional diplomatic response — all of this within 27 hours of April 13 — is documented in this cable. It reflects the immediate recognition across Arab capitals that the April 13 incidents had the potential to escalate into something uncontainable.

What the Embassy noted about itself

Paragraph 7 contains a sentence that is rarely cited in any literature on the Lebanese Civil War: “As Dept aware we are associated with the Phalange in the eyes of some Lebanese.”

The U.S. Embassy, in a classified cable on April 14, 1975, placed on record its awareness that its relationships with Lebanese political actors had created a perception of partiality — one that, the Embassy notes, could generate anti-American violence “if the situation deteriorates.” This sentence is in the diplomatic record. It has not been cited in the standard historical account of the Lebanese Civil War.

cables.excerpt: A two-section situation report filed at noon on April 15, 1975, documenting 80–90 dead throughout Lebanon, the spread of violence to Tripoli (three Christian churches bombed) and Sidon (three non-Phalangist villages rocketed and entered), and the Embassy’s own assessment that the casualty balance at this point ran against the Palestinian and Muslim side.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Two-section cable (3885/3886) · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 05 July 2006 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Conditions on the ground in Beirut remain unsettled with intermittent firing and explosions occurring in various parts of the city, as political efforts to defuse the situation have thus far failed to produce tangible results. American citizens continue to be safe, although a car belonging to an Embassy employee was bombed last night and foreigners, as well as Lebanese, are unable to move freely in the city. Tourists should be discouraged from visiting Lebanon at this time. Palestinians — the main elements of which have not yet thrown their full weight into the balance — and leftist parties continue to call for punishment of the Phalange. Strife over the last 24 hours has spread to other parts of the country and shown the first signs of assuming a confessional [sectarian] character.[1]

1.
The country passed a night described by a Beirut police official as “bad” and awoke to continued explosions and clashes in various localities. As casualty reports continue to rise — we would place the number killed to date at 80 to 90 —[2] and the Health Ministry issued appeals for blood donors and for doctors and nurses to report immediately to their hospitals, the major portion of the population in the capital at least remains hunkered down in their homes.

2.
Dekwaneh, Tel Zaatar, and Ain Ramanneh remained the primary Beirut centers of incidents (sniping, bombings, and shelling) during the evening and morning, but Sinn al Fil reportedly sustained considerable material damage. Palestinians are said to have occupied Quarantina Hospital[3] during the afternoon of April 14 and were reportedly rocketing Phalangist targets in Ashrafiye[4] from that position. Three large explosions (possibly rockets) have occurred in the Quarantine district near the port since dawn, the first killing one civilian and injuring three. A 4-kilogram package of plastique with a timer was removed from the Napoleon Hotel (one block off Hamra) around noon April 15.

3.
Security forces (police and gendarmerie with armored vehicles) have moved in strength in troubled areas, but their mission is not yet clear. One reasonably reliable report stated that Squad 16[5] moved against Phalange offices in Rue George Picot early this morning. Prime Minister Solh has again repeated his intention to apply the law and punish the culpable, but rejected proclamation of a state of emergency. PSP leader Kamal Jumblatt, who continues to play a key role among both the GOL leadership and those highly critical of the GOL, opposed calling out the army. Military sources inform us they are preparing for the possibility that the army might be called out at approximately 1900Z tonight.

4.
All American citizens [AMCITS] remain safe at the moment. Clashes, however, are beginning to affect the foreign community. A vehicle belonging to a member of the Embassy staff (DEA) was destroyed at approximately 0200Z while parked near his residence in Raouche. The explosive was apparently a single stick of dynamite tossed under the car, which bore white diplomatic plates. The French ambassador was awakened last evening when a stray bullet entered his bedroom; the Italian ambassador has moved into the city from his residence in an affected area.

5.
The airport is still operating and the access road is open. An Embassy officer returning from the airport this morning reported sighting several armed and uniformed fedayeen in the airport circle, but they made no effort to disrupt traffic. Pan American, however, reports it will run out of jet fuel as of 1100Z today, which will probably result in the cancellation or diversion of some flights. Refineries in Sidon and Tripoli have supplies but cannot deliver: tank trucks cannot pass Sidon; workers in Tripoli report high absenteeism and evidence of unknown elements preventing them from reaching the plant. Industry sources estimate local gas stations will begin to run out of gasoline by Wednesday or Thursday if resupply is not possible.[6]

6.
In view of unsettled conditions in Lebanon, the Embassy has informed the Department by separate cable that tourists should be discouraged from coming at this time. Most diplomatic and other social functions are being cancelled.

7.
On the political scene, there is considerable activity but no concrete results yet apparent. Arab League Secretary-General Riad arrived Beirut last evening and began a series of conciliation meetings, including sessions with Arab ambassadors in Beirut and with Abu Iyad (Fatah)[7] and Nayif Hawatmeh (PDFLP).[8] Arafat was not present and, to the best we can determine, has remained aloof from consultations. Latest reports place him in Damascus today after having spent part of yesterday in South Lebanon.[9] Riad has met with Solh and Frangieh and saw Jumblatt at the St. George Hotel this morning. A meeting between Riad and Gemayel has not yet been scheduled.

8.
Prime Minister Solh held a series of sessions during yesterday afternoon, including one with the cabinet that is reliably reported to have degenerated into a shouting match. Two ministers affiliated with Kamal Jumblatt’s PSP — Abbas Khalaf and Khaled Jumblatt — have announced their resignations, made contingent on Solh meeting their demands that those guilty (read: Phalange) in Sunday’s incidents be brought to “justice” and that the government restore order. As we noted in Beirut 4749, loss of Jumblatt’s support would knock the remaining prop from under the Solh government, which is already staggering.

9.
Fatah and other major fedayeen spokesmen are claiming their forces are showing real restraint in the face of Phalange “provocations.” We are unable to confirm this claim, but it is quite possibly true, since the head count to date appears to be in favor of the Phalange.[10] Splinter groups among the fedayeen and probably undisciplined elements of the more “moderate” organizations, however, do not appear to be exercising restraint, and it is questionable whether the major Palestinian groups can avoid a more aggressive stance indefinitely if the basic situation is not contained soon. Should PLO/Fatah take the decision to go all-out, residents of Beirut and other parts of the country will probably have little choice but to batten hatches and try to hold on. As we have reported over the last several years, we believe the fedayeen are well situated, particularly in the capital, for sustained urban warfare and terrorism which would take maximum toll in lives and property.[11]

10.
In addition to the prolongation of the current crisis — with the outlines of a denouement still not in sight — a disturbing element is the apparent spread of clashes geographically and indications that the strife may be taking a turn toward a Christian vs. Muslim/Palestinian conflict. Tripoli[12] witnessed two major demonstrations on April 14, in which at least two were killed and seven wounded, and three Christian churches were bombed last evening.[13] Yesterday’s events also included the gratuitous sacking of Chamoun’s NLP headquarters in Tripoli. NLP offices near the Foreign Ministry in Beirut were the object of an attempted rocketing this morning.

11.
Phalangist offices in Zahle and nearby Sadnail were bombed last evening. The Phalange office in Sidon was attacked and later rocketed from refugee camps outside Sidon. Three Christian — not Phalangist — villages in the Mieh Mieh region near Sidon were rocketed from camps.[14] According to one usually reliable Lebanese source, when the villagers did not return fire, Palestinians advanced into them and, at one village, seized the father and brother of a Lebanese security official and shot them.[15] Just as continuing Palestinian or Muslim casualties must eventually inflame the sentiment of even more moderate compatriots, so Christian losses will tend to engage the emotions of Christians who have thus far not supported the Phalange.[16]

GODLEY[17]

[INFO: AMMAN, ANKARA, ATHENS, CAIRO, DAMASCUS, LONDON, PARIS, ROME, TEL AVIV, USCINCEUR]

C O N F I D E N T I A L BEIRUT 4829

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS, LE, PLO
SUBJECT: BEIRUT SITREP - 1200Z
REFS: A) BEIRUT 4749; B) BEIRUT 4794

SUMMARY: CONDITIONS ON GROUND IN BEIRUT REMAINS UNSETTLED WITH INTERMITTENT FIRING AND EXPLOSIONS OCCURRING IN VARIOUS PARTS OF CITY AS POLITICAL EFFORTS TO DEFUSE EXPLOSIVE SITUATION THUS FAR HAVE FAILED TO PRODUCE TANGIBLE RESULTS. AMCITS CONTINUE TO BE SAFE ALTHOUGH CAR BELONGING TO EMBASSY EMPLOYEE BOMBED LAST NIGHT AND FOREIGNERS, AS WELL AS LEBANESE, UNABLE MOVE FREELY IN CITY. TOURISTS SHOULD BE DISCOURAGED FROM VISITING LEBANON AT THIS TIME. PALESTINIANS, MAIN ELEMENTS OF WHICH HAVE NOT YET THROWN FULL WEIGHT INTO BALANCE, AND LEFTIST PARTIES CONTINUE CALL FOR PUNISHMENT OF PHALANGE. STRIFE OVER LAST 24 HOURS HAS SPREAD TO OTHER PARTS OF COUNTRY AND SHOWN FIRST SIGNS OF ASSUMING CONFESSIONAL COLORATION. END SUMMARY.

1. COUNTRY PASSED NIGHT DESCRIBED BY BEIRUT POLICE OFFICIAL AS "BAD" AND AWOKE TO CONTINUED EXPLOSIONS AND CLASHES IN VARIOUS LOCALITIES. AS CASUALTY REPORTS CONTINUE TO RISE (WE WOULD PLACE NUMBER KILLED TO DATE AS 80 TO 90) AND HEALTH MINISTRY ISSUED APPEALS FOR BLOOD DONORS AND FOR DOCTORS AND NURSES TO REPORT IMMEDIATELY TO THEIR HOSPITALS, MAJOR PORTION OF POPULATION IN CAPITAL AT LEAST REMAINS HUNKERED DOWN IN THEIR HOMES.

2. DEKWANEH, TEL ZAATAR AND AIN RAMANNEH REMAINED PRIMARY BEIRUT CENTERS OF INCIDENTS (SNIPING, BOMBINGS AND SHELLING) DURING EVENING AND MORNING BUT SINN AL FIL REPORTEDLY SUSTAINED CONSIDERABLE MATERIAL DAMAGE. PALESTINIANS ARE SAID TO HAVE OCCUPIED QUARANTINA HOSPITAL DURING AFTERNOON APRIL 14 AND WERE REPORTEDLY ROCKETING PHALANGIST TARGETS IN ASHRAFIYE. THUS FAR SINCE DAWN, THREE LARGE EXPLOSIONS (POSSIBLY ROCKETS) HAVE OCCURRED IN QUARANTINE DISTRICT NEAR PORT, THE FIRST KILLING ONE CIVILIAN AND INJURING THREE. UPI FURTHER REPORTS EIGHT DEAD AND 30 WOUNDED THIS MORNING IN DEKWANEH AND FURN AS SHUBAK. AT ABOUT NOON APRIL 15, ARMY TECHNICIAN REMOVED 4 KILO PACKAGE OF PLASTIQUE WITH TIMER FROM NAPOLEON HOTEL (BLOCK OFF HAMRA).

3. AT LATEST REPORT SECURITY FORCES (POLICE AND GENDARMERIE WITH ARMORED VEHICLES) HAVE MOVED IN STRENGTH IN TROUBLED AREAS BUT THEIR MISSION IS NOT RPT NOT YET CLEAR. ONE REASONABLY RELIABLE REPORT STATED THAT SQUAD 16 MOVED AGAINST PHALANGE OFFICES IN RUE GEORGE PICOT EARLY THIS MORNING. PM SOLH HAS AGAIN REPEATED INTENTION TO APPLY THE LAW AND PUNISH THE CULPABLE BUT REJECTED PROCLAMATION OF STATE OF EMERGENCY AND SAID PSP LEADER KAMAL JUMBLATT, WHO GRACEFULLY CONTINUES TO PLAY KEY ROLE AMONG BOTH GOL LEADERSHIP AND THOSE HIGHLY CRITICAL OF GOL, OPPOSED CALLING OUT ARMY. AS OF EARLY AFTERNOON, MILITARY SOURCES INFORM US THEY ARE PREPARING FOR POSSIBILITY ARMY MIGHT BE CALLED OUT AT APPROX. 1900Z TONIGHT.

4. ALL AMCITS REMAIN SAFE AT MOMENT. CLASHES, HOWEVER, BEGINNING TO AFFECT FOREIGN COMMUNITY. VEHICLE BELONGING TO MEMBER OF EMBASSY STAFF (DEA) WAS DESTROYED AT APPROX. 0200Z WHILE PARKED NEAR HIS RESIDENCE IN RAOUCHE. EXPLOSIVE WAS APPARENTLY SINGLE STICK OF DYNAMITE TOSSED UNDER CAR WHICH BORE WHITE DIPLOMATIC PLATES. FRENCH AMB. WAS AWAKENED LAST EVENING WHEN STRAY BULLET ENTERED HIS BEDROOM; ITALIAN AMB. HAS MOVED INTO TOWN FROM RESIDENCE IN AFFECTED AREA OF CITY. AUB OPEN AND QUIET BUT ATTENDANCE WELL BELOW NORMAL.

5. AIRPORT STILL OPERATING AND ACCESS ROAD OPEN. EMBOFF WHO RETURNED FROM AIRPORT THIS MORNING REPORTS SIGHTING SEVERAL ARMED AND UNIFORMED FEDAYEEN IN AIRPORT CIRCLE BUT THEY MADE NO RPT NO EFFORT TO DISRUPT TRAFFIC. PAN AMERICAN, HOWEVER, REPORTS THAT IT WILL RUN OUT OF JET FUEL AS OF 1100Z TODAY WHICH WILL PROBABLY RESULT IN CANCELLATION OR DIVERSION OF SOME FLIGHTS. REFINERY IN SIDON HAS PLENTY OF JET FUEL AND OTHER PRODUCTS BUT TANK TRUCKS UNABLE TO PASS SIDON. REFINERY IN TRIPOLI ALSO CONTINUES TO OPERATE BUT REPORTS HIGH ABSENTEEISM AND EVIDENCE OF UNKNOWN ELEMENTS PREVENTING WORKERS FROM REACHING PLANT, POSSIBLY TO EMBARRASS PHALANGIST MINISTER OF PETROLEUM. WITH REFINED PRODUCTS FILLING STORAGE CAPACITY, IT IS POSSIBLE BOTH REFINERIES WILL HAVE CLOSED DOWN SOON UNLESS DELIVERIES TO CONSUMERS BECOME POSSIBLE. INDUSTRY SOURCES ESTIMATE LOCAL GAS STATIONS WILL BEGIN TO RUN OUT OF GASOLINE BY WEDNESDAY OR THURSDAY IF RESUPPLY NOT POSSIBLE.

6. IN VIEW OF UNSETTLED CONDITIONS IN LEBANON, EMBASSY HAS INFORMED DEPT. BY SEPTEL THAT TOURISTS SHOULD BE DISCOURAGED FROM COMING AT THIS TIME. EMBASSY CONTINUING TO COUNSEL EMPLOYEES AND AMCITS WHO INQUIRE TO KEEP MOVEMENTS AROUND BEIRUT TO ABSOLUTE MINIMUM. MOST DIPLOMATIC AND OTHER SOCIAL FUNCTIONS ARE BEING CANCELLED.

7. ON POLITICAL SCENE THERE IS CONSIDERABLE ACTIVITY BUT NO CONCRETE RESULTS YET APPARENT. ARAB LEAGUE SYG RIAD ARRIVED BEIRUT LAST EVENING AND BEGAN SERIES OF CONCILIATION MEETINGS, INCLUDING SESSION WITH ARAB AMBS. IN BEIRUT AND ABU IYAD (FATAH) AND NAYIF HAWATMEH (PDFLP). ARAFAT WAS NOT PRESENT AND, TO THE BEST WE CAN DETERMINE, HAS REMAINED ALOOF FROM CONSULTATIONS. LATEST REPORTS PLACE HIM IN DAMASCUS TODAY AFTER HAVING SPENT PART OF YESTERDAY IN SOUTH LEBANON. ACCORDING TO RELIABLE LEBANESE JOURNALIST, RIAD HAS MET WITH SOLH AND FRANJIE AND SAW JUMBLATT AT ST. GEORGE HOTEL THIS MORNING. MEETING BETWEEN RIAD AND GEMAYEL NOT RPT NOT YET SCHEDULED, BUT RIAD EXPECTED TO MAKE APPEARANCE AT MUSLIM/"PROGRESSIVE"/PALESTINIAN RALLY SET FOR 1500Z AT MAKASSED ASSOCIATION IN BEIRUT.

8. PM SOLH HELD SERIES OF SESSIONS DURING YESTERDAY AFTERNOON INCLUDING ONE WITH CABINET WHICH IS RELIABLY REPORTED TO HAVE DEGENERATED INTO SHOUTING MATCH. TWO MINISTERS AFFILIATED WITH KAMAL JUMBLATT'S PSP, ABBAS KHALAF AND KHALED JUMBLATT, HAVE ANNOUNCED THEIR RESIGNATIONS BUT MADE THEM CONTINGENT UPON SOLH'S MEETING THEIR DEMANDS THAT GUILTY (READ PHALANGE) IN SUNDAY'S SHOOT 'EM UP BE BROUGHT TO "JUSTICE" AND GOVT. RESTORE ORDER. SOLH HAS CONTINUED TO TALK ABOUT FOURTEEN PERSONS ARRESTED YESTERDAY BUT THIS HAS BROUGHT HIM LITTLE SURCEASE SINCE NO ONE, ESPECIALLY JUMBLATT, REALLY BELIEVES THEY ARE CULPABLE. AS WE NOTED IN BEIRUT 4749, LOSS OF JUMBLATT'S SUPPORT AND MINISTERS WOULD KNOCK REMAINING PROP FROM UNDER SOLH GOVT., WHICH IS ALREADY STAGGERING.

9. FEDAYEEN SPOKESMEN FOR MAJOR GROUPS, ESPECIALLY FATAH, ARE CLAIMING THEIR FORCES SHOWING REAL RESTRAINT IN FACE OF PHALANGE "PROVOCATIONS." WE UNABLE CONFIRM THIS CLAIM, BUT IT QUITE POSSIBLY TRUE, SINCE HEAD COUNT TO DATE APPEARS TO BE IN FAVOR OF PHALANGE. SPLINTER GROUPS AMONG FEDAYEEN AND PROBABLY UNDISCIPLINED ELEMENTS OF MORE "MODERATE" ORGANIZATIONS, HOWEVER, DO NOT APPEAR TO BE EXERCISING RESTRAINT AND IT IS QUESTIONABLE WHETHER MAJOR PALESTINIAN GROUPS CAN AVOID MORE AGGRESSIVE STANCE INDEFINITELY IF BASIC SITUATION IS NOT CONTAINED SOON. SHOULD PLO/FATAH TAKE DECISION TO GO ALL-OUT, RESIDENTS OF BEIRUT AND OTHER PARTS OF COUNTRY WILL PROBABLY HAVE LITTLE CHOICE BUT TO BATTEN HATCHES AND TRY TO HOLD ON. AS WE HAVE REPORTED OVER LAST SEVERAL YEARS, WE BELIEVE FEDAYEEN ARE WELL SITUATED, PARTICULARLY IN CAPITAL, FOR SUSTAINED URBAN WARFARE AND TERRORISM WHICH WOULD TAKE MAXIMUM TOLL IN LIVES AND PROPERTY.

10. IN ADDITION TO PROLONGATION OF CURRENT CRISIS WITH OUTLINES OF DENOUEMENT STILL NOT RPT NOT IN SIGHT, DISTURBING ELEMENT IS APPARENT SPREAD OF CLASHES GEOGRAPHICALLY AND INDICATIONS THAT STRIFE MAY BE TAKING TURN TOWARD CHRISTIAN VS. MUSLIM/PALESTINIAN CONFLICT. TRIPOLI WITNESSED TWO MAJOR DEMONSTRATIONS APRIL 14 IN WHICH AT LEAST TWO KILLED AND SEVEN WOUNDED AND THREE CHRISTIAN CHURCHES WERE BOMBED LAST EVENING. YESTERDAY'S EVENTS ALSO INCLUDED GRATUITOUS SACK OF CHAMOUN'S NLP HEADQUARTERS IN TRIPOLI. NLP OFFICES NEAR FOREIGN MINISTRY IN BEIRUT WERE OBJECT THIS MORNING OF ATTEMPTED ROCKETING. CHAMOUNIST MILITIA REPORTEDLY KILLED UNKNOWN PERSONS SEEKING TO EMPLACE ROCKET LAUNCHER ATOP NEARBY ROOFTOP.

11. PHALANGIST OFFICES IN ZAHLE AND NEARBY VILLAGE OF SADNAIL WERE BOMBED LAST EVENING AND PHALANGE OFFICE IN SIDON ATTACKED AND LATER ROCKETED FROM REFUGEE CAMPS OUTSIDE SIDON. THREE CHRISTIAN (NOT RPT NOT PHALANGIST) VILLAGES IN MIEH MIEH REGION IN VICINITY OF SIDON WERE ROCKETED FROM CAMPS. ACCORDING ONE USUALLY RELIABLE LEBANESE SOURCE, WHEN VILLAGERS DID NOT RETURN FIRE, PALESTINIANS ADVANCED INTO THEM AND, AT ONE, SEIZED FATHER AND BROTHER OF LEBANESE SECURITY OFFICIAL AND SHOT THEM. JUST AS CONTINUING PALESTINIAN OR MUSLIM CASUALTIES MUST EVENTUALLY INFLAME SENTIMENT OF EVEN MORE MODERATE COMPATRIOTS, SO CHRISTIAN LOSSES WILL TEND TO ENGAGE EMOTIONS OF CHRISTIANS WHO HAVE THUS FAR NOT SUPPORTED PHALANGE.

GODLEY

footnotes: "Confessional coloration": diplomatic language for violence that has begun to divide along religious community lines rather than remaining a dispute between specific armed groups. The cable uses this phrasing cautiously: the violence is showing "first signs" of assuming this character, not that it has fully become sectarian. This distinction matters — the Embassy is documenting a trajectory, not a completed transformation.

By noon on April 15 — less than 48 hours after April 13 — the Embassy estimated 80 to 90 dead throughout Lebanon. This figure, documented in this cable filed before 2:00 PM on April 15, 1975, does not appear in the standard account of the first days of the Lebanese Civil War.

Quarantina Hospital: the American University of Beirut-affiliated hospital in the Quarantine district near the Beirut port. The cable records that it was occupied by Palestinian forces on the afternoon of April 14 and used as a firing position against Ashrafiye, a predominantly Christian neighborhood. The Quarantina district itself — a mixed working-class neighborhood of Lebanese Christians, Kurds, and Armenians — would be overrun by Maronite militias in January 1976, approximately nine months after this cable.

Ashrafiye: predominantly Christian neighborhood in East Beirut. The cable documents that it was being rocketed from Quarantina Hospital — a medical facility under Geneva Convention protection — on April 14–15. This specific detail appears in this Embassy cable and does not figure in the standard account of these events.

Squad 16: an internal security unit of the Lebanese Army. The cable notes it was reportedly deployed against Phalange offices — a detail that, taken with the prior cable (1975BEIRUT04749, para 6B), documents the Lebanese Army taking some limited action against one side. Whether this represents state enforcement or political positioning is recorded as unclear by the Embassy.

The cable documents significant civilian infrastructure failure by noon on April 15 — less than 48 hours after April 13: airport fuel nearly exhausted, refineries blocked, civilian gasoline supply projected to fail by April 17–18. These logistics details appear in this cable and establish the speed at which the April 13 incidents produced country-wide disruption.

Abu Iyad: Salah Khalaf (1933–1991), Fatah’s security chief and Arafat’s designated deputy. This cable documents that on April 15, Riad was meeting with Abu Iyad directly. The subsequent cable (1975BEIRUT04860) records an unconfirmed report that Abu Iyad had been opposing a ceasefire for 36 hours before Arafat returned from Damascus. Read together, these two cables document Abu Iyad as the primary PLO interlocutor in Beirut during the critical April 14–15 period.

Nayif Hawatmeh (b. 1935): founder and leader of the PDFLP (Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine). The cable documents him in direct consultations with Arab League Secretary-General Riad on April 15, while Arafat was in Damascus. This is consistent with the PDFLP’s documented involvement in the April 13 events (cable 1975BEIRUT04749 attributes the initial Volkswagen driver to the PDFLP).

This cable documents that Arafat had "remained aloof from consultations" on April 15 and was in Damascus. This is consistent with and provides context for the subsequent cable (1975BEIRUT04860, paragraph 3), which records an unconfirmed report that Arafat had been in Damascus while Abu Iyad opposed a ceasefire in Beirut. The two cables, read sequentially, document Arafat’s physical absence from Beirut during the critical early-crisis period and provide the context in which the internal PLO command dispute may have occurred.

"Head count to date appears to be in favor of the Phalange": the Embassy’s own assessment on April 15, 1975, was that the casualty balance ran against the Palestinian/Muslim side, not in their favor. The Embassy presents this as partial corroboration of the Fatah restraint claim. This assessment appears in this cable. It has not been cited in the standard account of the Lebanese Civil War’s first days, which typically frames the April 13 bus attack as the initiating act of unprovoked Phalange violence.

This paragraph documents the Embassy’s long-standing assessment — based on "several years" of reporting — that the Palestinian armed forces were well positioned in Beirut for sustained urban warfare and terrorism. This assessment predates April 13, 1975, and contextualizes the structural military reality that made the April 13 incidents so significant: the PLO had the capacity to escalate to full urban warfare, and the Lebanese state did not have the capacity to prevent it.

Tripoli: Lebanon’s second-largest city, located in the north. With a predominantly Sunni Muslim population, Tripoli was a base for pro-Palestinian and leftist forces. The cable documents the spread of violence to Tripoli within 48 hours of April 13, including attacks on specifically Christian targets.

The bombing of three Christian churches in Tripoli on the evening of April 14 is documented in this cable. This event — representing targeted attacks on places of Christian worship within 24 hours of April 13 — appears in this Embassy cable. It does not appear in the standard account of the first days of the Lebanese Civil War.

The rocketing of three Christian villages in the Mieh Mieh region near Sidon — explicitly described as "not Phalangist" — is documented in this cable as occurring on April 14–15. The cable distinguishes these villages from Phalangist targets; they were not party combatants. This event appears in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of these events.

The cable reports, on the basis of one usually reliable source, that when the villagers of one of the Mieh Mieh region villages did not return fire, Palestinian forces advanced into the village and seized and shot a Lebanese security official’s father and brother. The Embassy sources this as a single-source report and presents it with appropriate qualification. The event — if accurate as reported — documents the taking and shooting of civilian family members in a non-combatant village that had declined to return fire. This appears in this cable.

Paragraph 11’s final sentence is one of the cable’s most analytically significant: "Just as continuing Palestinian or Muslim casualties must eventually inflame the sentiment of even more moderate compatriots, so Christian losses will tend to engage the emotions of Christians who have thus far not supported the Phalange." The Embassy is documenting, as of noon April 15, the dynamic by which a militia conflict was becoming a community conflict — and doing so symmetrically, attributing the same dynamic to both sides.

G. McMurtrie Godley (1917–1999), U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon. This is the third major cable filed by Godley in the April 13 crisis, following 1975BEIRUT04749 (April 14) and preceding 1975BEIRUT04860 (April 16). Together, the three cables document the continuous Embassy reporting from the first hours of the civil war through the first attempted ceasefire.

readerNarrative.headline: The Second Day: What Spread Beyond Beirut
readerNarrative.subheadline: This cable, filed April 15, 1975 at noon, documents how the violence of April 13 spread beyond Beirut within 48 hours. Three churches were bombed in Tripoli. Three non-combatant Christian villages near Sidon were rocketed and then entered. A hospital was occupied and used as a firing position. These events appear in this cable. They do not appear in the standard account of April 1975.
readerNarrative.summary: Less than 48 hours after April 13, 1975, the U.S. Embassy filed this two-section situation report as of noon on April 15. The casualty count had reached 80 to 90 throughout Lebanon. The cable documents the geographic spread of violence beyond Beirut: three Christian churches bombed in Tripoli, three non-Phalangist Christian villages near Sidon rocketed from refugee camps and then entered by armed forces. It also documents, on the basis of the Embassy’s own assessment, that the casualty balance at that point ran against the Palestinian and Muslim side — not against the Phalange.
keyRevelations: By noon on April 15 — less than 48 hours after April 13 — this cable records 80 to 90 dead throughout Lebanon. The Health Ministry was issuing appeals for blood donors and doctors. This figure is documented in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of these events.

This cable documents that three Christian churches were bombed in Tripoli on the evening of April 14, 1975. This event appears in paragraph 10 of this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of the first days of the Lebanese Civil War.

Three Christian villages in the Mieh Mieh region near Sidon — explicitly described as not Phalangist — were rocketed from Palestinian camps. When villagers did not return fire, the cable records that armed forces advanced into the villages and shot civilian family members of a Lebanese security official. This event appears in paragraph 11 of this cable. It does not appear in the standard account.

The Embassy’s own assessment at noon on April 15: “The head count to date appears to be in favor of the Phalange.” The Embassy presented this as partial corroboration of Fatah’s claim of restraint. This assessment is documented in this cable. It has not been cited in the standard account.

Arafat had remained aloof from all consultations by noon on April 15. He was in Damascus. Arab League Secretary-General Riad was meeting with Abu Iyad and Nayif Hawatmeh — but not Arafat. This absence, documented here, is consistent with the internal PLO command dispute described in the subsequent cable (1975BEIRUT04860).

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Forty-eight hours in

By noon on April 15, 1975 — less than 48 hours after April 13 — the U.S. Embassy estimated 80 to 90 people dead throughout Lebanon. The Health Ministry was calling for blood donors and ordering medical staff to report immediately. The major portion of the capital’s population, the cable records, remained hunkered down in their homes.

This cable, filed at the IMMEDIATE level in two sections, is the Embassy’s most detailed situational account of the crisis’s first 48 hours. It documents events in Beirut, in Tripoli, and in villages near Sidon. What happened outside Beirut does not appear in the standard account of these events.

What the cable documents outside Beirut

In Tripoli, Lebanon’s second city, two major demonstrations occurred on April 14. At least two people were killed and seven wounded. Three Christian churches were bombed that evening. The headquarters of the National Liberal Party — Camille Chamoun’s organization — was sacked.

Near Sidon, three villages in the Mieh Mieh region — the cable specifies they were Christian, and explicitly not Phalangist — were rocketed from nearby refugee camps. According to what the cable describes as a usually reliable Lebanese source, when the villagers did not return fire, armed forces advanced into the villages. At one village, the father and brother of a Lebanese security official were seized and shot.

The Embassy presents this as a single-source account and offers no characterization beyond the documentary record. The event appears in paragraph 11 of this cable, filed before 2:00 PM on April 15, 1975, on record at the State Department. It does not appear in the standard account of these days.

The Embassy’s own casualty assessment

Paragraph 9 of this cable contains a specific assessment: Fatah is claiming its forces are showing real restraint in the face of Phalange “provocations.” The Embassy states: “We are unable to confirm this claim, but it is quite possibly true, since the head count to date appears to be in favor of the Phalange.”

This is the U.S. Embassy’s own assessment, on the record, at noon on April 15. The casualty balance, in the Embassy’s judgment, ran against the Palestinian and Muslim side, not against the Kataeb. This appears in this cable. It has not been cited in the standard account of the Lebanese Civil War’s first days.

Arafat’s absence

Paragraph 7 records that Arab League Secretary-General Riad was meeting directly with Abu Iyad (Fatah’s security chief) and Nayif Hawatmeh (PDFLP leader) on April 15. Arafat “was not present” and had “remained aloof from consultations.” Latest reports placed him in Damascus.

Read alongside the subsequent cable (1975BEIRUT04860), which records an unconfirmed report that Arafat had been favoring a ceasefire for 36 hours while Abu Iyad opposed it, these two cables together document that Abu Iyad was the effective PLO decision-maker in Beirut during the critical period of April 14–15 — with Arafat geographically and apparently politically absent from the negotiations.

The Embassy’s forward-looking warning

The cable closes paragraph 9 with a direct assessment of what would happen if the PLO chose to escalate: residents of Beirut and other parts of the country “will probably have little choice but to batten hatches and try to hold on.” The Embassy notes it had been reporting for “several years” that Palestinian armed forces were positioned in the capital for “sustained urban warfare and terrorism.”

This assessment, documented before the civil war had fully begun, is what the Embassy understood the stakes to be on April 15, 1975. What it was warning about would not materialize — that escalation — for another year.

cables.subject: Beirut Situation Report — 1000Z
cables.excerpt: A situation report filed April 16, 1975, documenting the ceasefire negotiations that followed April 13. The cable records that the Kataeb delivered two suspects as agreed; the PLO then stated seven were sought. It also contains an unconfirmed report of an internal PLO command dispute — Arafat reportedly favoring a ceasefire for 36 hours while his deputy Abu Iyad opposed it.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 05 July 2006 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Fighting continues in troubled areas around Beirut as efforts are underway to implement effectively a ceasefire reportedly arranged for 1000Z [10:00 AM GMT, or midnight local time April 15/16].[1] We anticipate that even if eventually effective, complete end to fighting will take some hours.

1.
Apparent progress during the afternoon and night of April 15 toward implementing a ceasefire between Palestinians and Phalangists provides the first real basis for hope that the deteriorating situation in Beirut and the remainder of the country may be brought under control. Arab League Secretary-General Mahmud Riad[2] is credited by many local papers appearing the morning of April 16 with success in working out a modus vivendi between the contending elements, but it appears he had assistance from local figures, including President Frangieh[3] (still convalescing in the American University Hospital), Henri Pharaon,[4] and, possibly, Shia leader Imam Musa Sadr[5] (reports conflicting). Riad, who met with Palestinians and Lebanese “Progressive”[6] parties — but not with Phalangist leader Pierre Gemayel, with whom President Frangieh apparently handled contacts — will probably leave Beirut today around midday.

2.
The major development paving the way for efforts to bridge the gap between the combatants was the decision by Phalange leader Gemayel to accede to President Frangieh’s request that he turn over to GOL authorities two Phalangists implicated in Sunday’s incidents in Ain al-Rammaneh.[7] According to our information, the two suspects were delivered to GOL security officers at 2130Z on April 15. Prime Minister Solh officially announced the arrests at 2315Z.

A possible complication was the subsequent PLO statement that seven — not two — Phalangists were sought,[8] although WAFA[9] in an early morning release reportedly continued the line that the GOL continues to employ its good offices to contain the crisis. Somewhat more serious, in terms of efforts to enforce any ceasefire, was a reportedly Palestinian “rejection front”[10] assertion that its forces would not accept reconciliation with the Phalange.

3.
A reliable U.S. correspondent has informed us that Arafat, who has allegedly arrived in Beirut, estimated that twenty-four hours will be required for the ceasefire to be effective. Although the situation on the Palestinian side remains unclear, we also have an unconfirmed report that Arafat has been favoring a ceasefire for the last thirty-six hours but has been opposed by Fatah notable Abu Iyad,[11] whom Arafat left in charge of operations in Beirut when he returned to Damascus on April 14. If true, this internal conflict could account for both the delay in implementing the ceasefire and Arafat’s decision to resume charge locally.[12]

4.
Details of the reported ceasefire plan remain fragmentary. We originally heard the truce was to occur at 1200Z April 15 but it obviously did not hold. We are now informed by several sources that it went into effect as of 1000Z April 15 (midnight April 15/16 locally) and that efforts are now underway to get word to isolated units on both sides. The main sticking point will be the ability of “moderate” leadership on both sides — Phalange and Palestinian — to enforce their policy on elements that may not wish to see a peaceful resolution of the crisis. We have several reports of lower-level Phalangists who doubt the possibility of settlement and are prepared to fight on. Likewise, there are grounds for questioning the ability and/or willingness of the Palestinians to control completely the “rejectionists,” who probably include among their allies a number of local Muslim and leftist elements.

5.
Firing and explosions persisted throughout the night and into this morning, affecting areas that have been the scene of the fiercest fighting since Sunday. Roving bands also entered the center of town and Ras Beirut to plant explosive charges (mainly plastique) in Abdel Aziz Street and at a building housing former President Chamoun’s offices on Verdun Street. We would place the total dead to date throughout Lebanon at between 100 and 120.[13]

6.
During April 15, some efforts were made in various parts of the country to keep the strife from adopting a confessional [sectarian] character. The Maronite League, Higher Islamic Council, and National Organization (Muslim) met and reportedly agreed that a “misunderstanding between militias” must not be allowed to engage Muslim and Christian communities. A local “appeasement committee” was allegedly formed in Sidon under the leadership of Deputy Bizri[14] to keep lines of communication and reconciliation open between Muslims and Christians.

7.
The Solh Cabinet has appeared thus far to have played little direct role in events or efforts to arrange the ceasefire, and the Prime Minister is becoming increasingly isolated even among his own ministerial colleagues.[15] Some parliamentary deputies, including a number in the cabinet, attempted to hold a parliamentary session at 0800Z this morning, but were unable to obtain a quorum.

8.
Beirut airport is operating this morning at about 80 percent of normal, with one-third of its staff unable to reach the area. The airport has no fuel, but planes are refueling before or after Beirut and consequently flights are so far unaffected. AUB Hospital presently has food for eight days of operation.[16]

9.
All American citizens [AMCITS] are safe. The USIS Regional Service Center in Sinn al Fil and the Kennedy Center are closed, as are most businesses throughout town.

GODLEY[17]

C O N F I D E N T I A L BEIRUT 4860

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS, LE, PLO
SUBJECT: BEIRUT SITREP - 1000Z
REFS: A. BEIRUT 4845; B. BEIRUT 4844

SUMMARY: FIGHTING CONTINUES IN TROUBLE AREAS AROUND BEIRUT AS EFFORTS ARE UNDER WAY TO IMPLEMENT EFFECTIVELY CEASEFIRE WHICH WAS REPORTEDLY ARRANGED FOR 1000Z APR 15. WE ANTICIPATE THAT, EVEN IF EVENTUALLY EFFECTIVE, COMPLETE END TO FIGHTING WILL TAKE SOME HOURS. END SUMMARY.

1. APPARENT PROGRESS DURING AFTERNOON AND NIGHT APR 15 TOWARD IMPLEMENTING CEASEFIRE BETWEEN PALESTINIANS AND PHALANGISTS PROVIDES FIRST REAL BASIS FOR HOPE THAT DETERIORATING SITUATION IN BEIRUT AND REMAINDER OF COUNTRY MAY BE BROUGHT UNDER CONTROL. ARAB LEAGUE SYG MAHMUD RIAD IS CREDITED BY MANY LOCAL PAPERS APPEARING MORNING APR 16 WITH SUCCESS IN WORKING OUT MODUS VIVENDI BETWEEN CONTENDING ELEMENTS BUT IT APPEARS HE HAD ASSISTANCE OF LOCAL FIGURES, INCLUDING PRES FRANJIE (STILL CONVALESCING IN AUB HOSPITAL), HENRI PHARAON, AND, POSSIBLY, SHIITE LEADER IMAM MUSA SADR (REPORTS CONFLICTING). RIAD, WHO MET WITH PALESTINIANS AND LEBANESE "PROGRESSIVE" PARTIES (BUT NOT RPT NOT PHALANGIST LEADER, PIERRE GEMAYEL, WITH WHOM PRES FRANJIE APPARENTLY HANDLED CONTACTS), WILL PROBABLY LEAVE BEIRUT TODAY AT ABOUT MID-DAY.

2. MAJOR DEVELOPMENT PAVING WAY FOR EFFORTS TO BRIDGE GAP BETWEEN COMBATTANTS WAS DECISION BY PHALANGE LEADER GEMAYEL TO ACCEDE TO PRES FRANJIE'S REQUEST THAT HE TURN OVER TO GOL AUTHORITIES TWO PHALANGISTS IMPLICATED IN SUNDAY'S INCIDENTS IN AIN AL RAMMANEH. ACCORDING TO OUR INFORMATION, TWO SUSPECTS WERE DELIVERED TO GOL SECURITY OFFICERS AT 2130Z ON APR 15. PM SOLH OFFICIALLY ANNOUNCED ARRESTS AT 2315Z. POSSIBLE MINOR SNAG WAS SUBSEQUENT PLO STATEMENT THAT SEVEN RPT SEVEN PHALANGISTS WERE SOUGHT, ALTHOUGH WAFA IN EARLY MORNING RELEASE REPORTEDLY CONTINUED LINE THAT GOL CONTINUES EMPLOY ITS GOOD OFFICES TO CONTAIN CRISIS. SOMEWHAT MORE SERIOUS, IN TERMS OF EFFORTS TO ENFORCE ANY CEASEFIRE, WAS REPORTEDLY PALESTINIAN "REJECTION" FRONT ASSERTION THAT ITS FORCES WOULD NOT RPT NOT ACCEPT RECONCILIATION WITH PHALANGE.

3. RELIABLE US CORRESPONDENT HAS INFORMED US THAT ARAFAT, WHO HAS ALLEGEDLY ARRIVED IN BEIRUT, ESTIMATED THAT TWENTY-FOUR HOURS WILL BE REQUIRED FOR CEASEFIRE TO BE EFFECTIVE. ALTHOUGH SITUATION ON PALESTINIAN SIDE UNCLEAR AT THIS TIME, WE ALSO HAVE UNCONFIRMED REPORT THAT ARAFAT HAS BEEN FAVORING CEASEFIRE FOR LAST THIRTY-SIX HOURS, BUT HAS BEEN OPPOSED BY FATAH-NOTABLE ABU IYAD, WHOM ARAFAT LEFT IN CHARGE OF OPERATIONS IN BEIRUT WHEN HE RETURNED APR 14 TO DAMASCUS. IF TRUE, THIS INTERNAL CONFLICT COULD ACCOUNT FOR BOTH DELAY IN IMPLEMENTING CEASEFIRE AND ARAFAT'S DECISION TO RESUME CHARGE LOCALLY.

4. DETAILS OF REPORTED CEASEFIRE PLAN REMAIN FRAGMENTARY. WE ORIGINALLY HEARD TRUCE WAS TO OCCUR AT 1200Z APR 15 BUT IT OBVIOUSLY DID NOT HOLD. WE ARE NOW INFORMED BY SEVERAL SOURCES THAT IT WENT INTO EFFECT AS OF 1000Z APR 15 (MIDNIGHT APR 15/16 LOCALLY) AND THAT EFFORTS NOW UNDER WAY TO GET WORD TO ISOLATED UNITS ON BOTH SIDES. MAIN STICKING POINT WILL BE ABILITY OF "MODERATE" LEADERSHIP OF BOTH PHALANGE AND PALESTINIANS TO ENFORCE THEIR POLICY ON ELEMENTS WHO MAY NOT WISH TO SEE PEACEFUL RESOLUTION OF CRISIS. WE HAVE SEVERAL REPORTS OF LOWER LEVEL PHALANGISTS WHO DOUBT POSSIBILITY OF SETTLEMENT AND PREPARED TO FIGHT ON. LIKEWISE, THERE ARE GROUNDS FOR QUESTIONING ABILITY AND/OR WILLINGNESS OF PALESTINIANS TO CONTROL COMPLETELY "REJECTIONISTS", WHO PROBABLY INCLUDE AMONG THEIR ALLIES NUMBER OF LOCAL MUSLIM AND LEFTIST ELEMENTS.

5. FIRING AND EXPLOSIONS PERSISTED THROUGHOUT THE NIGHT AND INTO THIS MORNING AFFECTING AREAS WHICH HAVE BEEN SCENE OF FIERCEST FIGHTING SINCE SUNDAY. ROVING BANDS ALSO ENTERED CENTER OF TOWN AND RAS BEIRUT TO PLANT EXPLOSIVE CHARGES (MAINLY PLASTIQUE) IN ABDEL AZIZ STREET AND AT BUILDING HOUSING FORMER PRES CAMILLE CHAMOUN'S OFFICES IN VERDUN STREET. WE WOULD PLACE TOTAL DEAD TO DATE THROUGHOUT LEBANON AT BETWEEN 100 AND 120.

6. DURING APR 15, SOME EFFORTS WERE MADE IN VARIOUS PARTS OF COUNTRY TO KEEP STRIFE FROM ADOPTING CONFESSIONAL CHARACTER. MARONITE LEAGUE, HIGHER ISLAMIC COUNCIL AND NATIONAL ORG (MUSLIM) MET AND REPORTEDLY AGREED THAT "MISUNDERSTANDING BETWEEN MILITIAS" MUST NOT RPT NOT BE ALLOWED TO ENGAGE MUSLIM AND CHRISTIAN COMMUNITIES. LOCAL "APPEASEMENT COMMITTEE" ALLEGEDLY FORMED IN SIDON UNDER LEADERSHIP OF DEPUTY BIZRI TO KEEP LINES OF COMMUNICATION AND RECONCILIATION OPEN BETWEEN MUSLIMS AND CHRISTIANS.

7. SOLH CABINET HAS APPEARED THUS FAR TO HAVE PLAYED LITTLE DIRECT ROLE IN EVENTS OR EFFORTS TO ARRANGE CEASEFIRE AND PM IS BECOMING INCREASINGLY ISOLATED EVEN AMONG HIS OWN MINISTERIAL COLLEAGUES. SOME PARLIAMENTARY DEPUTIES, INCLUDING NUMBER IN CABINET, ATTEMPTED HOLD PARLIAMENTARY SESSION AT 0800Z THIS MORNING, BUT WERE UNABLE TO OBTAIN QUORUM.

8. BEIRUT AIRPORT IS OPERATING THIS MORNING AT ABOUT 80 PERCENT NORMAL WITH ONE-THIRD ITS STAFF UNABLE TO REACH AREA. AIRPORT HAS NO FUEL BUT PLANES ARE REFUELING BEFORE OR AFTER BEIRUT AND CONSEQUENTLY FLIGHTS SO FAR UNAFFECTED. AUB HOSPITAL PRESENTLY HAS FOOD FOR EIGHT DAYS OPERATION.

9. ALL AMCITS ARE SAFE. USIS REGIONAL SERVICE CENTER IN SINN AL FIL AND KENNEDY CENTER ARE CLOSED AS ARE MOST BUSINESSES THROUGHOUT TOWN.

GODLEY

CONFIDENTIAL NNN
footnotes: SITREP: Situation Report. A standardized diplomatic and military cable format providing a current assessment of conditions at a specific time. SITREP cables are filed at intervals during active crises to provide continuous situational awareness to Washington. The time designation "1000Z" refers to 10:00 AM Greenwich Mean Time, which was midnight local Beirut time on April 15/16, 1975.

Mahmoud Riad (1917–1992): Egyptian diplomat who served as Secretary-General of the Arab League from 1972 to 1979. Riad’s direct involvement in the Beirut negotiations within 72 hours of the April 13 incidents reflects the Arab League’s immediate recognition of the crisis’s regional implications. His presence also indicates that Egypt—then the dominant force in Arab League affairs under Sadat’s government—considered rapid containment a priority.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992), still hospitalized following gall bladder surgery on April 12—the day before the April 13 incidents. The cable notes he was handling contacts with Gemayel personally while convalescing, suggesting his political involvement did not require his physical presence in the executive offices.

Henri Pharaon (1902–1993): Lebanese politician, businessman, and diplomat who served as Lebanon’s Foreign Minister 1944–1945 and as a long-standing figure in Lebanese elite politics and inter-communal mediation. His involvement reflects the traditional Lebanese mechanism of managing political crises through established community notables with cross-sectarian relationships.

Imam Musa Sadr (1928–disappeared 1978): Iranian-born Lebanese Shia cleric who founded the Amal movement and gave the Lebanese Shia community unprecedented political visibility in the 1970s. Sadr was known as a cross-sectarian broker in Lebanese politics and had relationships across communal lines. His reported—though conflicted—involvement in the ceasefire mediation reflects his standing. Sadr disappeared during a visit to Libya in August 1978 under circumstances that remain unresolved.

The cable’s use of quotation marks around “Progressive” mirrors standard Embassy practice when reproducing a political self-designation without endorsing it. The Lebanese National Movement (LNM)—the coalition of leftist, pan-Arab, and Nasserist parties allied with the PLO—used “progressive” as its preferred self-description. Riad’s meeting structure—with Palestinians and LNM parties but not with Gemayel directly—reflects the political asymmetry of the negotiations: one side was at the table; the other communicated through President Frangieh.

The delivery of two suspects by the Kataeb to Lebanese government authorities represents a significant compliance with a state request. Gemayel’s decision to accede to Frangieh’s request—handing over Phalangists implicated in the April 13 bus attack—is documented in this cable at paragraph 2. The subsequent PLO demand for seven suspects is documented in the same paragraph. This documentary gap—between what was delivered and what was subsequently demanded—appears in this cable. It is not prominent in the standard historical account of the April 15–16 ceasefire negotiations.

The PLO’s public statement that seven Phalangists were sought—after two had been delivered—is recorded in this cable without characterization. The cable does not attribute motive; it records the statement and its timing relative to the deliveries.

WAFA: Wikalat Anba’a Filastiniyya (Palestine News Agency), the PLO’s official wire service, established in 1972. The cable references a WAFA release describing the Lebanese government as “employing its good offices”—official PLO public communication framing the Lebanese state’s role in containment-oriented terms, distinct from the simultaneous private demand for additional suspects.

The “rejection front” referenced in this cable denotes Palestinian factions that rejected negotiated accommodation with the Kataeb under any terms. The cable identifies this as “somewhat more serious” than the seven-suspect demand in terms of ceasefire enforcement. The existence of elements within the Palestinian political constellation in Beirut that opposed any accommodation with the Kataeb—documented here in April 1975—would become more consequential as the conflict deepened.

Abu Iyad: nom de guerre of Salah Khalaf (1933–1991), founding member of Fatah and head of its intelligence and security apparatus. The cable records—as unconfirmed—that Abu Iyad had opposed a ceasefire for 36 hours while serving as Arafat’s designated deputy in Beirut, and that this opposition may account for the delay in implementation. Abu Iyad was assassinated in Tunis in January 1991 by a gunman linked to the Abu Nidal Organization.

This paragraph contains information that this cable characterizes as “unconfirmed”: that Arafat had favored a ceasefire for 36 hours before returning to Beirut, but was opposed during that period by Abu Iyad. The Embassy presents this as one possible explanation for the ceasefire delay. If accurate, it documents an internal command dispute within PLO leadership in Beirut—with Arafat on one side and his security chief on the other—during the critical 36-hour window when the ceasefire failed to materialize. This report appears in this cable. It does not appear in the standard historical account of the April 15–16 ceasefire negotiations.

By the morning of April 16—three days after April 13—the U.S. Embassy estimated 100 to 120 dead throughout Lebanon. This figure contextualizes the speed of escalation from the initial incidents of April 13 to a country-wide armed conflict requiring Arab League mediation within 72 hours.

Deputy Bizri: likely a reference to a member of the Lebanese parliament from the Sidon area. The formation of a local “appeasement committee” in Sidon—documented here—represents civil society and political efforts from within Lebanon, across communal lines, to prevent the Beirut violence from triggering sectarian conflict in other cities.

The cable’s assessment that Prime Minister Rashid Solh is “becoming increasingly isolated even among his own ministerial colleagues” and that the cabinet has played “little direct role” in ceasefire efforts documents the functional collapse of Lebanese government authority in the crisis’s first 72 hours. The state’s role was mediated by community notables and the Arab League rather than by its own executive institutions.

The Embassy’s specific notation that AUB (American University of Beirut) Hospital had food stocks for eight days indicates it was tracking civilian institutional capacity as a crisis indicator—the kind of granular situational data that SITREP cables provide.

G. McMurtrie Godley (1917–1999), U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1974–1976. This is the second major cable filed by Godley in the April 13 crisis, following 1975BEIRUT04749 (filed April 14). Both were dispatched at the IMMEDIATE level, indicating continuous high-priority reporting throughout the crisis. The consistency of Godley’s assessment—cautiously optimistic about the ceasefire while noting its fragility—is characteristic of his reporting style throughout this period.
